TRE MUSIC ON THE WIND. Last night my heart was filled with woe:— My thought, were all of thee, Yet wayward Memory would not show Thy beauteous form to me: I strove in vain to call again Thy image to my mind. When lo ! a strain of music sweet Came wafted on the wind. The memories of our early days Came back—a glorious throng; • I Flaw once more upon thy face The love too deep for song: • I saw within thy eyes the light

That shone frit me alone ;- I lived again that radiant day Which made thee all my own. The g•alden years together spent In one unclouded home, That music to my fancy lent Beneath the starry dome. And when'at last the gladsome strain . .

- Ceased ringing in my ears. I turned and wandered on again, With eyes o'erbrimmed with tears. My heart was beating wild and fast; My soul was strangely stirred; Yet as I walked I thankful grew For all that I had heard. For if earth's music holds the power To bring thy face in view. And give me back in one short hour. The years of joy we knew,— I feel—l know—that when my feet Rest—all these wanderings o'er, A strain of heavenly music sweet Will wed our souls once more!

Doing nothing is doing ill. They rest best who work best. Branch establishment—A tree. With might and mane—The lion. The pink of propriety—The maiden's blush. Cut and dried—The man who was" withered by a glance." The fashionable woman in the forties is not generally ambitious to discover a new wrinkle. It is not what life has to bring to a man but what be is able to carry into it that will determine his happiness. Dignity is a good thing; but if you're in the rear of a big crowd and wish to see the procession, don't stand on it. Get on a barreL Who are the best men to send to war? Lawyers, because their charges are so great no one can stand them. Green: "You can't do anything without money, my boy!" Brown: "Oh, yes, you can." Greene "I'd like to know what." Brown: "Get in debt." First German student (fiercely) : "I challenge you to a duel, sir. Choose your weapons." Second student (after a moment's reflection) : Boxing glovss at one hundred yards." Fond mamma: "Why don't you take your dollie with you to the tea party?" Little Dot: I don't fink dollie would like folks to know zat she hasn't anyzing but 'summer clothes." Sneering is the infallible sign of innate vulgarity of spirit, and of a mean and base disposition, that waits only the opportunity to do that which will render it despicable as well. Magistrate (to woman charged with drunkenness) : "You must pay a fine of I five shillings." Prisoner: "Sure, then, I've but two shillings in the world." Magistrate: "Then you must go to prison. If you hadn't got drunk with your money you'd have had enough to pay the fine." COMMENCEMENT OF THE VANDERBILT FORTUNE.—An old New Yorker tells how the great Vanderbilt fortune began. In the early thirties Commodore Vanderbilt, the founder of the family, was running a small boat convey- ing passengers and freight from Staten Island to New York. A steamer plying between New York and Amboy on the Philadelphia route attempted to leave the dock at Whitehall when there was a strong tide against her. After making three unsuccessful attempts and return- ing to the dock, 'Vanderbilt, who was observing their operations, denounced the seamen as "a pack of fools." Gibbons, the owner ,of the steamer, said to him," My man, can you take her out?" "Yes," replied Vanderbilt. ."Come on board and-try then," said Gibbohs. Vander- bilt did so, and instead of trying to round the Battery against the strong tide he took the stream through ,the Buttermilk Channel around Governor's Island—a channel. little known then • except to the Whitehall 'boatmen. Gibbons made Vanderbilt captain and pilot of the boat soon after, and on-his death left him 825,000. The Com- modore's wife and family moved to New Brunswick and opened a restaurant and liquor saloon, and having the steamer's patronage, here commenced the great fortune of the house that Vanderbilt. -- THE VALUE or ACCENT.—At a trial in the Court of King's Bench as to an alleged piracy of the "Old Eng- lish Gentleman," oneief,the first witnesses put into the box was Cooke, the composer. "Now, sir"—said Sir James Scarlett in his cross-examination of Cooke, "you say that the -two melodies are identical but different What am Ito understand by that, sir?" "What I said," replied Cooke,-" was that the notes in the two, arrangements are the same but with a different accent .the one being in.common while the other is in triple . time; consequently the position of the accented notes is, different in the two copies.' "What is musical accent?" - Sir James flippantly inquired. "My terms for teaching music are a guinea a lesson,"&aid Cooke, much to the merriment of the court. •",Itio not want to know your terms for teaching," said the counsel; "I want you to explain to his lordship and the jury what is musical accent." Sir James waxed -wroth. "Can you see it?" he continued. " No." was the answer. "Can you feel it?" 'Well"—Cooke drawled out, "a musician can." After an appeal to the judge the examining counsel again put the question. "Will you explain to his lord- i ship and the jury—who are supposed to know nothing about music—the meaning of -what you call accent." "Musical accent," rejoined Cooke, "ha emphasis laid on certain note just in the game manner as you would lay stress on any word when speaking, in order to make yourself better understood. I will give you an illustra- tion, Sir James. If I were to say • you are a donkey,' the accent rests on donkey; but if instead I said 'you Me a donkey,' it rests en you, Sir James; and I have no doubt that the gentlemen of .the jury will corroborate me in this." The story is more personal than polite— nevertheless it is well worth telling as an instance of forcible illustration. It is useful, too, since it may serve to impress upon the minds of that very large circle of people who plume themselves on being musical, some faint notion of what accent in music really is. It is the outcome of that wonderful invention—the division of music into bars, but for which music might still be only the magical accomplishment of a few. Gentleman's Magasine. A HEROINE OF THE PRE-EMANCIPATION MM.—The American papers record amongst other victims of the influenza epidemic the name of Mrs. -Mlle° better known by her maiden name of Prudence Crandall. Miss Crandall belonged to what Mies Martineau-truly called the "martyr age" of the United Statesawhen the friends af human freedom had to work with the prospect of the gaol and Judge Lynch before their eyes. In 1832, Prudence Crandall, a young, gentle, and educated Quaker woman, opeoed a boarding And day school for girls at Canterbury, in the State of Connecticut. This academy was for the higher instruction of pupils who had passed through the classes of the common schools. A negro girl applied for admission. She was the daughter of a free black in comfortable circumstances; she was bright, intelligent, and a member of a Christian church. Miss Crandall decided to adsait her, and the other pupils made no objection whatever. But if they were "young and foolish," there were older heads to prevent such an unheard-of scandal. The Quaker schoolmistress was speedily informed by indignant parents that "they would not have it said that their daughters went to school with a nigger girl," and that Sarah Harris must therefore be expelled. Prudence Crandall was made of go New England stuff, and ref u-aiel to yield. The white children were withdrawn, and she then advertised in Garrison's Liberator that her school would be opeli to "young ladies and little misses of colour." The Canterbury people were still more in- dignant, ard a town's meeting was called to avert orabate the " nuisance" of a school where coloured children were to be educated. The resolutions adopted were couched in this spirit, and Mr. A. T. Judson, afterwards a judge of the United States District Court, waited upon ' Miss Crandall to represent to her the fixed determina- tion of the people that no such school should be per- mitted either in the town of Canterbury or in any pail of the State of Connecticut. When the coloured pupils came to Miss Crandall's they were subjected to mean and almost nameless persecutions, and, other means failing, the Legislature passed the retrospective "Black Law" of 1833 for the suppression of the school. The bells of Canterbury were set ringing for joy when it was known that this infamous law had been added to the statute book. Miss Crandall was arrested, and, refusing to give bonds for good behaviour, was actually sent to prison and placed for one night in the cell that had been previously occupied by a murderer. The disgrace thus inflicted ,upon the State of Connecticut was deep, and the effect was very different to what the promoters of the law had .expected. When Miss Crandall was tried for the "crime" of educating negro girls, the first jury disagreed, but the second convicted her. An appeal was made to the highest court of the State, and the whole proceedings were finally- quashed on technical grounds. After an attempt had been made to burn down the schoolhouse, Prudence Crandall left Canterbury, but re- 1 mained to the end of her long and useful life the friend of the negro. She lived to see the race emancipated and to witness strenuous and liberal efforts for the education of the coloured children—the "crime" for which she was imprisoned in a murderer's cell. Mr. Bradlaugh was in the House at the time when a division was called on Tuesday afternbon, on the subject of Ash Wednesday, but did not vote. Strange as it may appear, it is a fact that the hon. member abstains from voting on all purely religious questions.. _ _ _ _

A special messenger took a phonograph from Lon- don to Egypt and paid Mr. Stanley a . good round sum for talking into the instrument for an hour. Stanley gave the little machine a humorous lecture apologising for not confiding to it the details of his recent explorations. Dr. O. W. Holmes has been making merry over Socialist ideals in the• 'Atlantic Monthly," and points his moral through a dream about the planet Saturn, where they have no paupers, no thieves, and no money. To the question, "What are their amusements ?" the answer is "Intoxication and suicide are the chief recreations."

A handsome sum of pin money appears to have been given to Mdlle. Rattazzi, who was married the • other day to a Spanish grandee, Luis Villanova, the husband having presented to his charming wife the annual income from his famous tobacco plantation in Havana, supplying the cigars smoked by several European sovereigns, valued at £70,000 a year. Towards the close of March, the precise date not yet being determined, the Queen will leave for Aix- les-Bains. Her Majesty will occupy Mottet which since her Majesty resided there three years ago, has been re-christened the Villa Victoria, and is the dependance of the Hotel de l' Europe, and will probably return to England about the end of April. Hansard is in future to record the hour at which each member rises and sits down. This is an inno- vation which should inspire some alarm in the mind of Sir George Campbell and other gentlemen who very frequently claim the ear of the house. It will now be possible totell at the end of the session the exact amount of time consumed by each indivi- dual member, and it is haped that this circumstance will tend to check, the loquacity of certain hon. gentlemen. It has long been believed that married couples who are not only exposed to the same conditions of life, but the influence of whose minds must neces- sarily-react upon each other, assume a more or less strong facial resemblance. The Photographic Society of Geneva, Switzerland, with a view to determining this question,has made photographs of seventy-eight couples. The result is that in twenty-four cases the resemblance in the personal appearance of the husband and wife was greater than that of brother and sister ; in thirty cases it was equally great ; and in only twenty-four was there a total absence of resemblance.

."`I heard." writes a correspondent." a curious and characteristic story of Disraeli the other day. Once Lord 'Derby—then :Prime Minister—found fault with something Disraeli had done. Disraeli at the :time was Chancellor of the :Exchequer for thefirst time; and he was peremptorily summoned to St. James's-square. At once Lord Derby—who had a sharp •tongueand a fierce temper when he gave way trait—poured on Disraeli a lava-tide of re- proach. Disraeli sat absolutely silent, until Lord Derby, in final exasperation, said, have you nothing to say ?" Disraeli got up and left the house,never saying one word. "It was this mar- vellousself-control;" comments our correspondent, ." that probably.aecounts for his strange success." "Truth " saya :---To put it briefly, the Commis- sioners have found that all In " Parnellism and Crime "that wa.s new was not true,and that all that was true was not new. Everyone was aware that ?fir. Devitt had been a Fenian ; that some of the Parnellites had in former years been members 4, a Separatist Association; that there had been '1503,- u:tang; and that most of the Parnellites had joined an association to promote an wrarian agitation against the ,payment of excessive rents. Everyone knew, too, thatthe National League had received, moneys from albwho liked to. subscribe them, with- out asking for a certificate of character. All this was proved before the Commissioners ; not by the " Times' " witnesses, but by the admissions of the defendants. A Rembrandt has come to light in Paris in the most unexpected manner, and, as usual, a dealer who knew what he was looking at has • the credit and profit. Among the goods and chattels of an aged lady, who died at Pecq, was a musty-looking painting, on which the auctioneers put a .reserve price of 200 franca. When•the picture was under the hammer, however, the bidaeame freely until the price of 4,500 francs was -reached. This -showed that several persons had begun to think well of the neglected work. The dealer who bought it was within a few hours offered 15,000 francs for his treasure, which bears -Rembrandt's signature, with the date 1656, but he has hopes of obtaining a quar- ter of a million. How very much chagrined ,the heirs must be that they have allowed -a fortune to slip through their 'fingers. All flesh is indeed as grass and fish this Lent for the Roman Catholics of England; unless, indeed, the three stern prelates who have refused to take the Pope's paternal hint continue in their contumacy. Ten bishops have already published to their flocks the dispensation •; and among these, as might be ex- pected, is Cardinal Manning, though there are com- plaints of a certain fishy ambiguity in the phrases used by his Eminence in proclaiming the philan- thropic message of meat. It happened in 1866, and the first Lent of his arch-bishopric. that there was cholera in London, and that the cardinal issued a somewhat similar dispensation, which, when it was read in church, called forth from an aged Irish- woman the exclamations " This is what comes of having a Protestant Archbishop I " There was a terrible fuse at Constantinople, in consequence of a German photographer having rashly attempted to take an instantaneous photo- graph of the Sultan, as his Majesty was proceeding on horseback to the Mosque. Ile was detected by a functionary, and the guard at once rushed on him, smashed all his instruments to atoms' and dragged him off to prison, where he discovered that he was in a truly serious plight, for the Koran strictly for- bids the depicting of the human form, and his attempt to photograph the Sultan was therefore regarded as high treason of a peculiarly diabolical kind. If the culprit had not been a foreigner he would probably have been quietly strangled, or otherwise got rid of; but. thanks to the energetic intervention of his ambassador, he was released after a month's imprisonment, on condition that he quitted Turkey once and for ever. Bearing on the question of the manner , of Mr. Pyne's death, a very curious story is told. Just before starting for Ilolyhead, Mr. Pyne, says the London gossip of the "Liverpool Post," went to a colleague in the House of Commons, and handed him his watch, asking him to take care of it for him. The member was puzzled at this request, but accepted the commission. When no as came of poor Pyne's disappearance what was doubtless his original intention was carried out, and the watch was forwarded to his wife. On the dial there was roughly engraved the words, "Pay no rent:" This was one of Mr. Pyne's original devices. akin to his famous exploits in his castle. Whenever, in, troub- lone times, any of his poor neighbours cameato him for advice as to what they should do in fie() of a demand for rent, Pyne would shake his head. "I cannot give you advice on this subject," he said, "because Mr. Balfour says it is illegal. But I'll tell you what I'll do. I will show you what time of day it is," and, handing out his watch, the inquiring tenant read upon it the admonitory legend.

The final performance at Olympia was given on Satur- day night, and proof that the popularity of Barnum's Show remained unabated to the end was afforded by the unstinted applause with which the entertainment was greeted. Mr. Barnum, accompanied by the Lord Mayor and other distinguished visitors, occupied a box in the centre of the balcony, and at the conclusion of the per- formance he made a brief speech, in which he thanked the British public for the patronge accordpd to his show, and expressed a hope that he might visit 'England again next year.

-On Wednesday afternoon the-remains of the late Dr. Dale, who died On Sunday, at his residence, 163, Islington, Liverpool, were -interred at Daresbury Churehyard, near Warrington. A preliminary ser- vice was held in the morning in Brunswick Wesleyan Chap!. Moss-st., with which the deceased gentleman had for many years been connected. The widespread respect in which Dr. Dale was hifid was folly shown by the large congregation . present at the service. whichincladed many prcimmeric mem- bers of the Wesleyan body in Liverpool The body was encased in a coffin of polished oak witb brass mountings, and bearing the inscription, ' "Thomas Dale, died 16th February, 1890, aged 65 years." The mourners who followed the hearse and attended the service were Dr. T. A. Dale, Mr. W. R. Dale, and Mr. J. K. Dale, sons of the deceased; Dr.. Leigh, Mr. W. Kay, and Mr. Kirkham. Amongst‘ those also present in the chapel were Dr. Nevins, Dr. Thorne, Dr. Edis, and Messrs. E. Gilbert; W. Guyter, S. Townley, E. Hutchinson, John Dow, J. Ellison, W. Craze, J. Scarffe, J. Holt, J. A. Turner. E. Elliot, T. E. Jefferson, T. Frith, W. Ladyinan. J. W. Lloyd, and I. Mack. The ministers taking part in the service were the Revs. W. T. Ratcliffe, S. T. Hense, W. Middleton, H. Curnon, and W F; Slater, Professor of Biblical Exegesis at Didsbury In the course of an address the Rev. W. T. Ratcliffe paid a high tribute to the godly and useful life which Dr. Dale had spent. He had had ample opportunity of judging of this, their Personal friendship having extended over twenty-seven years. When the end was approaching Dr. Dale's Christian resignation was maintained without a murmur, and he displayed nothing but entire sub- mission to the will of God. All 'who knew him would give their prayful sympathy to the widow and family in their great bereavement. Dr. Dale would be much missed from his accustomed place in that chapel, and his absence from their meetings would long be deplored. At the conclusion of the service the body was conveyed to the Central Station, to be taken by the 12.30 train to Warring- ton. The Revs. W. F. Slater and S. T. House accom- panied the funeral party to Dargsbury. _

div.head: WARRINGTON AMATEUR PHOTOGRAPHIC. SOCIETY.
div.p: WARRINGTON AMATEUR PHOTOGRAPHIC. SOCIETY.

The third annual exhibition of lantern slides of the Warrington Amateur Photographic Society was held in the Co-operative Hall, on Tuesday evening. Those who were present were there at the invita- tion of the members, and evidently enjoyed the programme prepared for them. The chair was occu- pied by the President of the Society (Mr. T. J. Down), who opened the prodeedings with an address, in which he commented on the satisfactory progress the society had made since it came into existence, three or four years ago. He thought it was desirable that, in these busy rushing days, everybody should have a hobby ,of some kind, and he did not know of anything better than amateur photography, tas it took them out into the pleasantest parts of the country, and led to results which were a permanent source of instruction and enjoyment. He trusted that the exhibition that would be given that evening would be the means of those present taking an i interest n what ,they were doing, and becoming mem- bers of the society.—The views thrown upon the screen by the new lantern of the society were, of course, the work of the members, and it is due to them to say that they evidenced great progress since the first exhibition three years ago. The scenes presented were many of them near home, but some were from various parts of England, Scotland and the Isle of Man. The slides were taken in sections and in the intervals a musi- cal programme was proceeded with. The lantern mani- pulators, it may be stated, were Messrs. H. N. Houghton and W. H. Harrison, and it was explained that any little defects that might be apparent would probably be due to the fact that the lantern was a new one, and as yet under trial. The following was the musical pro- gramme, which was gone through as to every item in a most satisfactory style :—Pianoforte solo, Galop de bravoure, 4' Sans Souci," Miss E. A. Dalton ; song," My sweetheart when a boy," Mr. F. J. Dell : flute solo, "Jenny Jones," Mr. P. Brimelow ; song, "Heaven and earth,' Miss Isabel Monks : violin solo, fantasia, "La Traviata," Mr. A. Down • song," Ora pro Nobis," Mr. Alfred Cavanagh ; duet (flute and piano), "Fantasia on Scotch airs," Mr. P. Brtmelow and Miss Down; vocal duet, " Flow gently, Deva," Messrs. Dell and Cavanagh. After singing Heaven and earth," Miss Monks was recalled and sang" Needles and pins." Miss Down, it should be stated, efficiently acted as accompanist. What was in sonie respects a unique entertainment was brought te a close with the singing of the National Anthem.
THE GEOLOGY OF THE Sill? CANAL.

A lecture on the "Geology of the Ship Canal" was given in the Lecture Room, at the Museum, on Monday evening, by Mr. P. F. Kendall, late of Owen's College, and Lecturer to the Stockport Geo- logical Society. The lecture, which was under the auspices of the Museum Committee, was largely attended, and was illustrated by splendid lantern views thrown on a screen by Mr. F. W. Monks. The Lecturer remarked that there were several popular notions abroad regarding geologists. One of these was that they were people of a rather low type of intel- lect who derived pleasure from groping about in dirty placesatfter stones. Another notion was that geologists were a species of necromancers, who could see very much further through a millstone than the generality of people. Both of these ideas were erroneous. Geological methods were simply the application of commonsense to the el uci- dation of various problems which stared all intelligent people in the face. The con- struction of the Ship Canal had offered an altogether unique opportunity so far as Eng- land was concerned for the study of geology. It had this advantage over the making of a railway that there would be no embankments, except:of course down the estuary of the river, but they would have presented to their view, bit by bit, a clean cut section extending from Manchester to wnere the canal entered the river. They had a clean cut slice right through the country, and that was why the Ship Canal was of especial interest to geologists. He was sorry to say that Lan- cashire geologists had not availed themselves of that golden opportunity to the extent that might have been expected, but there was no reason why Warrington, having, as it has, a great advantage in situation, should not set the great towns of Manchester and Liverpool an example which might result in much good. (Applause,) Individuals had, it was true, taken advantage of the opportunity now offered, but it was really not a matter for individuals ; the work should be done by the Geological Societies which abound in this part of the country, and indeed there was no part of the country better provided with these societies. As Manchester and Liverpool had ap- parently conspired to neglect the canal, there was no reason why Warrington should not step to the front and do a duty which had been left to them or any one else to perform. (Hear, hear). Several lantern views were then given one of which was a portrait of the late Daniel Adamson., to whom, the lecturer remarked, if to any one man, they were indebted for the canal, Mr. Adamson, was also a geologist. The tbcks of the earliest period found on the canal were those of the Triassic period, represented by the red sandstone which contri- bute soconspicuous a feature to the scenery in the neigh- bourhood of Halton Castle. From a study of those rocks they were led to a tolerably clear picture of the times in which they were laid down. They found in these beds indications of salt which showed that they must have been deposited in extremely shallow water. It was from the same kind of deposits that the salt was obtained in the salt district around Northwich. The room having been completely darkened, the subject of the lecture was illustrated by a great number of lantern views which were thrown upon the screen with remarkable distinct- ness.

div.head: MISER FOUND READ.
div.p: A MISER FOUND READ.

, Considerable sensation has-been occasioned in Bramell, about three miles from Stockport, by the discovery of the dead body of Charles Woodcock, aged sixty-one. Woodcock was of miserly and very eccentric habits, and lived a solitary life in the village, and it was common for several days to .pass 'without his stirring out of the house. On Monday his nephew entered his lonely dwelling, and found his uncle lying dead on the Boor, with a wound on the back of thehead. The old man had evidently fallen from his chair while counting his wealth, for sums of gold and silver were found upon the floor and upon the table. Deceased lived the live of a recluse, and it is said he has a considerable sum of money in one of the district banks. Ile was subject t.) dizziness. It is believed he had been dead several days when the body was discovered.

div.head: ST. PAUL'S ANNUAL TEA PARTY.
div.p: ST. PAUL'S ANNUAL TEA PARTY.

The annual tea party in connaction with St. Paul's Church, Warrington, was held in the, Public Hall on Tuesday 'evening. The tea as usual was very numerously attended, there being about 600 persons present. The following is a list of the sub- cribers who gave either trays or subscriptions The Hon. L. W. Powys, the Lady Mary Powys, Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., M.P.. Lady Greenall, the Mayoress (Mrs. Fraucomb), Mr. J. Marson, Mrs. Marson, Mr. R.. Davies, Mrs.. Davies, Mr. P. Stubs, Mrs. Sutton, Mrs. T. Morris, Mrs. D. - Jones, Mrs. Smethurst, Mrs. Lawless, Mrs. Chantry, 'Mrs. Ashurst, Mrs. Braide, Mrs. Chorley, Mrs. Rowe, Messrs. Crosfield and Son, Mrs. J. Pierpoint, Mr. Kirkconnell, Mr. A. J. Jolley. Mrs. J. Tinsley, Mrs. Finney, Miss Finney, Miss ' -Burrows Messrs. Pear- son and Knowles, Mrs. Peers, Mrs. Craddock. Mrs. W. Tuilstall, Mr. T. Tunstall, 3lrs. %Yard, NI rs. J. Gibson, Miss liaison, Messrs. P. Walker and Son, Miss Garland, Mrs. Milling, Mrs. Jeans, Mr. Joseph Davies, Mrs. J. Hepherd, Mrs. Ferguson, Mr. Geddes, Mrs. J. Hesketh, Mr. Hutchinson, Miss Pierpoint, Miss White, Mrs. Wilkinson, Mr. W. Robinson, Mrs. Hedg- cock, Mrs. Craik, Mrs. Atherton. Mrs. Rathbone, Messrs. W. and J. Richardson, Mrs. W. Lawless, Mrs. Clive, Mrs. L. Greening, Mrs. Reid, Mrs. JosephLythgoe, Mr. R. Toft, Mrs. J. A. Sutton, Mrs. Greenou.ii, MN. Parsonage, Mrs. Marshall, Mrs. J. Lavran, Mrs. Hankinson, Mrs. H. Toft, Mrs. Griffiths, Mr. Murray, Mr. W. Gibson, Mrs. Peacock, Mrs. J. Whittle, Mrs. Bradley, Mrs. G. Fitton,Mrs. Highley, Mr. R. A. Naylor, Miss Bolton, Mrs. J. Parkinson' Mrs. Clare, Mrs. J. Wood, Mrs. Anderton, Mrs. Shillcockt Messrs. T. W. Nelson, and Co:, the Tanners-lane Tanning Co.' Mrs. G. Woods, Mrs. E. Woods, Mrs. Roberts, Mrs. Whalley, Mrs. Bates, Mrs. Hayes, Mrs. Birtles, Mr. Regers, Mrs. Alex. Baird,. Mr. Knowles, Mr. Evans, Mrs. Banks, and Mr. J. Smith. . .

After tea an entertainment was held, the chair being occupied by Mr. R. Davies. There were also on the platform the Rev. S. Wilkinson, the Rev. T. Emmott, Alderman T. Sutton, Messrs. D. Jones, J. Smethurst, and D. W. Finney. The hall was completely filled. The CHAIHNLN said that it gave him very much plea- sure to come amongst them, and to see the immense gathering which St. Paula parish had produced for that evening's tea party. He looked upon himself merely as a substitute for a better ,man, that better man being Sir Gilbert Greenall. (Applause.) He regretted very much that Sir Gilbert was notin a state of health—though he was not ill—which justified him in coming into a crowded, and perhaps a heated room that evening. He did not think they all of them quite understood what Sir Gilbert Greenall was doing for them in Warrington at the present time. If they recollected, he was anxious to make a present to the town of a handsome sum of money —several thousand pounds—for a jubilee gift. Theyhad been enabled by that gift to acquire a sort of little chapel at ease, belonging to St. Paul's parish, in Hoyle- st., called All Saints' Mission Room. (Hear, hear.) In addition to that, Sir Gilbert Greenall's generosity had enabled them to start the church of St. Peter's— (applause)—so that the parishioners of that rather poor parish will perhaps by the end of this year have the privilege and the great advantage of worshipping in a beautiful little church. There was also another thing of a useful kind which, owing to the generosity cf the gift, they were enabled to carry out at the present moment, and that was to acquire three houses which , were for sale adjoining Bank-st. Mission. They had acquired those three houses, and they would be added at some future time to Bank-at. Mission and school, and would form a most welcome and a most desired improve- ment to the poor building •there. (Hear, hear.) They had not yet quite exhausted the gift, for they had pur- chased a plot of land at the corner of Hopwood-at., in order to form the site of 'what they hoped would be a mission-room and school before very long. (Applause.) He was not quite done everryet, for whenever the public spirit of Warrington was advanced enough they might hope to have a church at Bank Quay, and the trustees had in hand the sum of £1;500 to start it with, all pro- ceeding from the bounteous gift of Sir Gilbert Greenall. (Applause.) He thought that it was only right that, when they were met there as an assembly of Church people, they should be told what was being done with the gift referred to, and to pay honour where honour was no, to the gentleman whose absence they regretted that night. (Hear, hear.) They had been told by a very witty Frenchman that England was a place which had only one sauce, and that was melted butter, and fifty religions. (Laughter.) But though they might differ in name, some going to church and some going to chapel, he hoped they might still regard England as an example to the world for the attempts which were made in it to do good to all classes, especially in the way of religious instruction. He was not undervaluing what was done in any other country, but he did say that the earnestness and the great efforts which had been made in England in the advancement of education, supple- mented by religion, had been an example which America and the whole world was following, and he did think it rested with everyone of them, however young, to do something to help towards the most desired consumma- tion of making this country a truly united, happy and religious kingdom. (Applause.) The Rev. S. WILKINSON said it hardly seemed like a party connected with St. Paul's not to have in the chair their genial and kind friend, Sir Gilbert Greenall, but while they deplored the worthy baronet's absence, they warmly welcomed Mr. Davies upon the platform. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Davies had been connected with the town of Warrington a great many years, and he (Mr. Wilkinson) did not think there was in the whole town a firmer friend or kinder supporter of everything which was good in Warrington, and especially in the parish of St. Paul's. (Applause.) Mr.' Wilkinson then referred to the loss their church had sustained by the death of Councillor Jolley, and alluding to the work of the parish, he said they had between 200 and 300 Church workers helping them, and these he thanked most sin- cerely for their labour of love. He also ex- pressed his thanks to the churchwardens, sidesmen, lay representatives Sunday and day school teachers, the choir, the ladies who helped in connection* with the mothers' meeting and girls friendly society, and those who assisted in connection with their most successful evening classes, temperance work, district visiting, Ix. They were most united in St. Paul's parish, and did their work in a Church of England way. (Hear, hear, and applause.) They had not had an exciting year, but they had started two works from which they hoped for much, One of these was a gymnasium in connection with the Sunday School. (Applause.) This had proved a most flourishing institution, and so far about fifty young men had joined it. He was one of those who thoroughly believed in muscular Christianity. He wanted to see their young men in the first place Christian young men, and in the next place manly young men, and he believed a gymnasium was a capital thing for doing something I towards both those ends. (Applause.) The next work they had undertaken was the removal of the church organ which, he believed, would result in many vivant- ages. (Applause.) 1 The first partof the musical programme was opened with a part song" Hark the distant hills "by the.choir. Afterwards Mr. Parr sang," Maid of Athens" -; Miss C. Hedgcock. " The Lost Chord " ; Mr. Potter. "Down In the deep " ; Mrs. Massey, "On the doorstep" -; Mr. Fryer," Blue Alsatian Mountains" ; and Miss C. Hedg- cock," Killarney." Humorous songs were also given by Mr. Rogers and a pianoforte solo by Mrs. Roberts. This part of the programme was very successfully ren- dered, in each instance the performer coming in for hearty applause. The second portion of the entertain- ment consisted of a dramatic rendering of" Vi(e Versa" an amusing piece. The characters in this were taken by Mr. Griffiths Mr. A. de C. Carson, Mr. J. Brady Moore, Mr. W. Griffiths, Mr. W. Worden. Mr. A. McFall, Mr. G. Griffiths, junr., Master F. Milling, Miss W. Griffiths, Miss Griffiths, and some schoolboys. This part of the programme provoked much merriment and was excellently rendered.

div.head: CATHERINE'S MISTAKE,
div.p: CATHERINE'S MISTAKE,
A SECRET FOR YEARS.
CHAPTER LVI. EXPLANATIONS.

Cram Arm returned ii;-the house and found Madame Bernstein awaiting her. They were both filled with dreary presentiments of evil in store. Cleland but half understood what had passed before her eyes that day; all she comprehended was, that her father had not committed the crime he had been on the verge of All beyond was a mystery to her; and now, sitting alone with the baroness by ,the firelight, in her father's study, she implored her, through her tears, to tell her what it meant—who was that strange dark man? and how had Miss Ware known her father 8,1 long ago? Madame Bernstein was MK) very unhappy—Un- happy,because Lina was feverish and ill with the ex- citement of the day; unhappy because of Catherine's strange light, and the wretched discovery that George Ingestre was really dead and in his grave. Still, she dried her tears and assumed it cheerfulness of manner, when she found that Cleland's sorrow was only aggravated by the display of her own. " I will tell you, my dear, as far as I know and have been enlightened to-day; but I must go back many years, and begin from the very beginning, or you will not understand how I came to know any- thing about your father's and uncle's affairs. Do you think you shall be tired, my child, before I have done?" _
'No. oh, no! tell the, and I will promise to listen." She laid her head down on the baroness's knees, and the lady stroked her hair tenderly, while sha con- tinued thus : , _

"You know my father WAS your grandfather's steward, and we, his family, lived at Westwood Farm, thus becoming very intimate with the young gentlemen up at the House (that is, here, at Redfe,m; It was always called 'The House' by us). They were fine, handsome boys all of them; but, my dear, your grandfather had committed a heinous in by them. They could not inherit his property, ncr even bear his name lawfully, for their 'mother was not hi wife, although she was alwtys called Mrs. Ingestre. Well, orie after another these fine boys dropped Into their graves. Two were drowned, one died of fever, and the fourth was flung from his horse; and the father, beginning to take it as a judgment of Heaven, married the mother, and a very few months after Georee Ross was born, the heir of all his pro- perty. Ede ard Maxall was his senior by about fout years, and it seemed hard that the younger brother &heel l stand before him. But still there was no such thing as jealousy between them, for they were both noble-hearted, open-handed fellows, and loved eacL other denrly. "So all the children not born in wedlock died hut Edward, and then his father add he Should share the Jamaica plantations, and his brother possess the English estate. So, when th-y were young men, the two went out to Um island together, the younger in- tending to return home SOOR. I went out a few months after, for s Mr. Clive, a planter out there, 'who had come over to see Mr. Ingestre on business, fell in love with me, and at stxteen I was a wife, and living abroad with my husband. The two Ingestree lived at Kingston, lat Spanish Town; still, we kept tap our old intimacy and correspondence. George did not return home so soon as he intended, but that was no wonder, for the life in Jamaica was an alluring one to both—courted, flattered, and every luxury of life at their command. • "Well, my dear, not very far from rue resided a family which I perfectly well knew had great attrac- tions for one of the Ingestres. The father was a native Spaniard, the mother a Spanish creole ; and they had one daughter—a graceful, lovely creature of fifteen or sixteen, not more, but quite a woman, I remember. I knew very little of them personally; but my black maid used to tell me there was is ,certain creole gentleman the father favoured, and the daughter would not listen to. / could guess the reason; for more than once I had seen George Tn- gestre waiting at night in the cinnamon grove at the .end of our street, evidently watching for someone. But it was no business of mine, and soon after that I left with my husband for St. Domingo, and remained there about eighteen months. " When I returned, the small-pox had broken out among the negroes on the Ingestre plantations. It raged like a plague; and the next I heard was that both the young men were down with it. Edward Maxall was reported dead, and, as I heard, buried two hours after; for the loathsome disease made this necessary in that climate. I was living at quite the opposite side of the island then, and all communica- tion with the infected portion was strictly forbidden pay government, so we heard very little of what was going on. "And now, who do you think I discovered living in a beautiful little house not half a mile from me? The lady whom you have known as Catherine Wace, my dear; but who confessed to me, in her hour of great trouble, that her true name WAS Catherine Ingestre; for George ROSA had married her, and they had lived together in that exquisite little house at such times as he could leave Kingston without suspicion. She had heard of the disease raging there, and was nearly frantic when they forbade her to leave the village. "The poor thing came to me for advice, and told me that not only her husband but her child also was at Kingston; for the father always kept it near him, he loved it so passionately. I did my best to com- fort her; but as to assist her in gaining the for- bidden ground, that was impossible, for we were closely watched. But at last some kind soul sent us word George was slowly recovering; so poor Catherine was forced to be content and remain as quiet as she could. "Soon after that I heard from my husband that the old squire was deed, and the heir wanted in Eng- land. I told Mrs. Ingestre the news, and she talked all that evening about the life she would lead at Red- fern as the Squire's lady, and I remember well telling of the neighbours she would have—the Draysons, Colonel Jones, and all the rest of it. Ah, me! who would have thought what was coming? "Well, my dear, the very next night, as I was sitting with her in the acacia harbour (I never smell a white acacia now, but I think of that night), a letter, all fumigated, was brought us by a sailor. He had come from Kingston, he said, where the small- pox was dying out, and the letter had been given him by a gentleman to deliver into Miss Franchi'a own hands. She opened the letter while I wit there (for the inscription seemed in her husband's hand), and Cleland dear, that cruel letter told that he was going to sail for England in three weeks' time; that their marriage had been no marriage at all, for it had not been performed according to the laws of his country, and consequently was not binding on him; that he must leave her, as it was impossible she should accompany him to his home. And then it told her the poor little boy was dead of the fell disease, and had been buried in the same coffin as its uncle.

"Ah, child! I cannot dwell upon that poor creature's woc. Her good name, her child was gone, and she had a second coming to share her life of shame. I took her into my house, and from that time until her little girl was born, she was not once conscious. George Ingestre, who, as we supposed, had survived, did net sail in three weeks' time; a great frieud and companion of his, Fernando Ponti, the creole. son Of a Spanish noble by a beautiful slave, stabbed him in the side. The man was hung, Cle," (hQrti the lady shuddered, and looked fearfully round the room). " He was hung, Cle, and Ingestre did not go to England for two months after; but he never noticed poor Catherine again. Her child was born, and my good husband allowed me to adopt it as my own, en condition the mother should never claim it in any way. She consented for the child's sake, and went away to Europe to be a governess, she said. She has supported herself in that way for very many years now, always writing to me and letting me know she was still alive. I wrote to her also, giving her a full account of Linn and all her pretty little ways; but they never met until I came to Westwood this year." madame—my father; is he not George Ross Ingestre? Did he not marry this lady?" " No, Cle; it seems George died, and Edward lived, and this man Ponti put it into his head to take his brother's name, and so inherit all the property. He did so, and, you see, has had to pay the penalty. Catherine thought she was going to marry her old love, and—oh, dear ! oh, dear; what a sad ending, to be sure !—how could Edward be such a wretch as to have another wife all the time!"

"Strange,' said Cleland, staring into the fire, "that she should not have known the difference between the two—mistaken one for the other." "They were very much alike in person and manner," was the reply, "only George was really the handsomest and the noblest-hearted of the two. And remember, she had never seen Edward, and believed, like all the rest, he was George. And to think that wicked creole wrote that letter, and plotted poor Catherine's ruin so thoroughly ! " "And now who will have Redfern, and all my father's money ? " .
"Ingram Rcss Ingestre, his first cousin." Cleland still looked into the fire. "Baroness, they cannot take me from him; I am his daughter?
" No, my child; you must be all in all to him now, he has no one else."
"/ will; / will never leave him." And Cleland kept her word. CHAPTER INIT. RETRIBUTION.

A MIDNIGHT ride; a graceless sinner abroad, when God spoke in his own language above the earth—spoke in the wind—spoke in the beating rain, and in the dark- ness of that tempestuous sky. Could that man ride out amid the voices of .that night and not listen tc them ?—live the life he had lived, and not hear it re- corded by them ?—sin as he had sinned, and yet not be awed by them? He pulled his hat over his brows, but he had no protection for his bare chest. The rain had soaked his wet clothes through and through, and his limbs were numbed with cold, still he did not knpw it; nor did he think of anything but the voices—the accusing voices abroad that night. Sorrow had not hardened this man's heart •.)f late. I true and worthy love had purified it from much evil; and now this nature of strong desires, of passionate impulses, of reckless deeds, %::.4 melted to listen to the angerstrutnp sound- ing above the wind. When he mounted the horse his daughter held, he had thought of Catherine as dead, and that thought brought but one other. A pistol was concealed in his breast, and he meant to die with her. He could not live, and she no more; he could not walk the earth, and know that she was beneath it. Self-inflicted death was the dreadful thing he contemplated when he implored his daughter's safety. _ But the love of a good woman had worked ii—chitnie in the old sinful nature of the man; the deed he con- templated was seen in all its awful crime. Two miles were kciircely passed before he flung the pistol far from him, and said: •6 God's will be done! lam not afraid of death, fear a lonely life much more; but I will do nc murder, and lose my soul forever. I will try to share heaven with Catherine."

And so he rode on, and the pistol lay in a field. Two hours after he passed it again on his way home. The wind had fallen, the rain had ceased, and the white moon flashed out at intervals from behind the wild, driving masses of cloud. His horse was lame, and he walked at its side, gently leading it. By the rare flashes of light shed on his face by the pale, watery moon, you could see his countenance was gentle and sad, too, for tears were quivering on the eyelashes and resting on the furrows of the cheek. Often he leaned his head upon the horse's neck, and his lips moved—it might have been in prayer. They journeyed on through the heavy roads like this, until the park was close at hand. Then theh.,rse became lamer than ever, and the master seemed more ;Ind more tender of giving it pain. The shortest to the house lay through the park and past the little church. and Ingestre, still leading the horse, guided it carefully beneath the dark masses of trees. Chap 57 The graveyard was uninclosed, and the path wound close under the wooden porch, which had a bench on either side. Ingestre halted here to rest the horse awhile, and, holding the reins, sat down on the seat to watch the scudding clouds and the white wan moon. •. Suddenly she burst forth with superb radiance, singing. her beams over tree, and grass, and grave— over the weary horse, the sorrowful man, and over— yes, over a second figure, crouching in the farthest corner of the porch, staring with all its wild eyes at Ingestre as he leaned forward to watch the moon and sky. 'f he horse turned its head and whinnied gently; the master spoke an encouraging word, and rose to go. The moon still lighted up the place, and at a sound —a low, deep sigh—he started, turned, and met those eyes. " Catherine !" and he was kneeling at her feet, embracing, kissing them and her stone cold hands.

She seemed to have been abroad all that dreadful night, for she had no coverinn•b on her head, and her long hair hung dripping withwet round her shoulders. Her dress, too, was saturated, and her face white and blue with exposure to the cold. Ho asked how long she had been there. She tried to answer, but her lips formed no words. He took her In his arms, and warmed her chilled blood with the heat of his own; he tenderly kissed the white lips, and chafed her stone cold hands.

"Catherine, only speak to me, only say that you forgive me the injury I have done you, and I will humbly go away and never torment you with my presence any more. Only forgive me!" Her only reply was to dash his hands away—to shrink from him, and cower farther into the corner. "How dare he say those words?" she cried. "flow dare he hunt her thus—or speak to her, when—'

"Catherine, if you love me, I have every right. Listen: She is dead!" "Dead! who is dead now?" she moaned, wringing her hands woefully. "My wife. She died to-night--a terrible death, too, and I stood by the bedside unknown to her. I did not hope for this release, Catherine; I did not pray for it; I was not bad enough for that. I thought the summons was to your deathbed, and instead I found my wife, a horrible sight (she had been run over in Lowmoor), with not an hour to live. She is dead now, Catherine, but I have no hope that you will either love or marry me. It was George you if ,VE,I, not Edward, the thief, who stole your children's patri- mony. No, you mast hate me!" Her bitter tears were the only reply to his word. "It I had but known my brother was really married, I would have cut off my hand before I consented to do:this thing. I only suspected it afterwards from a threat the creole used. He died, and I could find no proof of my suspicion; but that was the secret a the toleration I had for the creature I believed your son."

And here he shuddered, for he thought if that face among the reeds, lying in the moonshine now, and staring up at the stars. "Catherine, can you believe me ? " ' Yes, I believe you," was the husky reply. *May I not lead you into your own house ? " he said presently, for her strange state alarmed him. "No ; let me die here. I have wandered all rout.d the place, but came back here to die!' "Not to die. Oh, Catherine, for my wretched sake, not to die! Let me take you in my arms—let me put you on my horse! Die here you must not, torl,,rn creature that you are! God pardon Inn for mak 11,4 such misery. What shall I ever do to atone?" fle lifted her Alp, and placed her on the gentle horse pawing at his side. She made no opposition; she seemed too utterly exhausted to deny him anything. And thus, one arm supporting her, the other guiding the horse, lLy moved on towards the house. Neither Cleland nor the baroness was astonished at theburden he brought in and laid upon the sofa. She was quite insensible, and an hour after was raving in the height of delirium.

div.head: CHAPTER LVIIL THS END OF ALL.
div.p: CHAPTER LVIIL THS END OF ALL.

Tim next morning, at an early hour, Parkins entered with a grave, startled face the room where his master paced up and down (he had not been in bed all night, nor changed the wet clothes he had swum the lake in), and begged his presence in the hall. Ingestre had suspicion of what he was about to see there, and, witl- a curling lip, obeyed the summons, for he had no fancy for the sight he was called upon to witness. And there surely, in the middle.of the hall, lay the dead body of Maxall, Domingo weeping over it, and kissing the clammy face. "He was blown over Keighley Bridge last night, sir," said the butler, "and drowned in the lake. He was not quite sober when he left the Ingestre Arms. and Judges warned him from the bridge, but he wou:d go, and this is what came of it; but how Domingo came to rind him I don't know. You see the nigger is wringing wet, too." Then the poor black looked up, and told his tale most piteously. He had followed his master the night before, but had lost him in the shadows of the chest- nut grove. Patiently he had waited there until dawn, when, to his horror, he saw a hat floating on the lake, and the boat drifting about. He plunged into the water and swam towards the island, where 111 made sure something else belonging to Mr. Ingestre lay, and then he came upon the body of Maxall, and with the corpse lashed to him he swam back to shore, and brought it all the way to the house on his back. "And oh, masse, now him quite dead, I tell you secret—can't harm him now. I tell you secret 'bout Massa Maxall. He am your own child, Fare ; he am my poor sister's child, sere, and yours as well. She died, care, long, long 'go; but Massa Ponti took her son and put him in the little one's place that used to run about your feet—'inember, ma.ssa, the little one you loved?" Domingo evidently still thought his master George Ross Ingestre. Edward Maxall turned away. His punishment was greater than he could bear. The murderer of his beloved boy Ross was a child of his own! That day about noon a letter was put into Limes bands. It was from Ingram, and these the contents : "MY OWN,—I set sail for Italy to-night. The wretch is off; but I am after him, and will hunt him down like a dog. Riga has given me full permission. The order won't protect him, he has broken their laws. Let all remain at Redfern as it was until I return. George Ross is still master. Adieu, my heart ! Kind remembrances to madame and Miss Ingestre." Three months went on, and Catherine slowly re- covered from her great illness. She had resolved to leave England for ever with the baroness. and that

resolve was well known to Edward Maxall. He was, Indeed, an altered man now. The scandal of his contemplated marriage, and the subsequent discovery it led to, had been lathe mouths of all —shire. He had been told to resign his position as a magistrate, and he had done so with ex- cellent grace; and given up, beside' every other post of public trust or emolument he had held. And on the particular day I speak of, he walked along beneath the Op avenue, his hands thrust in his pockets, think- ing ot all this, and thinking how life with such shame would once have been insupportable; but now h:s spirit was so broken that he accepted both the life and the shame without a murmur.

Catherine had fixed this day, too, for her de- parture, and he had no hope that he should ever see her face again. Their intercourse, since she had lain beneath his roof (scarcely his, though), had been of the most re- stricted kind; never had he seen her alone, and never had he dared to wish it. Deeply injured as she bed been by him, he felt he had no right even to love her. He did not anticipate that she would so much as hid hitn farewell, and when he thought of this he covered lug face and wept. He was a desolate and htart, broken man, remember.

When the tears had had their, way, and his eyes looked out again over the spring landscape, he WV Catherine slowly coming towards him where he stood. Slai stopped once to gather a primrose growing at the foot of an elm, and then came certainly towards lion. When he was sure of this, he almost thought it would have been more merciful not to have ktidden

him that last farewell. She held out her hand, and a faint flush made her pale face beautiful. "Will you not take it ? " she said. "Shall we not part friends?" Something in her voice, her downcast face, nu.le, lijLn shiver all over and look at it most eagerly. Ordr for an instant; he sighed bitterly, arid turned "Not for me—not for me," he muttered; "it Lever was mine, and that is the greatest pain," "What was never yours, Edward?" "Your love, Catherine—your 10V..) "It was yours." "Catherine!" "And is saw. Yes, is now!" shs repeated, passionately. " I came into your house, saw, and loved you. No ?natter what likeness you bore to my dead hus- band, it was you I loved then, and you I love now. I have tried to think otherwise, but I cannot. I have tried to believe you everything that is false and bad. and I cannot. I have tried to believe you everything but what I love, and I cannot. I cannot leave you- I cannot tear myself away from you. I love yea, and must live where you are. I will be your child's servant as long as I live; but I will love and serve r you, too, for evermore!" _ Than he kneeled down at her feet, beneath the tree and clasped both arms round her figure. He lifted his quivering face to hers, and she stooped down and tenderly kissed it. After that she never left him. A year elapsed and Ingram Ingestre returned tc' Redfern. Then Edward Maxall, with his wife and daughter, went abroad. He retained only his private fortune, and a hand- some annuity settled on Catherine by Ingram. His passionate love fDr her never abated; she era! the hope of his life and became to him even more than he anticipated: The man was much changed, but not for the worse: and five years after, when he visited England wilt" Cle and a little son, to celebrate the birth of an heir to Redfern, many said that either Italy or his wife had made the Ingeatre of old days a younger and • better man. Grave' pale, quiet-eyed Cleland never left her father, The girl's heart could hold no other love than his and the beloved brother's. The exiles are happy and united in themselves, and Edward Masan never regrets that he is no longer George Ross Ingeatre of Redfern. Ingram made an excellent lord of the manor, and Line an admirable lady. Somewhat fond of gaietY and dress, perhaps; showing of her pretty little self to the beet advantage, and wilful to the last; but as her husband remained utterly blind to these weak- nesses, they never marred his happiness in any way. Be never told the fate of the creole Ponti ; but none doubted that through Ingram's means he had been. made to pay the penalty of his crimes. The baroness still resides at Westwood, and Mr. Kent visits there very often—on professional matterS. be says.
THIII END.

div.head: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
div.p: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.

HOUSE OF LORDS.—MONDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at a quarter-past four o'clock. AUSTRALIAN FEDERATION.—Lord KNUTSFORD, replying to the Earl of Belmore, said the result of the preliminary conference on Australian federation must be accepted as most satisfactory to all who believe, as the Government did, that the prosperity, the welfare, and the strength of those great colonies would he materially increased and secured by a closer union under some form of federation, Upon which the colonists must decide, and which would ieave large powers to the local legislatures. MISCELLANEOUS.—Lord Cnoss informed Lord Norton that the Reformatory and Parochial Schools Bill would be re-introduced. The Hares' Preservation Bill was read second time; and Earl CADOGAN, replying to Lord Dun- raven, said it was undoubtedly the intention of the Government to obtain the judgment of Parliament upon the proposals for increasing the number of occupying tenants in Ireland and for extending to that country the principles of local self-government. The house adjourned at ten minutes past five o'clock.
HOCSE OF COMMONS.-MONDAY.

Mr. SAMUEL SMITH interrogated Baron de Worms regarding the alleged flogging of West Austra- lian aborigines by their white masters, but Baron de Worms professed ignorance of the matter. Mr. GOSCHEN, being interrogated by Colonel Hughes regarding the Property tax, said he was unable at present to give any information either as to remission or imixkition of taxa- tion, THE PARNELL Conuvrisstow.—Mr. PARNELL asked what stoPs the Government intended to take regarding the Parnell Commission, and Mr. W. He hoped it would be in his power to move this resolution on Monday. THE ADDRESS —The debate on the Address was re- Slimed by Mr. W. Pease to amend the laws re- lating to slavery; and a bill introduced by Mr. H. J. Wilson to amend the law relating to the qualification of guardians of the poor. The house adjourned at five minutes past twelve o'clock.
HOUSE OF LORDS.—TuEsnmr.

DISRAELL—The LORD CHAN- CELLOR informed the House that he had received from Mr. Disraeli, Assistant Clerk of Parliaments, a letter announcing his resignation. Their lordships' good Wishes would follow that gentleman in his retirement, after his long occupation of a scat at the table of the Rouse. (Hear, hear.) This motion having been agreed to, the Lord Chancellor stated that subject to the approval of the House he had appointed Mr. Thesiger, Clerk of Presentations, to the vacant post; and he be- lieved that a bett,•r appointment could not have been Made. Sir Henry James and Mr. John Orley took part in the debate, which closed at midnight, 'When a division was taken For Mr. Parnell's Amendment 240 Against

The debate on the Address was adjourned until next week, Channing brought a Bill to amend the Agricul- .'r„l',WHoldings Act, and it was read a first time. The House adjourned at a quarter-past twelve. HOUSE OF COMMONS, WEDNESDAY. beSpe,ker tookthe chair shortly after two o'clock. ADDRESS AND SCOTCH LEGISLATION. Dr. CLARICE ii4)ved as, an amendment to the Address "that wail desirable, while retaining the supremacy rthe Imperial Parliament, to devolve upon a legislature Scotland the consideration of the domestic affairs of tet country." Mr. Madonusarms, while agreeing with - fir Clarke that the neglect of Scotch business in the se was deplorable, and also the indifference of Eng- members to legislation for the sister country, Rict it was both premature and inopportune to propose establishment of a separate Scotch Legislature. Mr. 12, enawyonia moved to amend the amendment by ex- stessicg a general concurrence in the principle of ,cctch members dealing with Scotch affairs. Mr. , .u,'-`l-knstoNE, following the Lord-advocate, said it his intention to give a vote in consonance that of othis official, but on grounds totally differ- , Flt- After protesting against the Lord-Advocate's im- glta,tion of garrulity by Scotch members, Mr. Gladstone a n'ended that the state of Scotch private business was Serious grievance, and a serious change was about to 0417' „,roPosed on that account. When the House divided . Donald Cratrferd's amendment it was lost by a oitieritY of 166, and the debate was adjourned. BILIS.—The following new bills were brought in: • aaLvir• Barclay—Bill to empower local authorities to • hoici.;ll.ire land, and to facilitate the sub-division of large Mr. Teter M'Donald—Bill to amend the law b,_ankrupte,y ia Ireland. eeived thilir assurance that they would take into careful consideration thc, measures submitted to them, which she trusted might become the basis of legislation that would promote the happiness and welfare of her faithful people. The House adjourned at twenty-five minutsa to five o'clock.

QuEsrimis, &c.—Mr. GOSCIIIIN informed Mr. Howard Vincent that it was intended to reintroduce the bill for the appointment of a public trustee. Mr. Goschen also replied to Mr. H. H. Fowler with reference to interest on a portion of the National Debt. Mr. Balfour declined to give Mr. P. O'Brien particulars of evicted farms that had beentaken by new tenants. Other questions had reference to the investment of trust money in colonial stocks, Mr. Clifford Lloyd's positions in the Civil Service, and Scottish Crofter colonists in Western Canada. Mr. W. H. Smith, replying to Mr. Rowntree, said that £8,302,659 had been applied for by way of loans under the Land Purchase (Ireland Acts, 1885 and 1888, and £8,575,828 has been advanced. Mr. Balfour, in answer to Mr. M. Healy, denied that there had been any persecution of Roman Catholic policemen in Dublin. THE ADDRESS.

On the resumption of the debate on the address another amendment, for devolving upon Scotch members the consideration of Scotch business, was discussed. It was rejected by 181 to 141. Mr. Stanfield moved an amendment regretting that no promise had been made of legislation for the amendment of local government in Great Britain. Mr. LONG for the Government asked whether it was best to put a long list of measures in the Queen's Speech which had little or no chance of passing, or to limit the list to those which would probably pass, and to be ready to extend the list if possible. The Govern- ment, he said considered themselves fortunate in having been able to put the Local Government Bill on the statute-book, and would do their best to supplement it with other useful measures, and it would rest with the House to assist them in completing the work. Mr. PICKERSGILL and Mr. JAMES ROWLANDS supported the amendment, and the debate was adjourned. The House adjourned at five minutes past twelve o'clock.

div.head: O'SHEA. DIVORCE CASE.
div.p: THE O'SHEA. DIVORCE CASE.
THE MOTIONS FOR ATTACHMENT.

In the Divorce Court, on Tuesday, before Justice Butt, the motions for attachment against the "Freeman's Journal," the "New York Herald," and the '• Star " were renewed. The Solicitor-General, for the plaintiff. read comments in the London letter of the " Freeman's Journal "of the 4th January, on Captain O'Shea's divorce action against Mr. Parnell, desciibing the action as "a new plot," and he asked that Mr. John Porter, publisher of the paper, and Mr. James Tuohy, London correspon- dent of the paper, should be punished for transgressing the rules of the Court.—Sir Charles Russell submitted that the comments in the " Freeman's Journal" were called forth by the action of Captain O'Shea in discussing proceedings of a delicate nature with a newspaper repre- sentative, and authorizing their publication in a Conser- vative evening journal.—Justice Butt dismissed the motions against the " Star " and " New Ycrk Herald," but in regard to the " Freeman's Journal," its London representative, Mr. 'James Tuohy, was fined £lOO and condemned in costs.

div.head: INFLUENZA.
div.p: THE INFLUENZA.

RAILWAY OFFICIALS INCAPACITAT ED. lufluenza continues to prevail with great severity in Wimborne. A number of railway officials are incapaci- tated, and on Tuesday afternoon Dr. Sydney Parkinson, medical officer of health for the Wimborne and Cranborne district, died after a short attack of the malady.

CHESHIRE. The influenza epidemic in Cheshire is producing serious results. In Crewe there are over 2,000 cases, and at Nantwich 1,000. The death returns this quarter will be exceptionally heavy. The number of deaths certified as being due to influenza is not so large, but deaths due to pneumonia, one of the after-consequences of influenza, are numerous. Doctors are working night and day attending patents.

div.head: CHESTER.
div.p: CHESTER.

Influenza is prevailing to extent in Chester and its surrounding neighbourhood. The out- break of the epidemic first became noticeable about a fortnight since. It is stated by a medical practitioner to be similar in type to the Russian disease, but differing somewhat in point of degree. Its symptoms are muscu- lar pains, accompanied by headache, with or without catarrhal symptoms, and followed by muscular :and ner- vous depression. FLINTSHIRE AND DENBIGHSHIRE.

The influenza epidemic is still very prevalent in Flint. shire and Denbighshire, and some hundreds of people have been seized with the complaint since its first appear- ance. The deaths, however, are few, the epidemic being of a mild form. The public schools in Holywell have been closed for a fortnight, and fresh cases daily break- ing out, the medical officer has declined to allow them to be reopened. The schools at Denbigh, Bodfari, and Tremerichion are also closed. SPREAD OF THE EPIDEMIC AT LEEDS.

The fLii; Mercury" of Tuesday says :—A fort- night ago there seemed grounds for hoping that Leeds was about to escape the fate of other towns. Up to that time there had been, as far as could be ascertained, very few cases of Russian influenza. We regret to say that such is no longer the state of things. The epidemic is spreading—we fear with considerable rapidity—and there is now a large number of sufferers. The attack is sudden; a person may feel in tolerably good health and two or three hours afterwards be completely pros- trated.

div.head: PARNELI, COMMISSION.
div.p: THE PARNELI, COMMISSION.

A meeting of the Liberal leaders took place on Tuesday evening, at the House of Commons, at which Lord Her- schen was present, to consider the form of the amend- ment to the Government motion en the report of the Commission. No decision has been come to by the leaders of the Opposition with respect to the Government motion on the report. There is a strong feeling in Opposition circles that reparation should be made to Mr. Parnell and those concerned with him in the inquiry, and it is pro- bable that Mr. Gladstone's energies will be directed to this end. The difficulty of meeting the Government is not one that the Irish members have personally endeav- oured to solve, as they have left themselves in the hands of the Liberal leaders. • Another telegeam says :—lt is now regarded as improb- able that the debate on Mr. Smith's motion respecting the Commission report will take place before the week after next. Owing to the exigencies of the financial year. certain supplementary estimates and a vote on account will have to be dealt with as soon as the Address is disposed of, and this business, it is expected, will occupy the whole of next week. The London correspondent of the "Freeman's Journal" says :—Mr. Parnell is anxious for the appoint. ment of a Select Committee to inquire into the forgeries conspiracy, and if it be admissible to grant such a proposal on the motion of Mr. Smith, he will take that opportunity of preferring his demand. LORD R. CHURCHILL AND THE REPORT. A London correspondent understands that Lord R. ' Churchill substantially agrees with the view taken by the Opposition of the Commission report. He thinks that all the more serious charges have been disproved, and thilt those which have been established art of compara- tively little importance. Mkt. W. S. CAINE AND THE REPORT.

Mr. W. S. Caine (writes a London correspondent) is having the report reprinted for distribution to each of his constituents. It will be accompanied by a letter expressing the writer's satisfaction that Mr. Parnell and his incriminated colleagues have been exonerated from the personal charges. Mr. Caine explained his position to a friend in the lobby on Monday evening. The ex- planation is characteristic and epigrammatic. It will live. "My position," said the hon. member, "has lain in a nutshell. Until the Commission reported I could neither dine with these gentlemen nor put them in prison —now I can do both." RESIGNATION OF MR. HOUSTON. Mr. Houston has sent in his resignation of the secre- taryship of the Irish Loyal and Patriotic Union. A special meeting of the executive committee has been con- vened for an early day to consider the matter. THE TIMES AND THE COMMISSION EXPENSES. A London correspondent states that the project of raising a subscription to cover the expenses of the " Times " has been mooted, but it finds no great favour among the Unionist party. The truth is that though they are attempting to put the best face on it. they are altogether sick of the " Times " charges, and feel that they have done irreparable injury to their own cause.
