div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 22, 1800
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 22, 1800

MURDER AND ATTEMPTED MURDER BY A FATHER, A terrible affair is reported from Litlington, about four miles from Royston, Cambridgeshire, a labourer named Walter Laurence haying killed one child and in- jured another so fearfully that it is not expected to re- cover. Mrs. Laurence was getting the children ready for school, when the husband seized a billhook, used for trimming hedges, and struck his little boy, aged four years, inflicting a fearful gash on his head. 'His wife rescued the child, and he then struck his daughter, aged eight years, and she shortly afterwards succumbed. Laurence is statedto have been strange in his manner lately. The boy, died on Wednesday.
MESSRS. BRUNNER-, MOND, AND CO.,
GOLD FIELDS IN CHINA.
SUDDEN DEATH OF MR. BIGGAR, M.P.

?Mr. Joseph Gillis Biggar, M.P., a prominent member of the Yarnell4 party, died auddenly on Wednesday morning at hisfesidence, Cl*hain Common. For some months it had been evident Mi. Biggar was not in good health, and, since the commencement of the present ses- sion, his growing weakness has been so apparent that his brother Nationalist whips had more than once urged him to go abroad for a change, but he always persistently refused to adept their suggestions. He found it neces- aary to leave the House early each evening since he cesumed his Parliamentary duties last week, but he insisted on performing his full share of the whips' work up to the time of leaving, and he had not gone away until physically incapable of doing any more work. The hon. member, though aware that something was radi- cally wrong with him, did not know the exact nature of his complaint, which, remarkably enough, was not actu- ally established until Tuesday night. For a week or two he had been taking cod liver oil, and within the last few days had applied to his medical adviser for liniment to rub on his chest. Dr. Kenny, who arrived from Ireland on Tuesday to take part in the division on Mr. Parnell's amendment, encountered Mr. Biggar ashe was entering Palace Yard, and was so struck with the change in the latter's ap- pearance since their last meeting that he arranged to make a thoroqgh examination of him in the course of the evening. About seven o'clock Mr. Biggar proceeded to the room recently set apart for the use of the Irish whips, and, in the presence of Mr. Carew. Dr. Kenny made a minute examination of the invalid. Although the distance from the House is not far, Mr. Biggar was quite exhausted when he entered the whips' room, and he asked to sit down for a few moments before he was able to say a word. After removing his coat he had to sit down again to rest himself, and the same thing occurred after taking off his vest. On the stethescope being applied it was at once apparent that Mr. Biggar was suffering from a cardiac glen- ' tion, and after the hon. member retired Dr. Kenny conveyed the intelligence to Mr. Carew. During the remainder ot the sitting Mr. Biggar, although obviously in considerable pain, remained at his post, and did not leave the House until nearly half-past 12 o'clock. He dined at the House, but after dining he I was observed to be unusually quiet, sitting in the corner of the tearoom by himself, and holding his pocket handkerchief to his mouth almost conti- nually. On leaving the House, Chief Inspector Horsley, who happened te be standing outside the members' entrance at the time, was much struck with Mr. Biggar's appearance, and he asked if he should call a cab for the hon. member. Mr. Biggar thanked Mr. Horsley for his offer, but said thatan Irish member had already summoned a hansom. The moment afterwards the vehicle drew up opposite the entrance, and Mr. Big- gar drove to his residence, 124, Sugden-road, Clapham Common. As soon as the news of the hon. member's death reached the Irish Parliamentary Office, on Wednes- day, a number of Nationalist members proceeded to Clapham to do what they could in the matter. It is very fortunate that Dr. Kenny made the examination oni Tuesday, for this precaution will probably obviate the necessity for an inquest. At six o'clock on Wednesday morning Mr. Biggar complained of shortness of breath, and his housekeeper was called up. While Dr. Alahony was being fetched, Mr. Biggar died. Heart disease was the cause of death. Mr. Biggar was born at Belfast in 1828, and was unmarried. He has represented county Cavan since 1874, sitting for the undivided county from that year intil 1885, and for the western division of the county since. At the last election he was not opposed, and at the previous general election he was returned by a majority of 4,846. He was very popular amongst the members of the Home Rule party generally: Mr. Biggar carried on an extensive business as a provision merchant, and had shops in various large towns of the United

_ Kingdom. Mr. Parnell, who was down at the House of Commons early on Wednesday, was greatly affected on hearing of the death of the member for Cavan, He said :" It will be impossible to replace him. He was my first and for a long time my only friend and colleague. At half past four in the afternoon a meeting of the Executive of the Irish National League was held in the conference room of the House of Commons, Mr. T. P, O'Connor presiding. A resolution was unanimously passed expressing profound sorrow at the unexpected death of its vice-president, and recording its conviction that Mr. Biggar's distinguished services entitled him to the grateful and affectionate memory of his countrymen. A Belfast correspondent says the news was received with great surprise by the people of Belfast, his native town. Mr. Biggar was well-known there, and even amongst those politically opposed to him was regarded las a warm-hearted and kindly man and his career as a I Belfast merchant was successful and honourable.

By the death of Mr. Biggar, says a correspondent, the parliamentary temperance party loses an ardent member. He has supported Sir Wilfrid Lawson ever since his entry into Parliament, and has shown great interest in temperance measures, especially those relating to Ire- land, though he seldom publicly advocated temperance. After the rising of the House on Wednesday evening, as the Speaker was leaving the chair, he spoke to Mr. Swift APNeil and expressed his great regret at Mr. Biggar's death, desiring him to communicate to his col- leagues his sympathy with them in the loss they had sustained. _
No inquest will be necessary, as Dr. Kenny on Wednes- day gave a certificate of death based upon his examina- tion of the deceased on the previous evening.

div.head: LIMITED.
div.p: LIMITED.

The 18th half-yearly meeting of the shareholders of Messrs. Brunner, Mond, and Co., Limited, took place at the Law Association-rooms, Cook-street, Liverpool, on Thursday. Mr. John Crosfield, chair- man of the directors, presided. The report was as follows :—" The balance sheet and profit and loss account certified by the auditors and now presented, show a balance to the credit of profit and loss account on the working of the half-year ended on the 31st December, 1889, of £120,639165. 10d., which, with the amount of £15,734 15s. id., brought forward from the previous half-year, makes a total of £138,374 lls. 11d. The directors propose to deal with the above balance as follows : s. d.

Dividend on the preference capital, at 7 per cent, per annum 11,943 15 0 Dividend on the Ordinary capital, at 30 per cent, per annum Amount to be written off patents ac- count 2,500 0 0 Amount to be placed to suspense account 13a1anc,e to be carried forward 13,805 16 11

The directors propose again to place to suspense account a sum of £20,000 towards meeting the cost of the re- modelling of a portion of the plant, which is in progress The sum of £6,500 has been written off freehold land account, in order to reduce to a reasonable figure the cost of adjoining lands which the directors have felt bound in the interest of the company to purchase during the last few months, and for which they have been com- pelled to pay fancy prices. The directors who retire by rotation are Mr. Henry Brunner, Mr. Holland, and Mr. Galloway, all of whom are eligible for re-election. The report was, on the motion of the chairman, passed unanimously. The retiring directors were re-elected, and the auditors, Messrs. T. W. Read and Co., reappointed.

div.head: CREWE MURDER.
div.p: THE CREWE MURDER.

LETTER FROM THE PRISONER RICHARD. The particular phase of the evidence in the enquiries made before the coroner and the magistrates respecting the murder of Richard Davies which created most dis- cussion was that which referred to the feeling existing between the members of the family. It was stated both by those who have known the murdered man for years in Crewe,and his neighbours at the Hough,that he tyran- nized over the whole of the family in a very harsh manner. The neighbours of the deceased at the Hough distinctly affirmed that rows were frequent, and that he had assaulted his wife. At the inquest Mrs. Davies stated with perfect composure and deliberation that the murdered man lived on good terms with the prisoners accused of his murder, and with the rest of the family, including herself. At the last hearing of the case before the county Bench Mrs. Davies was askeel the question, " On what terms was George with his father ?" and she replied. "Be was on good terms, for anything I know of." With regard to Richard, she said that he was on good terms with his father when he was at home with her at the Hough. On being asked if all the mem- bers of the family lived on good terms at the Hough, she answered rather indistinctly, and after a pause, that they had to make themselves co-nfortable, and added something to the effect that he (meaning her hus- band) was not comfortable with them. It is now hinted that previously to this Mrs. Davies had received a letter from her son Richard on this subject; but be this as it may, a letter was received by Mrs. Davies from Richard on Monday. In it he expressed his grief for the events that had taken place, and his contrition for the part lie had borne in them. He went on to urge his mother to speak without reserve upon the subject of the relations 'in which the family stood to the deceased, and made a touching appeal to her to speak the truth on the matter. The letter was of such a character that it moved the members of the family very considerably. Enquiries as to the state of the health of the widow are replied to by assertions that she is fairly well. Those who have met her say that she feels the trouble that has fallen upon her deeply, but bears it remarkably well. She states that if ' the boys had reason to dislike their father, they were free to leave his employ and make their own way. The shop in Victoria-street is still closed, and it is understood that the widow has relinquished an idea she had of still carrying on the business. The shop will therefore be let. With the power the widow has to sell a portion of the property, and thus redeem the mort- gages on the rest, it is considered that she will be able to live fairly comfortably on the income fromithe remainder, coupled with what she can obtain for the cultivation of the small farm at the Hough. Since the prisoners have been at the gaol at linutsford, it is found that Richard has become deeply impressed with the seriousness of Ws position, and is manifestly suffering acute mental pain. George shows little altera- tion, and as the prisoners are confined in separate cells and will not see each other again until they are brought to the assizes, it is very unlikely that any fresh com- munications will be made by them to the police officials. Up to the present they have not been visited by anyone on behalf of their friends, but they doubtless will be interviewed as to their defence.

div.head: ROMANTIC SUICIDE.
div.p: A ROMANTIC SUICIDE.

A sad case of suicide through grief was reported from Jersey on Monday morning. A young woman died two or three days ago, and a young man, who was engaged to her, was so affected that he has committed suicide by shooting himself through the head.

div.head: THREE MEN DROWNED.
div.p: THREE MEN DROWNED.

A Queenstown telegram says that despatches received per the Cunard steamer, Aurania, tram New York, on Saturday night, state that the second officer and three men of the British steamer Black Prince were drowned at Countzuloloos on the 29u1t., by the swamping of the ship's boat in which they were attempting to land while a heavy sea was running.
THE BOLTON WORKHOUSE SCANDAL.

At a special meeting of the Bolton Guardians, on Mon- day, in connection with the recent workhouse scandal, a letter was received from Dr. Marsh, medical officer, ten- dering his resignation, and solemnly declaring that no undue intimacy existed between him and the deceased nurse. The idea of a further inquiry must, it is under- stood, be now abandoned.

div.head: CHESS CHAMPIONSHIP MATCH.
div.p: THE CHESS CHAMPIONSHIP MATCH.

A CURIOUS TERMINATION. NEW Yortx, WEDNESDAY.—The chess match at Havana between Mr. Gunsber„., and M. Tchigorin has had an unexpected ending. Both players have won nine games and it was supposed that the twenty-fourth game, which was to have been played to-day, would determine the winner; but the Chess Club decided to declare the match a draw as it stood, and the gains was accordingly not played. The score is as under :—Twenty-three games played : Mr. Gunsberg won nine, M. Tchigorin nine, and five were drawn.

div.head: FIGHTING IN CENTRAL AFRICA. HORRIBLE MASSACRE,
div.p: FIGHTING IN CENTRAL AFRICA. HORRIBLE MASSACRE,

Native letters received from the Victoria Nyanza report that Mwanga, aided by the Europeans, has re- gained the throne of Uganda. There was severe fighting, in which King Kalema and his Arab allies were com- pletely annihilated, very few Arabs surviving the massacre which subsequently took place. During the engagement a dhew on the lake conveying a number of important Arabs and a quantity of powder and ammuni- tion was blown up, all on board being killed. Uganda is now in the hands of Mwanga and the Europeans.

div.head: -..• THE MINISTERIAL HUSH LAND BILL.
div.p: -..• THE MINISTERIAL HUSH LAND BILL.

The sum to be advanced in connection with the Irish Land Purchase Bill will not be limited to £20,000,000. The main principle embodied in the measure will, it is understood, be the same as that on which the Ashbourne Acts were based ; but the securities for the loans will be of a local character. The exact nature of the securi- ties has not yet transpired. Provisions will be included in the bill for amalgamating the Landed Estates Court, of which Mr. Justice Munroe is president, and the Land Commission into a great agrarian tribunal for the settle- ment of disputes conmected with the land. Arrange- ments will also be proposed whereby the transfer of land shall be simplified and cheapened.

MR. GLADSTONE'S GOLDEN WEDDING MEMORIAL. The parishioners of Hawarden, of both political parties, have just decided to erect as a memorial of Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone's golden wedding a handsome foun- tain opposite the main entrance to the Castle grounds. It will be triangular in shape, richly carved, and have on panels medallion portraits of Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone and the arms of the Gladstone and Glynne families. The body of the memorial is to be composed of Manley and Storeton stone, and the portraits are to be carved in Mansfield stone. The site is about the centre of the vil- lage. The members of Mr. Gladstone's family are also to commemorate the event by erecting a new main porch to the Castle, in keeping with the architectural features of the building.

div.head: ELECTION INTELLIGENCE.
div.p: ELECTION INTELLIGENCE.
Monday next has been fixed for the nomination for West Waterford, and the polling for the following Mon- day. UNIONIST CANDIDATE FOR NORTH ST. PANCRAS.

_ Mr. H. IL Graham, who fought one of the St. Pancras divisions in 1888, has been elected as the Unionist candi- date for North St. Pancras. On Tuesday afternoon a deputation from the North St. Pancras Conservatives waited upon Mr. Graham and informed him of the deci- sion, which was unanimous. This being so Mr. Graham agreed to become the candidate, in opposition to Mr. Thomas Henry Bolton, who has been adopted by the Gladstonian party. The campaign will not be com- menced until after the funefal of Lord Lamingtcn.

div.head: MID-GLAMORGAN ELECTION.
div.p: MID-GLAMORGAN ELECTION.

Mr. Samuel Thomas Evans, Ravensworth, Neath, Radical, was the only candidate on Thursday nominated at Neath for the vacancy in the representation of Mid- Glamorgan, caused by the death of Mr. C. R. M. Talbot, the late father of the House of Commons. Subsequently Mr. Evans was declared duly elected. The new mem- ber is a solicitor by profession, waseducated at Aberyst- with University, is first B.A. London, and a fluent speaker in Welsh and English. His election has been hailed with delight throughout the principality.

div.head: EMIN PASHA'S FUTURE.
div.p: EMIN PASHA'S FUTURE.

A Berlin correspondent states that Emin l'asha has wired to his friends that he does not approve of the sub- scriptions which some newspapers propose to raise on his behalf, and he totally objects to the sensatiou.st articles which have lately been published in Germany with a view of creating ill-feeling between .iiiinself and Mr. Stanley. Whether he'remains in Europe dr goes back to the equatorial regions depends, first, on his health, and,.secondly, on an Understanding to be con- cluded between Germany and England, without which it is impossible for him to think of regaining his former influence with the African natives. '

div.head: DEATH OF COUNT ANDILASSY.
div.p: DEATH OF COUNT ANDILASSY.

A telegram from Vienna, dated Wednesday night says —Count Julius Anarassy, late Austro-Hengarian Minister of Foreign Affairs, died at.Voloica. in Istila, on Tuesday morning after a very painful illness. M. Tioza announced on Tuesday that the Government intended to bring in a Bill authorising the erection of a monument to the late statesman, in recognition 9f his services to the Throne and country. VIENNA,,WEDNESDAY NIGHT.—The Emperor ha .4 written a letter of condolence to Countess Andrassy in the most sympathetic terms. The body of the deceased states- man will arrive at Pesth from Volosca at 11 to-morrow morning, and the great entrance hall of the Academy of Sciences is being beautifully decorated with palms and ferns for the reception of the body, which will lie in state for one day, and be shown to the general public. On Friday the funeral takes place, and the body will be con- veyed to Terebes.

div.head: EXCITING SCENES AT A FIRE. Two PERSONS KILLED. _
div.p: EXCITING SCENES AT A FIRE. Two PERSONS KILLED. _

A fatal and destructive fire raged for over an hour and a half, on Tuesday morning, on the premises of Messrs. Gay, Armstrong, and Company, fur and skin merchants, Felix-st., Westminster Bridge-road. As an engine was hastening to the scene, an old wonian, attempting to cross the road, ran directly in front of it, with the result that she was knocked down the wheels passing over her, severing her head from her body. She was taken to St. Thomas's Hospital, but has not yet been identified. Dur- ing the progress of the fire, a fireman named Sydney A. Crowe, twenty-five years of age, who had only been five months in the service, was knocked down by a falling beam and instantly killed, while another fireman named J. W. Hansell was severely injured. They were conveyed on stretchers to St. Thomas's Hospital. Several exciting scenes were witnessed during the removal of the persons in the houses immediately adjoining the burning build- ing. The fire was finally subdued about three o'clock, not, however, until it had consumed Messrs. Gay and Armstrong's property, the damage being estimated at £lO,OOO. The cause of the fire is unknown.

div.head: CHARGE OF SHOOTING A LONDON
div.p: THE CHARGE OF SHOOTING A LONDON
M.P.

On Wednesday, at the Richmond Police Court, Eliza- beth Vincent, a young lady, twenty-two years of age, was brought up on remand, charged with having at- tempted to feloniously kill and murder Lewis Henry Isaacs, by shooting him at 110, Church-road, Richmond, on October 8, 1889. When the case was adjourned on the former hearing, the Bench suggested that the pri- soner should obtain legal assistance. Accordingly, on Wednesday Mr. Duerdin Dutton defended, and Mr. St. John Wontner again appeared for the prosecutor, who is M.P. for Walworth. Mr. Ragge Price presided over a full bench of magistrates. The public interest in the 'lease was shown by a thronged court, and the arrival of the prisoner, who is A young woman of very prepos- sessing appearance, from Holloway: Gaol, was witnessed by a large crowd, who had assembled in the streets.— major Isaacs, re-called, produced the document spoken of at the former hearing, from which a piece had been torn. He saw by this document that it was not £lO,OOO but £20,000 that the prisoner demanded. The age of the prisoner had been stated at twenty-two, but she had completed her twenty-seventh year.—Cross-examined by Mr. Dutton 1. He asked the prisoner whether any other persons were in the house, and she said the person re- ferred to was in the country.—Do you undertake to say on your honour as a gentleman that the pistol did not go off accidentally 2—No, I cannot say that.—Did she not say that if you did not sign the document she would shoot herself and make the whole thing public ?—Yes, I think she said that.—You naturally objected to her hav- ing a document in her posgession with your signa- ture ?—Yes; she had one already before I went there.— Mr. Matthias Noot, surgeon, 8, Kensington Park-road, was called, and described the injuries which Major Isaacs sustained by the pistol shot. He found a wound on the right arm, which had the appearance of a gun- shot wound. He took Major Isaacs home from his sur- gery, and had since attended him with Sir William McCormack. The bullet was still embedded in the upper third of the arm.—The Chairman then read over the formal charge to the prisoner.—Mr. Dutton : Pri- soner reserves her defence.—The Chairman: You will be committed to take your trial at the Central Criminal Court on March 3rd.

div.head: LABOUR AND CAPITAL
div.p: LABOUR AND CAPITAL

The West Lancashire Coalowners' Association on Tues- day resolved to inform the miners that "the state of trade does not warrant any further advance" in wages. At a meeting of Welsh coal-owners on Tuesday, at Chester, it was decided that a scheme of federation was necessary, and the announcement was made that colliery proprietors representing an output of eighty million tons were prepared to join such an organisations. MINERS' WAGES IN LANCASEIIRE.

The members of the West Lancashire Coalowners' Asso- ciation met in Manchester on Tuesday, in response to a letter from the miners' representatives, to consider the demand for an advance of 10 per cent, in wages. A resolution was passed declaring that the state of trade does not at present warrant any further advance in ' wages. The coalowners in the Manchester district have individually informed their men .that until there is al further advance in price they cannot entertain any appli- cation for an advance in wages. PROTECTION FOR SAILORS. A deputation representing a large number of British seamen waited upon the president of the Board of Trade on Tuesday with a view to obtain the support of the Government to the Load-line Bill. Sir W. Harcourt introduced the deputation, and Mr. S. Plimsoll was one of the speakers. Sir M. Hicks-Beach, in reply, did not deny that there was loss of life through over-loading, but said the question to ask was, "Is our legislation defective ?' He did not think it was so defective as stated. He believed in a compulsory load-line, and was disposed to support the second reading of the bill; still he did not think they could quite ignore the foreign difficulty. Sir W. Harceurt's suggestion that the Govern- ment should take up the bill would be considered, but he could not say more. RETIREMENT OF MR. BROADFIURST. Mr. Broadhurst, M.P., secretary to the Trades Union Congress Parliamentary Committee, has audressed a letter to the chairman of the committee announcing his intention to retire from the secretaryship at the end of the congress year. " The cause of my retirement," Mr. Broadhurst writes, "is the inroad made by chronic disease during the last two years into what was formerly a robust constitution, and which necessitates the careful husbanding of my strength. I am glad to inform the trades that during the 15 years I have acted as secretary to the committee I have never been more in harmony with my collegues than at present. I hope and believe that we are only on the threshold of new and great advances in the position of labour. I am confident that the congress has a great future before it, and that the trades will wisely guide its policy to successful issues." THE EIGHT HOURS QUESTION.—IMPORTANT

div.head: DEPUTATIONS.
div.p: DEPUTATIONS.

A deputation, pr;:e—tie:scli-frOM—the miners of the United Kingdom, waited upon Lord Randolph Churchill and Lord Dunraven on Tuesday to obtain their support to the Eight Hours Bill for miners. Lord Dunraven was in sympathy with the miners, and did not see why, under certain circumstances, the State should not inter- fere to regulate the hours of labour. Lord R. Churchill expressed surprise that the Home Secretary had taken up the position that the Legislature would be unlikely to place restrictions on adult labour. He did not attach much importance to Mr. Matthews's prophecies, and thought it extremely likely that the Home Secretary spoke without previous consultation with his colleagues. So far as he was concerned, hs saw nothing at present to warrant opposition to the unanimous demand of the representatives of labour. The deputation afterwards waited upon Mr. Gladstone, who was convinced that eight hours was a reasonable limit for underground labour. But the question was—how was that limit to be I attained? There were in deciding this question two points needing consideration. The miners should first take the case of a collier who wished to work more than eight hours, and then consider how the eight hours limit would affect his own and other trades. It was a subject 1 he reserved for careful consideration, while remaining free to act in the way his judgment and sense of right dictated. Mr. John Morley, M.P., replying to a Belfast corres- pondent who wrote respecting the Eight Hours Bill and other questions, says he is obligaffor the letter, though he scarcely agrees with a single word of it. His corres- pondent opens up questions which it would taken. treatise to deal with. He adds "So far as the eight hours proposal is concerned, you appear to wish to force restriction upon workers whether they like it or not. That is not my notion of liberty.

SATURDAY. FEBRUARY 22, 1890.

The LAST night a Town's Meeting was held 'Waterworks in the Public Hall to take into comsider- Purchase' tion the Warrington Extension, Water, and Improvement Bill. There was a fair attend- ance; and considerable ground was covered in the 4..15cu55i0n which :ensued, but it was evident that

the ratepayers are not as yet in a position to aPprove the Bill. It was, therefore, wisely resolved to adjourn the meeting until Monday week. It is quite natural and advisable that the minds of the ratepayers of Warrington should be exercised • upon such a large transaction as the proposal to Purchase the property of the Warrington Water Works Company. The subject is one which has fr°lll time to time for many years been before the community, and the opinion may be said to be universal that it is desirable that the Works should become the property of the town, if they can be acquired upon reasonable terms. The question is --what are reasonable terms? and upon this Point there isnecessarily some diversity of opinion. ~, BeeMS to be the view of a number of the rate- Payers that the Corporation will be acting un- Wisely, if they purchase the Works upon any terms „. Which will result, even temporarily, in an aildi- 'aM, however small, to the rates of the borough. tut this is surely a narrow view to take of the in- terests of the town. Everything has its price; if a thing is worth having it is worth paying for; and to Pay for a thing involves, as a rule, some sacri- , ace---a sacrifice which should be proportionate to, arid not beyond, the gain to be ultimately Obtained. It is unreasonable, as it seems to s to contend, as some ratepayers do, that the Water Works ought not ta be purchased if the tratisaetion will add anything to the rates. It caight to be sufficient to show that the burden will be light, and that, in a few years, there will be no burden at all, whilst the inhabitants will be paying tfr the money they have borrowed out of the profits ef the undertakiag. This was done in the case of the Purchase of the Gas Works; and we believe it can be done in the purchase of the Water Works. Mr. .1. L. TUNSTILL has prepared an able and ex- haustive financial report which we print in another e°lunio, and from which it will be seen that it is Possible to give the Company thirty years' purchase of the maximum annual dividends, and arrange for b tu.l.°lving and repaying the capital sum upon such sarais that "the greatest possible risk" would /,:r43 an increase upon the rates of 31d. in the pound. he reader must not, however, jump to the colt- that the increase will be one of 3d.; for the amount will necessarily be less, if, in the first Itlace, the Parliamentary Committee extends the ifule of repayment beyond 60 years; or, secondly the Sinking Fund be suspended for two or three 3:eara ; or, thirdly, if the revenue from the sale of ter should continue to grow as it has grown dur- -I,llg the past three years. The bringing into :Peration of any one of these factors would reduce the rate below aid. in the pound, while the concur- , Operation of all three would mean that the pur- :"aae would be effected without an addition to the sates of as much as a farthing in the pound. We are rring now solely to the financial side of the ya'ntletfiti°n ; but we are fully aware that there are 15-eg important matters to take into account as the frr°Bl3ects of a large and unfailing supply of water °lll the present sources; the condition of mains ;nail other working plant; and the nature and ne,With a view to their future application, of the TrPowers which the Corporation would acquire. bas are all considerations which the ratepayers Zaire to take into account, and as to which full „ reliable information should be given, if the vroPe. tr yis a good property, as we believe it to be, Will gain in repute rather than lose by searching 'aqui (1,1 rY• The Water Works Company have un- tie6tionably made a largo sum of money out of ,growth of Warrington. They have been in a ixieraitio‘o to appropriate what is called "unearned einent and it is because we think this incre- : ba-Tut shou'ld for the future be secured by the Alabitauts—the real earners—that we earnestly eate the acquirement of the Water Works 111)°n t ernis which will be fair alike to the Company t 4) the Corporation.

nal THE debate on Mr. PARNELL B l'tunriByin amendment to the Address which a- condemned the administration of oh —oYernlTlent in Ireland was brought .b a close, defellliesdaY night, when the amendment was tha aird by a majority of 67. It is significant Biob"he Majority is so small, in view of the divi- of h eing taken so soon after the publication e report of the Parnell Commission. Mr. ie4lna may boast of the success of coercion teeirlitrlisd Lilmt it is evident that some of the l have o once supported the Government ha their misgivings ; and, further, that they ye next an eye to what is likely to happen at the scli e'ecti°a• The Tann SECRETARY showed him- ' a 8 usual' cynical and self--conceited in the 1-413,1e,ebeh Which he made on Tuesday night. He tiorrad to scorn the idea that the better condi- nf Ireland to-clay was in any degree rermuta.ble to what he contemptuously tv,,el:l'ed to as "the union of hearts" be- the people of Ireland and of England. nil,,aad was certainly more tranquil, but this was ad -.wing to the Coercian Act, and its resolute 4111istration by the "brave Mr. BALFOUR !" tnaY be asked, if the people of the sister isle pe. -,,iv48-T.1131y ceased to e mischievous because their or L mislaid is crippled, is it nOt folly, is it ao rnaci - they d nes; for the Government to propose, as °l3l'opose, to yut weapons of resistance and 'r6BBioxv in their lands by extending local self-
government F Mr. BALFOUR, it seems to us, is playing a game, and it does not suit him to aeknow-
lodge that the game is going against him. He knows, just as every other politician knows, that Ireland has been more influenced for good by Mr.

GLADSTONE'S adhesion to the cause of Home Rule than by all the Coercion Acts that - were ever placed upon the Statute Book. If things were going quite as well as the Irish Secretary would have the Tories believe, we may be sure that there would be less of that all-prevailing dread of a dissolution which at the present moment governs every action of the Tory / arty. Mr. JOHN MORLEY, who spoke immediately before the divi- sion was taken, completely riddled the Irish Secretary with argumentative shot and shell. He quoted from a speech made by Mr. Bsiroun, in which he said that the conduct of Mr. GLADSTONE was" disgraceful" for "attempting to rouse the working classes of England and of Scotland by telling them that the rights which they enjoyed on this side of St. George's Channel are denied to their brothers on the other side?" " But," con- tinued Mr. Montsy, "What did the Home Secre- tary say to-night ? He said in words, in reply to my right hon. friend the member for the Stirling Burghs, We could not do this or that in con- nection with the dockers' strike.' Why? 'Be- cause the statutory enactments protect and guard trade combinations which do not protect and guard agrarian combinations.' (Loud opposition cheers.) Why, that is the very thing we have been saying, and it was for saying that very thing that the Chief Secretary attacked Mr. GLADSTONE for disgraceful conduct. (Opposition cheers.)" Touch- ing the use which the Irish Secretary made of his stock-in-trade, the inflammatory language of ' United Ireland," Mr. MORLEY reminded the House, amid lusty cheers, of what by way of con- trast, the "Times " had published. He said : There is nothing in " United Ireland "in its most exasperated moments comparable in enormity with the charge brought by your own ally and confeder- ate—(loud and prolonged Opposition cheers)— against colleagues -of your own—(cheers, and a Voice on the Ministerial side : I.ot . colleagues of ours.) Are they not your colleagues? Then turn them out of the House. (Great Opposition cheers.) There is nothing so vile as what was done by your ally and confederate in the press, which charges your colleagues with meeting at a railway station, and there, a mouth before the Phcenix Park murder, deliberately niaking themselves participants in the plot which ended in that murder. (Loud Opposit'on cheers.)

Mr. MORLEY had yet another knock down blow for Mr. BALFOUR ; for, with reference to jury pack- ing, he convicted him of quoting Mr. CROMPTON. Q.C., as giving unqualified testimony to the manner in which the judge performed his duty and the jury discharged theirs, when, as a matter of fact, Mr. CROMPTON had said something which was in effect exactly the reverse. In a letter on the subject the English Q.C. remarks :—" I said noth- ing in favour of the way in which the prosecution was conducted on the part of the Crown. On the contrary, I denounced the way in which the jury was packed. (Opposition cheers.) The result of what I say is that a trial by jury so selected can- not be called trial by jury at all, but rather a trial by 12 men selected by the Crown, and presided over by a judge of the Superior Court." And yet this is the sort of administration of the law upon which the Irish Secretary prides himself, and with regard to which Englishmen and Irishmen are expected to" Rest and be thankful." But not so. There is a feeling in men's hearts which is deeper than cynicism ;it is the love of justice. That feeling has been stirred—it has been aroused—and it will not be satisfied until Ireland is free from end to end from Balfourism and all its works.
Cardinal h has been interesting to observe Manning how the proposal of the EMPEROR of

Germany to hold an international , Conference on the labour question has been re- ceived in various quarters. It has been treated on the one hand as a mere electioneering move to secure the vote of German Socialists; and on the other as a sincere and honest endeavour to alleviate the lot of the working-classes. It may be that both motives have operated in causing the EMPEROR WILLIAM to issue his Rescripts, and it is no discredit to him if, like ordinary mortals, he has acted from mixed motives. But, why concern ourselves with the motives; for has it not been said that, if motives were always visible, men would of ten blush for their most brilliant actions ? The main point is—ls it worth while to hold such a conference? We are strongly of opinion that it. is a step in the right direction. It is hardly possible harm can come of it, and it is just possible that much good may be done. Cardinal MANNING, who has had a large experience in work big amongst the poorest of the poor, is emphatically in favour of the holding of an International Con- ference. In a letter to the editor of the "Deutsche Revue," he says :

You ask me what I think of the invitation of the Emperor of Germany to the European Powers to meet in conference on the subject of labour, and the state of the millions in every country who live by the wages of labour. I think this Imperial act the wisest and the worthiest that has proceeded from any Sovereign of our times. The condition of the wage-earning people of every European country is a grave danger to every European State. The hours of labour, the employment of women and children, the scantiness of wage, the uncertainties of employ- ment, the fierce competition fostered by modern political economy, the destruction of domestic life resulting from all these and other kindred causes have rendered it impossible for men to live a human life. How can a man who works fifteen or sixteen hours a day live the life of a father to his children? tlow can a woman who is absent from home all day long do the. duties of a mother? Domestic life is impossible. But on the domestic life of the people the whole political order of human society reposes. If the foundation be ruined, what will become of the superstructure? The Emperor William has, therefore, shown himself to be a true and far- sighted statesman.

We have given the Cardinal's expression of opinion in full, because we regard it as an important pro- nouncement upon an important subject. It may be that the German Emperor, like many a man before him, will find that it is one thing to sympa- thise with suffering humanity in the struggle for existence, and quite another to find a remedy that will do good without doing mischief. But it is something to make the attempt; mid if monarchs and statesmen can, along with the toiling millions, set their hearts and minds upon improving the lot of the lowly, it will be strange indeed if no- thing good should come of it. Why should it not be possible to take into considera- tion, at an international conference, how far great standing armies—war, and the preparation for war—drain the life-blood of communities ? It will not be denied that, if each of the standing armies of Europe could, by international arrange- ment, be reduc,Hl one half it would be means directly and indirectly of benefiting the workers by lessening the burden of taxation. It may be in the nature of a dream, but we are hopeful of a time when the soldiers of the world will be the peace-preservers of the 'world—an inteniational police, so to speak; swortv-Ao-eariy—aut-the man- dates of International Councils, and thus render resistance as impossible as is, broadly speaking, resistance to the police force of a community.

/ But it is more immediately with the hours of labour and the conditions of labour that the proposed conference will concern itself ; and, if its representatives go to work in a business- like manner, it must result, to say the least of it, in a mass of information being collected which will be of value to the workers themselves. So far as we can perceive, our continental competi- tors—Germany not excepted—have longer hours of work, and pay less for work, than on the whole is the rule in this country. There must be a cause or causes for this, and it is especially in the interest of foreign workers that these causes should be ascertained in order that they may profit by applying a remedy. English workmen are also interested in the issue ; for if they can bring their continental brethren more nearly into line with themselves, there will be good ground for hoping that the movement which is now being made for further reducing the hours of labour will be ulti- mately successful: For ourselves, we hail all intentational effort as making for rightebusness and peace ; it is in the direction of that longed- for era of which the inspired ploughman sings :
When man to man the world o'er. Shall brothere be for a' that.
" MUM AND GO."
The death rate for Warrington for the week, ending February 19th, was very large ; it was equal to 37 per 1,000.

Captain O'Shea has succeeded in his motion for attachment against the "Freeman's Journal"; hut has failed in his proceedings for attachment against the " Star " and the "New York Herald." It remains now to be seen whether he will succeed in his motion for de-tachment—from Mrs. O'Shea.

Ernest Benzon, the Jubilee Plunger, after squandering £250,000 in a couple of years, is sent to goal, for three months, for obtaining money under false pretences. What a commentary on a fast and foolish life !
The gods are just, and of our pleasant Twee Make instruments to scourge us.

Victor Meyer, a German professor, says :—" We may reasonably hope that chemistry will teach us to make the fibre of wood a source of human food:' This is encouraging. Wonder what form the food will take F Will it come in the shape of " sycamore " sandwiches, " poplar " puddings, or " deal " dumplings?

_ Shrove Tuesday is still observed as a day of holiday—and pancakes; but there are few, except amongst the Roman Catholics, who associate the day and its name—the day when, in olden times, the people were shriven of their sins, prior to mak- ing merry and eating fritters.

The special attention to eating on Shrove Tues- day was by way, we suppose, of preparing for the first 4ay of Lent, which, commences on the day following— Ash Wednesday. The " Ash " comes from the custom, instituted in the sixth century, of sprinkling ashes on the forehead, and tracing the form of a cross in them. Parliament still takes some note of Ash Wednesday ; it commences busi- ness an hour or two later. Pity that some of the members cannot be made to appear in sackcloth and ashes, for there is no denying that they are sinful souls.

The principal resolution to be submitted to the conference to he held OA the sth inst., at the Na- tional Liberal Club, declares—" That the time has now arrived when the people of Scotland and Wales should be entrusted with the management of their own affairs, still preserving the supremacy of the Imperial Parliament." We are getting ox ; it can he said of the world? PA in gralileo's days, that "it moves,"

Lord Randolph Churchill's Liquor 13i11 will serve to keep his lordship in evidence ; but it is not at all likely that it will find its way on the statute book. I{e is simply a private member now ; and a private member is very small beer in this matter of dealing with the nation's drink. As for the present Govern- ment, they are not likely to touch the question again. They are still staggered by the memory of their huge failure in trying to perpetrate a fraud upon the country.

The Emperor William is "going it" on the labour question. The Minister of War, carrying out the views of his master, is about to give orders for the erection of model dwellings for the work- men engaged on military works at Spandau. It is estimated that the expenditure will amount to 13 million marks. 'the saddlers who were about to go on strike have had their case inquired into, and they are to have an increase of wages. The new broom ie so far sweeping clean.

--- •The German Emperor is not to be left alone in his rdory as a Reformer: for his Imperial brother of China is also "on the job." He is said to be overhauling every department of the State, and has issued a Rescript in which he gives a broad hint to the official chiefs who "only visit their offices once in several months." Kuang Tsu is wakening everybody up, and has given the Peking owners of opium and gambling dens such a fright that they have shut up shop, Bravo Kuang Tau

There was something new at the gathering at St. Barnabas' School, Warrington.on Monday evening; there was" harmony." The entertainment in ad of the fund for wiping off the school debt was very successful, and it is to be followed by other efforts. Now that things are getting ship-shape, it is to be hoped the managers, who have shaken off the shackles, will be well supported by gifts for the bazaar which is about to be held with the object of removing the burden upon the school.

The Warrington Amateur Photographic Society are to be congratulated on the progress they have made in the three years of their ex:stence. The exhibition of lantern slides, given on Tuesday evening, afforded abundant evidence of a develop- ment amongst the members of the artistic faculty. Composition and perspective are being studied with good effect. It is worthy of mention that, although the slides embraced many scenes of interest in Great Britain, one of the prettiest pictures was a view of the high road not far from Thelwall village.

The miners seem to be making headway with their agitation for Parliamentary limitation of the hours of work to eight per day. Two prominent Torins—Lord R. Churchill and Lord Dunraven— have "tumbled to" the proposal in the easiest fashion. Mr. Gladstone shows himself more cau- tious; he doubts whether Parliament would be justified in prohibiting a man—for that is what it comes to—from working more than eight hours, if he wished to do so. He makes it clear, however, that he thinks eight hours is quite long enough for work underground. •

Mr. Robert Davies sings the praises of his client, Sir Gilbert Greenall, in the very best style' and it is to be hoped he will be well paid for it. But he was altogether too modest at St. Paul's tea party, on Tuesday evening, in speaking of himself as a mere "substitute for a better man." If Mr. Davies liad Sir Gilbert's brass, along with his own brains, we are quite sure that he would give every- thing that is good in Warrington such a helping along as would be felt for a generation.

Take, for instance, the remark Mr. Davies made that, "although they might differ in name, and some go to church and others to chapel, he thought they might regard their England as an example to the world for the: attempts which were made in it to do good to all classes, especially in the way of religious education." Such an observatior reveals a broad mind; and is diametrically opposEd to the narrowness which Sir Gilbert Greenall exhibited in confining the Jubilee Gift, of which we have heard so much, to a single sect in the town. 4 gift to the town should be above sects and parties.

The mo-nt-1;lir--oneeting. w.a...S held on Wednesday under the presidency of the Vicar. Present : Messrs. W. Handley, W. Hankinson, J. Pritchard, and J. D. Jones (librarian.) It was reported that during the past month, there had been 2,260 volumes isSued from the library, of which 1,719 were fiction. Twenty-one volumes had also byen consulted in the reference department. A number of books had been presented. ST. PAUL'S SUNDAY SCHOOL, WIDNES. A miscellaneous entertainment, arranged by Mr. T. div.p: BRPOOL BOUNDARIES BILL.

As the result of a poll of the citizens of Liverpool on the question of the extension of the municipal boundaries, it was found that about 33,000 votes have been recorded in favour of the bill which the Corporation are promoting, and 0,880 against. The bill proposes to make the municipal boundaries co- terminous with the Parliamentary limits.

ACCIDENT AT NORTON About noon on Wednesday a singular accident happened at Norton on the Ship Canal Works. A valuable horse belonging to Sir Richard Brooke, of Norton Priory, was engaged in drawing timber in the plantation adjoining the temporary railway, when, in consequence of an engine and a number of heavily-laden trucks passing, the animal became affrighted. and, although held by a son of Mr. Fergusson, darted in front of the engine, and was cut to pieces. The' lad had a vsry narrow escape, and is to be complimented on the manner in which he clung to the horse, with the object of preventing it from rushing on the line..

Since last Sunday week the Dean of Bangor has been lying seriously ill at the residence of Col. Geo. ifcCorquodale J.P., the Willows, Newton. On the night of the day named the rev, gentleman was preaching in St. Peters' Church, Newton, when he was noticed to be unwell. His,remarks came to an abrupt termination, and the preacher retired to the vestry. It was found that, his indisposition was so serious that he was removed to the Willows, which adjoins the church,and he was attended by Dr. J. W. Watkins, of Newton. He has since been under that gentleman's care and attention, and on Wednesday afternoon last he was reported to be much better and unless there was a relapse the Dean would probably be removed to Bangor in a few days. A RUNCORN DOCTOR AND HIS DOG.

Mr. Bartholomew Mangan, M.D., of Church-st., was summoned before the Runcorn magistrates, on Monday, to answer a charge of allowing his dog to be at large, unniuzzled. The doctor sent a boy to court with a letter, in which he practically admitted the offence, but the Chairman (Mr. Brundrit) announced th it the case would be adjourned for a week, and if Dr. Mangan did not then appear a warrant would be issued to compel him to do so. Mr. Brundrit said no distinction could be made between a doctor and other defendants at that court.—ln regard to the muzzling order, the Bench fined a chemical labourer from Weston, named Joseph Frod- sham, in tho sum of ed. and costs, for permitting his dog to be at large. div.head: BREAKING A WOMAN'S LEO AT WIDNES.
div.p: BREAKING A WOMAN'S LEO AT WIDNES.

At Widnes Police Court. on Monday, J'A-i; Conlan, Pear-St., was charged with causing grievious bodily harm to Catherine Simpson, a married woman. From the statement made by Inspector Keighley, it appeared that on Saturday night the parties were in the Royal Hotel, Hutchinson-st., together with another woman named Mrs. Potter. Whilst standing at the bar, they entered into a heated conversation, and the prisoner, it was alleged, deliberately took hold of Mrs. Simpson by the shoulders, and pushed her down. On those present assisting her to rise, it was found that her leg was broken.—Dr. Hutchinson said direct violence, by a kick or a blow, most have been used to break the limb. The woman would not be able to come out of doors for at least a month—The prisoner said h neither gave her a kick, or a blow.—On the application of Inspector Keighley, the prisoner was remanded for a week, but he was liberated on bail, himself in £4O, and two sureties of £2O each.

DESERTING A BLIND WIFE AT WIDNES. There was brought before the Widnes magistrates, on Monday, a chemical labourer, named John McCormack, of North-st., who was called upon to answer a charge of deserting his wife. Mt. .1. Treacy, the relieving officer, deposed that the woman was suffering from blindness, and was unable to maintain herself. She had been chargeable to the Union since the Bth of October last, and the cost of her maintenance had been £35 12s. ed. The prisoner, who had not been in regular employment for years, had been out of the town, and had not at- tempted to communicate, either w ith his wife, or the Guardians.—The prisoner said he had been working at a Jarrow chemical works, and had earned 28s. per Week. —lnspector Keighley informed the Bench that the pri- soner had been 18 times previously before the court, on charges of drunkenness, assaults, and other offences, and had served two terms, of three months each, in gaol. He was now sentenced to three weeks' hard labour._

FROFITADIE FOWL KEEPING AT WIDNES.

There are various opinions held as to the profit or loss attending the keeping of fowl. and the subject a few years ago was dealt with in a series of special articles in this journal. It is generally conceeded that the fowl keeper must haves good" run" for his hens, if success is to a tend his efforts, but a Widnes tradesman has just achieved a remarkable success without this adjunct. Mr. Rose, stationer and tobacconist, Victoria-st., is the possessor of nine hens and a e,ock,which roost in an ordin- ary wooden cote in the yard of his own house, and go scratching in the back passages of the houses. During the two months commencing the 14th December and ending 14th February the fowl have laid no less than 209 eggs a remarkable record for the winter months as eggs for the greater part of the time were selling at 2i each, and the hens did not cost more than 10d per week to feed, it is plain that Mr. Rose has found lien keeping very profitable indeed. The fowls are hardy cross-bred birds.

COAL CONTRACTS AND COLLDIRY ACCIDENT:S. At the St. Helens County Court, on Wednesday, before Judge Butler, an action was brought by James Withing- ton, Hyde, Platt-lane Colliery, Wigan, against Mort, Liddell, and Co., chemical manufacturers, Widnes, to recover £32 19s. 9d. for coal slack sold and delivered according to contract, and the defendants made a counter-claim for £134 6s. Bd. for alleged breach of con- tract. Mr. Mulholland, instructed by Mr. John S. Hopwood. solicitor, Wigan, appeared for the plaintiff; and Mr. Pugh, instructed by Mr. Seddon B. Smith, of Liverpool, appeared for the defendants. The case for the plaintiff was that in May last the plaintiff entered into a contract with the defendants to supply 200 tons per week of Platt-lane Colliery slack. In the following month (June) plaintiff began to send the slack,but found that he could not supply Flatt-lane because of a fall of roof and flooding in the mine but he sent Garswood hall slack instead. A correspondence ensued between the parties, the defendants insisting upon the kind of slack stipulated,and the plaintiff replying that as the colliery was r ,t working he could not do so, but would send the other kind. It was contended that a clause in the con- tract known as the " strike" clause released him from strict fulfilment of his engagement because it included such accidents as had happened. Mr. Pugh, on behalf of the defendants, urged in. support of the counterclaim that the" strike "clause could net apply to such a con- tract unless there was some dispute between masters and men, or unless it was extended to include a" stop- page "or an " accident" clause. After a lengthy hear- ing his Honour reserved judgment, which lie stated, would be given in the Liverpool County Court.

div.head: FATAL FALL AT EARLESTOWN.
div.p: FATAL FALL AT EARLESTOWN.

_ On Monday. Mr. W. T. Husband, the deputy. coroner, held an inquest at the New Market Inn, Earlestown, touching the death of Wm. Woods, years of age, of 24, Derby-st., who died early on the previous Friday mornirig, from injuries received on ithe Thursday. The deceased was engaged in tarring the roof of some back pre nises near the shop of Mr. Samuel Carrington, baker, Earle-st., when a young man named Joseph Keswick saw him fall back- wards,slip from the roof, and drop a distance of 14 feet to the ground. An alarm was given and Mr. Carrington, Keswick, and another man named Sedgwick found Woods lying unconscious on his back. He was carried into Carrington's house, where Dr. Paterson. was called. It was stated that . .

no bones were broken. but he was seriously suffer- ing from the shock he had received. The unfortu- nate man was removed home in a trap, and was subsequently attended by Dr. Overton, assistant to Dr. Watkins. The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death." div.head: RUNCORN MUSICAL SOCIETY.
div.p: RUNCORN MUSICAL SOCIETY.

The second qoncert of the season was given in the Drill Hall, Oreenway-road. on Moiplay evening, be- fore a large, and fashionable assemblage. The first part, of the programme consisted of " The Rose Maiden," a cantata adapted from the German, and set to music of considerable beauty by Frederick . Cowen. The ,numerous choreseS ,in the Composition afforded full scope for the display of the ability of the choir, which was about 120 voices strong. The different' parts w(re fairly well balanced, and their work was distinguished by precision, power, and harmony, the whole performance of the choir being of a highly finished and artistic character. The " Bridal Chorus" quite took the audience by.storrq, and by a repetition of the gem only c-uld the enthusiastic applause be silenced. The principals were ..Miss Fanny, Boutlieur (soprano), Miss Frances Haskoll.(contralto), Mr. Leyman Jackson (tenor), Mr. Eaton Batty (baritone) ; and with the ex- ception of Miss Haskell are vocalists well known to Runcorn audiences. Miss Bouffieur was in capital voice and sang the music put down to the part of Roseblossom with much success. Her, best effort was undoubtedly " illoomon my roses," which was rendered with charming effect. MIA Haskoll, Who'is possessed of a voice of very wide rangeonade a faVoUrable impression by her artistic method and power of expression. Mr. Jackson was scarcely in his best form. His voice had all its customary clearness of tone, but his enunciation was' rather indis- tinct, and detracted somewhat from his vocalisation. The powerful voice "of Mr. Batty was heard to consider- all!e advantage; and hearty applause was accorded for his rendering df " Where the gloomy pine trees rustle." , The orchestral score of the cantata is difficult of execution, 1 but the band of over '3O instrumentalists, under the leadership of Mf. F. Duncanson, proved fully equal to , the task, and throughout the concert their performances were a rich mu,ical treat. The second part of the pro- gramme was as follows :—Overture "Poet and Peasant," Sttyq4 ; 010 and chorus" Nazareth," solo—Mr. Eaton Batty, Golino4 ; vocal! waltz " II Racio," Miss Fanny Bouffieur, Arditi ; selection (by desire) " Pirates of Penzance." Sullivan ; song "Alas those Chimes," (Vraritaim) Miss Frances Haskoll. Wallace ;song " Death of Nelson," Mr. FermoUr Jackson, Brake's; finale festival arrangement of the " National Anthem," Princi- pals,- Orchestra 'and' Chorus, Costa. Mr. E. Wynne I Humphreys officiated as conductor with his accustomed skill, and to his efforts the success of the concert was in a large measure due.

TEE ALLEGED LNTIMIDATION AT CREWE. Sir Richard Moon presided on Thursday at the half- yearly meeting of the London and North-Western Rail- way Company. Mr. Tomkinson, Liberal candidate for the Eddisbury Division, moved the desirability of a p 1 tic inquiry into the charges of dismissing and intimi- dating workmen at Crewe. A prolonged discussion ensued, the Chairman totally denying the charges. The motion was ultimately rejected by 73 to 39 votes. A motion by Mr. Schwann, M.P., to post a notice at Crewe works declaring non-interference in political matters with the employes was also lost. - -

• DEATH OF MR. JOHN LOVELL. Mr. John Lovell, manager and editor of the "Liver- pool Mercury," died somewhat suddenly on Thursday . morning. Mr. Lovell had been unwell for some weeks past, but no serious apprehensions had been entertained regarding him. He was appointed manager of the Press Association at its inception in 1869. and ten years later was appointed managing editor of the" Liverpool Mercury." The cause of death is attributed to the effects of an attack of Russian influenza. He was 54 years of age. In addition to contributing largely to periodical literature, Mr. Lovell had translated and edited the "Nouveau Robinson Suisse" of Slahl.
THE TERRIBLE MINE EXPLOSION. IN _FRANCE.

..... --- NEVERS, THERSDAV.—Up to this morning thirty-eight dead bodies and thirteen injured miners have been re- covered from the colliery near Decize, where the terrible accident occurred on :Tuesday evening. Five of the injured expired almost immediately they were brought up. An inquiry has been opened into ths causes of the disaster, but the result is not set known. It is believed, however, to have been due to an explosion of fire-damp. AU the authorities are at the pit.

FRODSHAM V. BIRKENHEAD WANDERERS.—TheSC clubs met at Frodsham on Saturday in wet weather, The visitors kicked off, and in the first half Frodsham obtained 1 try and 1 minor to the visitors a minor. The try was obtained by Rogers from a capital run from the centre, and it was disappointing that the attempt at goal failed. Nothing was added in the second half, although some fine play was noticed on behalf of both teams. The pick of the players for Frodsham were Webb, Clough, and Lightfoot, whilst for the visitors Sutherland played ex- cellently.

WIDNES V. TOTTINGTON.—This return fixture was played at Tottington on Saturday. The visitors were not fully represented, and consequently suffered against the strong team which had been arranged against them. Dayeres, who played well for the home team, succeeded in obtaining two tries, in one of which he ran half the length ot the f.. 1,1 after receiving a pass from Fogg. The visitors played an excellent all round game, and several times had hard lines of scoring. The game ended in a win for Tottington by two tries and two minors to Widnes nil.

SUITOR V. WIDNILS Sr. MAILY'S.—This match was played at Widnes on Saturday in wretched weather. Sutton lost the toss and Thomson kicked off against the wind, the ball going into touch. Play at once became very fast and exciting, both lines in turn being visited, until the Sutton forwards by a combined dribble took the oval over the line and Gamble grounding, scored. Again the Sutton forwards showed up well, as from a scrim- mage they took the ball over the line again, Quillan scor- ing. Johnson took the place kick but failed: Half . _ _

tie—Score: Sutton. 2 tries, 1 minors ; St. Mary's, nil. Widnes re-started and pressed their visitors, but they could not break through the splendid defence. Sutton won a hardly contested game by 2 tries and 2 minors, to 1 minor.

RUNCORN v. NEW BRIGHTON.--SatUrdfly saw these well-known teams engaged in open hostility on the ground of the Runcormans. The weather was quite a contrast to that which had prevailed during the week, the frost having given way on Friday evening, and dur- ing the time that the match proceeded rain fell heavily, and made it most uncomfortable for spectators. Both teams were minus important players, the homesters be- ing without the services of Davies, Rigby, Hughes, whilst Luya, whose performances create a great amount of interest, was absent from the visitors' side. The teams were represented as follows :—Runcorn J. W. Brazendale, (hack) ; 11. Crompton, W. Riley, and J. Clarke, (three-quarter backs) ; H. Hughes, and W. E. Evans, (half-hacks); W. H. Broady, W. Faulkner. R. Dolan, P. Riley..E. Davies, A. Hampson, J. Gayter, G. Lee, and F. Hancock (forwards). New Brighton: W. Barry,(back); W. H. Male, F. Edwards, and F. P. Jones, (three-quarter backs) ; Q. J. Leitch, and W. Jackson (half-backs) ; R. F. Muir, W. Eugecombe, H. K. Patterson W. A. Williams, J. M. Colman W. D. Miller, R. B. Esk 9 rigge, R. E. Smith, and J. H. Williams (for- wards). Immediately the teams appeared on the ground they were heartily cheered. The visitors started the ball, and Faulkner returned in fine style. This was the signal for some warm work, and Leitch secured posses- sion of the sphere but was splendidly collared by Han- cock, and thus prevented from doing any material mis- chief. In the New Brighton half play was afterwards continued, when Barry come to tfie relief, and pressure was thus removed, that player kicking the ball well out. A little later on Male secured a pass from Barber and endeavoured to break through the Run- corn backs, tut Riley was on the alert, and put a check on his dangerous career. Rileys' collaring was superb, and was vociferously applauded. Faulkner then, by some smart dribbling, worked the ball into the visitor's territory; but New Brighton put in some fine defensive tactics, and Hughes' efforts were thus checked. He, however, made a determined effort to get over, and the performance was worthy of more suc- cess. Crompton was apparently the most feared of the Runcorn team, and a careful watch was put upon him, and notwithstanding his attempts he was forcibly pro hibited from getting many chances to improve matters Broady, before the whistle was blown for half time, suc ceeded in getting over; but Brazendale failed at goal. In the second half the game was much faster; but the rain which was falling had the effect of spoiling the ground, and interfering to aconsiderable extent with good play. Crompton shone out conspicuously, but a good chance was missed by a pass not being taken. Hughes later on received the ball from Evans, and made a dashing run, and the sphere eventually got into the hands of Cromp- ton, who got over, and afterwards kicked a goal. The game still continued to be hotly played, and Hancock succeeded in crossing the line, from a scrimmage, but no goal resulted. At the close of play Runcorn had I goal. 2 tries, and 5 minors to their credit, whilst .New Brighton had not made a single register.

PENKETH. 3IUTUIL IMPROVEMENT AbSOcIATION. At the weekly meeting of the above on Wednes- day evening, Mr. Thomas Gandy, read an able and interesting essay on "Birds," Mr. James Watson in the chair. There was a good attendance of members and the subject was given full justice by Mr. Gandy who is at home in all matters respecting the feathered tribes. Several members took part in the usual after discussion.

div.head: LYAI34.
div.p: LYAI34.

CHURCH TitsTony.—The second of a series of lectures on " Church history " was given by the Rector (the Rev. G. W. Guest), in the Parochial Schoolroom, on Monday t vening. There was a large attendance. Mr. R. Oddie manipulated lantern slides illustrative of the lecture. SocrAL T&.—On Tuesday evening the annual social tea and entertainment in connection with the Parish Church took place in the Parochial Schoolroom. The tea tables were presided over by the lady members of the congregation, Subsequently a miscellaneous entertain- ment was given.

FuDzmut.—The funeral of Mrs. Taylor, of the Cross. Lamm, who died at her residence on Saturday, took place in the Parish Churchyard on Tuesday morning. The services in the church and at the graveside were , conducted by the Rector. The funeral arrangements were carried out by Mr. Ferris. Man3' beautiful wreaths and floral tributes were sent by the relatives and friends of the deceased lady. CONGREGATIONAL BAND OP Hop.—On Monday evening an entertainpent and meeting in connection with this society waslneld in the Congregational Schoolroom, the pastor (the Rev. Charles Clay), presiding. The Rev. J. A. Mee.son, M.A., LL.B., of Manchester, delivered an address. At-intervals songs, recitations, and dialogues werq. given by the members, nine of whom also took part in a dialogue, entitled "Mrs. Dawson's Sunday 'Visi— tors."

WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL.—Considerable improve- ments are being made in the Wesleyan Sunday Schools. Not only has the gallery been removed but two addi- tional class rooms are being added at the north-east corner, in continuation of a new porch. An entrance to one class room will be from the porch, and the second entrance will be direct from the large rooms. When the improvements are completed there will be five class- rooms besides the vestry. SUDDEN DEATH OF A LYMM FARMER.—On Tuesday afternoon, an awfully sudden death took place at Norton Railway Station. Mr. John Haslam a farmer, residing at Heatley, near Lymm, was on the platform waiting for a train, when he was seen to suddenly stagger and fall down. Medical aid was at once sent for, but before a doctor arrived life was extinct. Deceased had, it is be- lieved, suffered from heart disease. Information was sent to the coroner, but he did not think an inquest

SAYIN4 FARHWRLL.—On Wednesday, Mr. and Mrs. Wright, and Mr. P. J. Maim and family, left Lymm for New Zealand via London. On Monday evening a fare- well gathering took place in the Primitive Methodist Chapel, Eagle Brow. The congregation of the chapel had tea together, and subsequently addresses were de- livered by Mr. and Mrs. Wright, the Rev. W. Evans, Mr. Noden (Dunham Massey), Mr. Warha.m (Dunham Massey), and Mr. Owen (Warrington.) The choir also-• sang at intervals.
