div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
THREE YouNo THIEVES.

Yesterday morning, at the Warrington Police Court,' three lads named Thomas Musgrove, (14), Thomas Quinn (10), and Thomas Cunliffe (10), pleaded guilty to having stolen five gross of leather laces from a stall in the market kept by William Beswick, general dealer, of Horsemar- ket-street. Four gross of the laces had been recovered. The Magistrates directed that Musgrove should have twelve strokes with the birch rod, and the other two prisoners six strokes each.
ALLEGED THEFT AT ORFORD.

Yesterday,at the Warrington Occasional Cou rt,a woman named Mary Coyne was brought up on a charge of having stolen an apron, a pair of stockings, a shawl, and twelve ounces of yarn, of the value of 10s., the property of Dennis Mannion, at Orford, on the tenth of last October. Coyne at that time lodged with the prosecutor, and it is alleged that she took the articles named away with her. She was remanded to the Petty Sessions to be held at Newton to-day (Saturday.)
ONE WAY OF " DOCTORING " 7'103 INFLUENZA.

A navvy named William Jones, who was before the Warrington magistrates on Monday on a charge of drunkenness, candidly admitted the offence, but advanced the excuse that he had been suffering from "what they call the influenza." He was advised to try whiskey as a remedy, and took three glasses of that fiery liquid. The result was that he could not find his way home, and so he lay down in Knutsford-road. He was extremely sorry for what had happened, and said it would act as a warning. A fine of 2s. ed. and costs was imposed.
ASSAULTING A WIFE.

Michael Corless' 4, Howard-street, a wiredrawer, ap- peared before the Warrington magistrates, on Tuesday, in answer to a summons issued by his wife alleging an assault upon her on the 18th inst. She stated that her husband came home, but she did not speak to him, tkough he used very bad language to her in the hearing of their daughter. She could live with him no longer, and all she wanted was a separation. Corless pleaded guilty to the charge, and was bound over to keep the peace for six months in one surety of £5, or in default one month's imprisonment. A MOTFIER AND CHILD CHARGED WITH THEFT.

At the Warrington County Petty Sessions, on Wednes- day, Florence Slade, a little girl, was charged with hav- ing stolen a woollen shawl from the shop of John Lowe and Sons, tailors and drapers, Golberne, on the night of the 18th inst., and was remanded until the Newton Petty Sessions, to be held this (Saturday) morning. At the same Court Fanny Slade, the girl's mother, was re- manded on a charge of having stolen a table cloth from a shop in High-st., Gclborne, kept by Charles Withnall. One of the witnesses, a constable, said that on appre- hending her at her home he found 41 pawntickets there.
THEFTS BY AN EARLESTOWN _HOUSEKEEPER.

At the County Petty Sessions at Warrington, on Wed- nesday morning, an elderly woman named Margaret Naylor was brought up on a charge of having stolen three sheets, three pieces of cloth, and other articles, from the house of James- Henderson, a tailor, who lives at Newton Common. The prosecutor said that Naylor had been acting as his housekeeper, and the offence .alleged against her was that she had taken the articles and pledged them without his knowledge. She pleaded guilty, and handed in a written statement to the Bench to the effect that she intended to redeem the goods. The magistrates sent her to prison for a week, wahout hard labour.

A CAUTION TO THOSE CONCERNED. Persons who make themselves amenable to the law for neglecting to regularly send their children to school will do well to take notice of the recent action of the Warrington magistrates. The Act under which proceed- ings are taken makes it compulsory on the part of parents to produce in court the children with regard to -whom they are summoned, but many decline to do so. 'There is, however, a penalty of 205., including costs, for the offence, and on Tuesday the magistrates imposed it in the case of a defendant named Hughes. The penalty was also imposed last week, in the case of a person named Spofford, whose wife had persistently refused w bring her boy to court when summoned.

div.head: KEEPING AN UNREGISTEEED LODOING-HOESE.
div.p: KEEPING AN UNREGISTEEED LODOING-HOESE.

_ At the Warrington' Police Court, on Monday, William Spafford, navvy, 49, New-road, Latchford, was sum- moned for keeping an unregistered lodging-house on the sth February. Inspector Norman said that the defend- ant's house was visited on the stl. inst., and 15 persons were found in it. The house was adapted for only seven. The matter was reported to the Sanitary Committee, who, however, decided to take no action on Mrs. Spafford promising to get rid of her lodgers the same day. Four days later a visit was paid to the house, and on that occasion 16 persons were found there. The Bench inflicted a penalty of 20s. and costs. Two MONTHS FOB WIFE ASSAULT. Lawrence Spencer, employed at the Bank Quay spelter works, appeared before the Warrington magistrates on Saturday on a charge of having assaulted his wife on the day previous. Mr. A. Browne defended. Mrs. Spencer said that when her husband came in on Friday afternoon, he asked her for his dinner and this not being ready he struck her over the back and arms with a poker, her left arm being broken. In answer to Mr. Browne, she admitted !laving used provoking language, calling her husband "Ann Cook's bully," but she said she did not threaten him with a knife. She did not want her husband sent to gaol, but the bench com- mitted him for two months. Complainant afterwards applied for a judicial separation, but this was not , granted HUSBAND AND WIFE LOCKED UP. At the Warrington Police Court, on Wednesday, a bricksetter, named John Parnell, was brought up in cus- tody on a charge of having been drunk and disorderly,in Mersey-et., on the night previous. He was also charged with having assaulted his wife, Elizabeth Parnell. Evi- dence was called in support of the charge of drunken- ness, and a witness named Smith said that he saw pri- soner beating his wife unmercifully because she would not give him money; he assaulted her in a "frightful manner," and created a great disturbance in the street A charge of drunkenness against the wife was also pre- ferred, and it was stated that afterher husband had been locked up she went to the Police Station and used very bad language. She refused to go to her lodgings, and, as she was drunk, she was detained. She now declared that her husband had not assaulted her, but the magis- trates considered the charge against him proved, and fined him 20s. and costs,or a fortnights' imprisonment in default of payment. The female prisoner wasdischarg,ed.

A VULCAN WORM/LE FALLS AMONG THIEVES. Two girls of bad character, named Winifred Burke and Elizabeth Ellen Fleming, were brought before the War- rington magistrates on Wednesday, on a ciiarge of having picked the pocket of Richard Yates, a striker, employed at the Vulcan foundry, in Buttermarket-street, on the night previous. The Chief Constable (Mr. Hum), stated that opt Tuesday night the prosecutor received his wages at the Vulcan, and came to Warrington, where he con- sumed a quantity of beer. He met the prisoners in the Kings Arms public-house, and paid for drink for them. Afterwards he went into Buttermarket-street, accom- panied by the prisoners, and it was alleged that Fleming put her hand in the trousers pocket of Yates, and took out the money, some of which fell on the ground. In the meantime Burke was standing a short distance away and the two made off together, but were afterwards ap- prehended. The magistrates, after hearing the evidence of several witnesses, expressed the opinion that the case was one of great suspicion, but the evidence was not sufficient to warrant a conviction. Prisoners were there- fore discharged.

div.head: MINOR CASES. WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT.
div.p: MINOR CASES. WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT.
SATTI.R.DAY.—Before Alderman Burgess and Councillor

Voisey. DESERTING A FAMILT.—Thomas Griffiths, an under- hand puddler, was charged on a warrant with haying deserted his wife and family, whereby they had become chargeable to the Union. Fourteen shillings were claimed by the Guardians, and a remand of a fortnight was granted to allow the prisoner to pay the money. MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Francomb) and Alderman Sutton. _ _

BERATIOIIR.—Mary France and John Powell were charged with having been guilty of improper be- haviour.—France was sent to prison for a fortnight, and Powell was fined 10s, and costs. DRUNKENNESS. The following persons were dealt with for this offence :—Thomas Johnson, in Bridge-st., cm Saturday night, fined 55., including costs; Thomas Adams, in Winwick-road, on Saturday, sixth appear- ance, sent to prison for a month ; Peter Ford, in Tan- ner's-lane, on the 9th inst., fined ss. and costs • Henry Bithell, in Orford-st., on the 12th inst., fined ss. and costs; Mary Gibbons, in Bridge-st., on the Bth inst., fined ss. and costs.

DISORDERLY BEHAVIOUR.—Joseph Bate and Mary Bate were brought up on warrant charged with having been disorderly in Rose-yard, on the 7th of last September. They were each ordered to be bound over to be of good behaviout, in their own recognisancos, and to pay ss. costs each. • CHIMNEY ON Film—William Jones, summoned for having allowed the chimney of his house to be on fire, was fined 3s. 6d. BYE-LAW OFFENCE.—Thomas William Urey was sum- moned as the driver of a horse and cart for having allowed, on the 17th inst., certain liquid to run from the cart on to Buttermarket-st. John H. Fleming. jun., the owner of the cart, was summoned for having allowed the offence. The cases were dismissed on Mr. Fleming paying the costs, 7s. TIIESDAY.—Before Mr. W. Owen and Mr. E. M. Crosfield. SCHOOL ATTENDANCE CASES.—A number of people were summoned at the instance of the School Attendance Committee, for having neglected to send their childre. regularly to school, and were fined in various amounts Mr. George Riley appeared to prosecute. WEDNESDAY' .—Bef ore Alderman Holmes, Capt. Nicholson, and Mr. J. Fairclough. THE7T OF A COAT.—Patrick Kilroy, a labouring man, was charged with having stolen a coat, value El, from the shop of Alice Hatton, tripe dealer, Mersey-st.,

between Sunday night and Monday niorning. He was sent to prison for a month, with hard labour. THIIRSDAY.—Before Alderman Sutton and Captain Ridgeway. Dstamsrmvss.—For this offence James Carney was fined 2s. ed., including costs, and Sarah O'Brien was sent to prison for a month. FRlDAY.—Before Mr. John White and Dr. Gornall. DRUNKENNESS.—The following persons were dealt with for this offence :—Michael Kelly, in Museum-st., fined ss. and costs; and Martin Curley in Stanley-st., fined 53. and casts.
THE MAINTENANCE Of' A MOTHER. —Thomas Barker, brewery labourer, wias ordered to pay is. a week towards the maintenance of his mother. Mr. A. Browne repre- sented the defendant.
ALLEGED ASSADLTS.—Edward Dillon was charged with having assaulted Elizabeth Plinston, in Rose and Crown. St., on the day previous. The case was dismissed.
WARRINGTON OCCASIONAL COURT. MONDAL—Before Mr. P. Stubs.

MISCELLANEOUS.— Thomas W.right, James Higham,i Joseph Hawkins, Annie Holmes, Ellen McCormick, and Annie Clarke, were charged with doing wilful damage to the extent of 18s.' to a haystack, the property of Stephen Deane, on Saturday last, at Poulton. The three female prisoners were also charged with sleeping out at the same time and place. For the first offence each of the male prisoners was fined 10s. including costs, and the female prisoners were fined for the damage 3s. or seven days, and for vagrancy they were committed to prison for 14 days.—Patrick Donoghbe was charged with being drunk and disorderly, at Golborne, on the 18th inst., and with assaulting P.C.'s Mounsey and Da.ven- port, whilst acting in the execution of their duty. Evidence in support of the charge was given, and the Iprisoner was remanded to the Newton Sessions, to be held to-diy (Saturday).—Elizabeth Lawrinson, for being drunk and disorderly, at Poulton, on Saturday, was fined 10s. and costs, or in default 14 days' imprison- ment.
WARRINGTON COUNTY PETTY SESSIONS. WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr.. Rigby, (in the chair), and Mr. G. Comber.

DRUNKENNESS. —James Coyne, for having been drunk on the highway at Penketh, on the 4th inst., was reprimanded and dismissed- ASSAULT.—Johp Bibby, for having assaulted Sarah Maxfield, was bound over in his own recognisances to be of good behaviour, and was ordered to pay the costa of the case.
THFI MUZZLING ORDER.—George Walker, summoned for having, on the Bth inst.. allowed his dog to be at larp, unmuzzleci, at Burtonwood, was ordered to pay a fine of is. and costs.

div.head: FOOTBALL.
div.p: FOOTBALL.

*„. Secretaries of Football Chita are requested to note that reports of matches played on Saturday must,be sent to the head office, Bewsey-atreet, Warrington, not later than ten o'clock on Wednesday morning.
RUGBY.

WARRINGTON " A " v. MANCHESTER RANGERS "A."— The return fixture between these teams was played on the Wilderspool enclosure, on Saturday, in miserable weather, rain falling throughout the match. Owing to the visiters arriving shorthanded, neither displayed their full strength; but notwithstanding this and the ulafavour- able weather, a fairly interesting game was witnessed. Manchester kicked off, and no return being forthcoming, play was lathe home quarters. The scene of operations was soon changed, however, for succeeding some ex- changes between the rival backs Gadd failed to gather Webster's final kicks, which enabled Mather to run in under the posts, the place failing. A fast dribble by rnsworth was returned by Gadd, but Holmes almost dropped a goal directly afterwards, and a minor was concealed Berry was next prominent by finely stopping HigginlyAtom, and a fine spell of passing by Rowe, Mather, Jolley, and Webster, resulted in the lattergetting a try. From the drop ont Daniels ran strongly and Rowe threw across a scrimmage to Mather, but the latter's pass was intercepted. A lot of interesting looSe play ensued, the Rangers eventually dashing to the home line, but Molyneaux, and Berry by some short passes quickly relieved. Molyneaux, Davies, and Thornley then started a dribble to their opponents territory, but this was more than neutralized by Tyacke getting clean away from a pack, Webster saving a sure try at his own quarter flag. Subsequently Mather dodged his opponents in a line-out, and threw across to Jolley, who run in unopposed under the posts, Webster kicking a goal. The drop out was still! of little advantage to the visiting team, for a long kick by Neild almost re,ulted in a try, and another minor was ' forced immediately after, Warrington passing over with 1-2-3 to the good, Restarting, a lot of loose play monopo- lized the game for some time, Jolley in the end almost rushing in but Gadd ran the ball grandly to halfway. By the aid of some good play by Beard, Unsworth, and Davies, the home team again attacked, and a kick by Unsworth, which was rapidly followed up by the same player enabled Beard to score in a good position, the place failing. Berry, who was now playing fullback, returned the drop-out finely, but immediately afterwards he wasoblige4l to save a determined rush by Tyacke, Storer, and Taylor. The Rangers were now handicapped greatly by Gadd having to retire. Daniels was the next to put the Manchester team on the defence, and Rowe threw finely to Jolley, who forced a minor by a drop at goal. After some long kicks by Jolley, the Rangers gradu- ally forced their way to the Warrington quarters, and obliged the home team to concede a minor to avert dis- aster, This was their only effort, for Neild, Thornley, and Uusworth soon got away to neutral territory, and Jolley getting possession from Rowe put in a tall punt, from which Webster scored. A minor was soon afterwards conceded, and then Jolley again got away and threw smartly to Webster, who ran in easily and grounded behind the posts. Following the drop-out Daniels ran well into the visitors' quarters, and a dribble started by Jolley and Mather resulted in Holmes getting a try near the posts, the place again failing. The visitors again dropped out, but were pressed back immediately. Jolley running well threw to Webster, who got his fourth try, which was converted by Jolley, Warrington winning by 2 goals, 6 tries, 5 minors to 1 minor. Teams Warrington: Holmes, back; Daniels, Jolley, and Webster, threequarter-backs ' • Mather and Rowe, half-backs; Beard, Molyneux, Davies, Thornley, Nield, Berry, Wood- ward, and Unsworth, forwards. Rangers: Gadd, back; Higgingbottom, Tyacke, and Irwin, threequarters ; Vickers, and Storer half backs • Bishop, Taylor, Cox, Jones, Taylor, Johnson, and A. N. Other forwards.

div.head: WARRINGTON v. MANCHESTER RANGERS.
div.p: WARRINGTON v. MANCHESTER RANGERS.

The return fixture between these clubs took place at Rosholme on Saturday, when, despite the fact that War- rington were without the aid of Barnes, P. R. Lawless, Nevins, and Antrobus, they confirmed the previous meeting this season, coming out of the fray victorious. The Rangers had made a special effort for the occasion, and the strongest team it has been their lot to place in any engagement this season was placed on the field. The weather was miserable and the ground was slippery and heavy going thus rendering true football a difficulty.

The Rangers started, and Pearson at once showed up until E. Dillon blocked the way, and a shortrun and passed to Dmsohue settled play at the half-way flag. Hill responded to a dribble of the Warrington forwards, and then Evans averted danger by a smart punt well into the Rangers' quarters. After some give and take play Meehan dribbled thiough the opposing defence and located play near the Warrington goal, and some pass- ing by the home backs was checked by the effective tackling of Massey. Again the homesters tried to score, this time Sabin rounding his opponents, and although ' Randles made a good attempt to floor his man the stalwart Ranger used his strength to advantage and got in near the corner flag, Hill making a feeble attempt at the place. The drop eut still found play at the Warrington end, and Sabin made another effort to get in, but no mistake was made this time. Warrington now warmed to their work, and a fine rush of the visiting forwards, chief amongst others being Eyres, W. Dillon, and Little- wood, caused some anxiety. A free kick taken by Fair Turner was well followed up by W. Dillon and a reply averted. Frank Turner now headed a combined dribble, and a beautiful cross dribble by Bate took play under the Rangers' goal. Lawless ineffectually tried to cross the line, and Herbert Hasleham by a short run moment- arily relieved. A tricky kick by Speakman was followed by a drop at goal by Evans, this last point forcing a minor. Evans and Massey shone with brilliant runs and kicking soon after the drop out, and although the Rangers paid a flying visit to the Warrington quarters, Evans got possession, and ran from his own quarter flag to within a yard from the Rangers' line. Radcliffe replied, and Povey from the line-out ran and punted along the touch. Fair Turner made a desperate attempt to score, but being foiled placed the oval at his comrade's feet and the leather being finally sent over a race took place, Massey outdistancing his opponents and gaining a try. Frank Turner took the place and kicked a fire goal. From the restart Warrington still remained on the aggressive, and although Boscow was tested, he was /lever found wanting, and equal to any emergency. Another capital run by Evans and a fine run and kick by , Massey again raised the hopes of the visitors' supporters, but a minute from the call of half-time Ratcliffe gained possession near the Warrington quarter flag, and running strongly ran in near the post, Hill kicking a goal, bringing half-time with the score—Rangers, 1-1-0; Warrington, 1-0-1. Frank Turner restarted, Evans and Ratcliffe exchanging kicks, the oval being finally deposited in touch near the home quarter flag. By degrees the Rangers worked the oval to half way, but Massey made the Mancestrians beat a hasty retreat with a useful kick well into touch. Another penalty kick fell to Warrington, and Fair Turner taking it, his kick was met by Sabin. The latter sent the oval to Boscow, who punted down the field to his forwards, who dribbled on owing to the failure of a Rangers' player retaining possession. Meanwhile Boscow bad been on the alert, and following up at top speed joined in the scramble, with the result that the oval was taken over, , and the Warrington custodian successfully notched a try, Frank Turner making a good though unsuccessfullaid , for premier honours. A minor followed to the Warring- I tonians' credit immediately upon the drop out. A , spell of give and take play followed, and the visiting

forwards, who were rtayin,g a grand game, now swept down in a body on the home goal. Nearing the line, Massey joined in the movement,which ws noay cqnfined to three. Another try astak Icerfd bie:Massey, the kick at goal being futile. The-drOp 'olat found play '`at half- way, and some passing by the visitors' backs was luckily checked by Hamblett, who by these means took play to Warrington goal. It was left to Lawless to relieve, for clashing round the pack he evaded Meehan and sent the oval to the halfway flag. Again the War- rington forwards demonstrated usefulness when thoroughly combined by rushing to the line, where Frank Turnez and Bandies both experienced hard lines in not securing tangible points. Radcliffe next essayed a shot at goal, the ball going dead. This was followed by some pretty play on behalf of Bate, who tricked his opponents, and throwing to Evans, that player threw across to Massey, but the pass was short, otherwise a certain score would have resulted. A drop at goal by Evans just missed its mark. As a last hope for the Rangers the ball was passed to Sabin, but Evans judging his man with admirable precision brought him to mother earth, and following this the whistle sounded for no side, the score reading Warrington, one goal, two tries, three minors ; Rangers, one goal, one try, one minor. The play of Warrington was far superior to that cf the Rangers, and cur local club undoubtedly owe their vic- tory to combination, This was specially noticeable in the second half, the forwards distinguishing themselves in a remarkable manner. Boscow made a capital full back, not making the semblance of a mist Ore. Too much praise cannot be awarded Evans, avII gave a brilliant exposition of wing three-quarter play. Massey also deserves praise, whilst it is only fair to state that Speakman was severely handicapped, this being his first turnout this season. Bate played his usual scientific game, and Lawless never showed signs of relaxation. The forwards one and all played a good honest game. Teams: Mancheher Rangers: D. Hill, back; H. Radcliffe, Sabin, and A. Hammett, three-qnarter backs; A. Storer and J. Meehan, half banks; Herbert Hasleham, Harry Hasleliam, E. Mee, S. Grange, G. Ibbotson, W. , Storer' W. Pearson R. Hamnett, and A. McDougall. forwards. Warrington: J. Boscow, back; J. W. Evans, J. Speakman, and J. T. Massey, three-quarter backs; J. Bate and J. Lawless, half backs; Fair. Turner, Frank Turner W. Dillon, E. Dillon, W. Povey, W. Bandies, R. LittlewOod, T. Donoghue, and B. Eyres, forwards.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 22, 1890.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 22, 1890.
NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS. . FOOTBALL-RUGBY.

To-day's matches :—Warrington v. Oldham at Old- ham ; Runcorn v. Huddersfield at Huddersfield ; Widnes v. Rochdale St. Clements at Widnes; St Helens,v. Aspull at St. Helens; St. Helens Recs. v. Tyldeslev at Tyldes- ley.

It was not the Welshmen but the Englishmen, who had to eat the leek in the international encounter on Saturday. The match took place at Dewsbury, in miser- able weather, min and sleet falling the whole of the time. The English team answered to their "tames to a man, but there were three changes among the visitors, one of them being the inclusion of Lloyd among the three-quarters, of whom there were four. This experi- ment was tried against Scotland with much success.

The game taken as a whole was pretty evenly fought, but whilst this is granted, the Welshmen were the superiorlot. From the start they pressed the Englishmen, and there were several packed scrimmages in the latters' 25, of which England got the worst. It soon became apparent that the English backs were not shaping as was expected. They allowed their opponents to become dangerous several times, and had Mitchell not been in grand form the score against them would have been greater. Later on there were signs of activity, bow- over, and after Stoddart had stopped a rush England forced the first minor. Wales did plenty of aggressive work, their forwards shining especially and outclassing those on the other side. England obtained two other minors before half time, but nothing tangible accrued.

Before the second half had progressed five minutes there were some capital tactics by the Welsh three-quar- ter backs, which ended in Stadden scoring the first and only try. A smart attack upon the English goal fol- lowed, and although Valentine succeeded in relieving slightly he mulled the ball. Wales defended well and kept their charge intact up to the finish winning by one try and one minor, to three minors. Bancroft was very safe at full back, and of the three-quarters Gould and Gwynn put in some splendid play. Stadden played a very fine game throughout, and he was well backed up by Thomas. The forwards were a'capital lot. On the English side the play of Stoddart and Valentine was disappointing, though it must be admitted that they had few chances, especially the Swintonian. Mitchell could not have been improved upon, and Fox was about the best man on the field. Forward, flan- cock, Lowrie, Evershed, „ and Hickson were the most conspicuous. England can hardly look forward to the big match of a fortnight hence with any degree of con- fidence.

The "Lancet " says :—We are indebted to a corespondent for the following list of football casualties in the present season, commencing the first week in Septem- ber last, to the third week in the past month of Janu- ary, taken from a carefully tabulated record of such casualities as have been publicly announced :—Deaths. 13. Fractures: Legs, 15; arms, 4 ; collarbones, 11. Injuries: Spines, 3; noses 1; knee, 1 ; ankle, 1 ; cheek, 1.

div.head: MISCELLANEOUS.
div.p: MISCELLANEOUS.

During the present week an interesting chess match between the redoubted chess champions Mr. H. E. Bird of London, and Herr E. Lasker, of Berlin has been going on at the Liverpool Chess Club. Herr Lasker is but a young player, who came into prominence by winning the Hauptonnier in the German Congress at Breslau, and by winning the second prize in the Masters' Internation- al Tournament, at Amsterdam in September. Since carrying off these honours, Herr Luker has added to his laurels by beating Herr Misses, the winner of the third place in the Breslau International Tournament. Mr. Bird has been before the British public as a chess player for many years. He is the oldest living master of the game, and his recent success in winning the National Tourna- ment, held in London last November, entitles him to the honoured designation of champion of England. In the present contest the winning of the first seven games will entitle the competitor to the coveted honours of the event.

The contest between the teams of the Warrington and Bournemouth gymnasium, in the National Challenge Shield ompetition, will not take place to-Jay, as first announcecd, but next Saturday. The postponement is due to the fact that Mr. Alexander, the director of the Warrington team, is also leader of the Chester team, which meets the Dublin contingent to-day in the first round.
WARRINGTON BANKRUPTCY COURT.

A sitting of this Court was held yesterday, before the Registrar, Captain Nicholson. THB BANKITITVITT OF A STATIONER.—John Woolsten- croft, stationer, late of 37, Horsemarket-st. and now residing at 14, Mill-st., appeared to undergo his first public examination. A receiving order was made against the debtor on his own petition, and he was adjudged bankrupt on his own application. In his statement to the Official Receiver bankrupt said that by trade he is a journeyman bookbinder. About October, 1887, he commenced business as a stationer at 37. Horsemarket-st., without any capital. Owing to losses in trade he had to execute a deed of assignment for the benefit of his creditors on June 27th, 1889. The trustee, Mr. John Mainlwaring, realised the estate, and had paid 2s. in the £to all the creditors except four, to satisfy whose claims he still held £l2 2s. 4d. Debtor now worked at his trade. He first became aware that he was insolvent in June, 1889, and suspended payment of his debts when he executed the deed of assignment. He alleged that he had not con- tracted any debts with a knowledge of his insolvency. The bankrupt put down his deficiency at £l2l 2s. 11d. The bankrupt admitted that he had not, within the past three years, prepared any statement of his affairs, and that he never took stock, except for the trustee under the deed of assignment. He also stated that, not having kept any account thereof,he could not,for the past three years, say what income he had been making, nor give any more accurate account of his expenditure for ' household and personal purposes than that it had amounted to about £2 a week. In explanation of the fact that he disclosed no assets he made the following statements—" All my assets are in the hands of Mr. Mainwaring. The furniture at 14 Mill-st. belongs to my mother-in-law, Mrs. Pritchard, wile purchased it herself. My life policy has lapsed. The dwelling-house 14 Mill- st. is in my wife's name." The Official Receiver reported that the bankrupt appeared to have resorted to the Bank- ruptcy Court in consequence of the service on him of a judgment summons. The debtor alleged bad trade and want of capital as the causes of his failure. After vari- ous questions had been put to the debtor by the Official Receiver, the examination was adjourned until the 21st March. RB BRAMICALL AND BISSET., BUILDERS.—JOIHI BrAMball and James Bissel, builders. Sidg-st., appeared on an adjourned examination. Mr. Dibb, the official rveiver, asked that the public examination might be closed,if there was no opposition on the part of creditors. They had now filed their accounts, and he believed that they had done the best they could, although the accounts were not such as we would have wished to have seen.' If ever there was a case in which his persistency in regard to accounts was justified it was this one. Mr. Bramhall had over andiover again persisted that his books contained a com- plete record of his transactions, but there was a sum of £llO odd at this moment unaccounted for. He did not, however, think that the bankrupts could do anything more. The public examination was then closed.

div.head: PRESENTATION TO THE REV. E. MOORE.
div.p: PRESENTATION TO THE REV. E. MOORE.

Clnaltursday eveningt ,the Rev. E. Meorettuatii- lateliZtinister f toiborde-st. liaptiat Or&Ca, Kval presented with an illuminated address, a handsome and valuable gold watch, and a purse of gold which had been subscribed for by members of the Golb6rne- st. Church and townspeople generally. The presen- tation took place iii the Golborne-st. schoolroom, Mr. T. Hill presiding over ,the lsxge gathering which was present. Amongst those on the platform and in the audiencel in addition to Me and Mrs. Moore, were the Rev. J. Yonge, Rev. J. W. Varley, Rev. E. H. Jackson, Rev. F. R. Roberts, Mr. Wm. Roberts, Mr. John Fieldhouse (who presided later on in the evening), &c. Letters of apology for non- attendance were read from the Rev. E. S. Kenworthy Cliffe), and Mr. E. J. Hall. The following are the words of the address :=--" To the Rev. Edward Moore.—Sir,— Upon the termination of your pastorate of the Baptist Church, Golborne-st., War- rington, we, the undersigned, beg to assure you of our sincere regard and earnest wish for your future happinese and prosperity. The eight year during which you have been our pastor will ever be memorable in our history, for during that period all debt has been removed from the church property, the chapel has been completely renovated, and recently £l4O, or thereabouts, has been raised towards the rebuilding and the enlargement of the school. In addition to the usual duties of the ministry which have been preformed by you, we rejoice. because of the valnable and constant part undertaken by you in the Sunday'school, and remember with pleasure your manly and fearless advocacy" of moral and social reforms. Your place in our memory and affection is assured and we pray for you and your family God's richest blessing always and wherever you may be. Signed on behalf of the subscribers, Warrington, 20th February, 1890. Thomas Hall, Joseph Hall, Renjamin Few, John Fieldhouse, deacons ; John Fieldhouse, Samuel Gough, E. James Hall, Norman Balmford, Alfred Field- house, Samuel Fernley (secretary), testimonial com— mittee." The address is in book form, bound in morocco and gold, and has been handsomely illuminated by Messrs. Brookes and Son, of Warrington. The gold watch, supplied by Messrs. Woods and Son, of Warring- ton, has Mr. Moore's monooyam finely engraved on the back, and inside there is the following inscription n— " Presented to the Rev. G. Moore on the occasion of his resigning the pastorate of the Golborne-st. Baptist Church, Warrington, by the members and friends.' February, 1890.' The CHAIRMAN said that meeting was not altogether without either its pleasures or its pain. It was always pleasant to receive new friends, but it was, not always pleasant to part with old ones, and especially when they had been working together so long and in se good a cause. Mr. Moore's connection with them had been unbroken by any unpleasantness betwixt him and the church, and this had not contributed to the step he had taken in resigning his pastorate of Golborne-st. Chapel. He (the Chairman) endorsed everything that was said in the address with regard to Mr. Moore, but he should like to add something with regard to Mr. Moore's indefati- gable labours in connection with the Sunday School. Ever since he had first come amongst them he had taken a deep interest in the Sabbath School and had never been away from it except when preaching elsewhere or ill. His labours in the Sunday school had been very much appreciated by the young people, who had not been un-' mindful of his teaching. (Applause.) Mr. FIELDHOUSE then made the presentation to Mr. Moore. He remarked that he came to Warrington just a little before Mr. Moore's ministry began at the place, and he had therefore the opportunity of watching Mr. Moore's conduct and the value of his ministrations amongst them, which, he was sure had been duly appreciated. (Hear, 'hear.) Great changes had taken place in connection with that church since Mr. Moore came to it. He (Mr. Fieldhouse) remembered the first Sunday he came to the church. It was a cold cheerleas morning, and the service was as cheerless as the morning. The singing was so slow that he wondered when they would get to the end of a hymn, and the organ was sadly out of tune. (Laughter.) All these things had now being rectified. Thechoir were now able to sing praises with understanding, and the organ had been put in a thorough state of repair. When they took a retrospect of the past and considered the great improvements that had been made in the chapel for the comfort of worshippers, the marvel to him was how so much had been done during the eight years of Mr. Moore's ministrations. (Hear, hear). The Gospel Mr. Moore preached when he first came amongst them was the same gospel that he preached in his farewell sermon, and there were many ministers of which that could not be said after eight years service. (Hear, hear). In making that presentation he sincerely hoped and trusted that Mr. Moore's life might be long spared, and that the gospel proclaimed by him during the last eight years would be proclaimed by him for many years to come. He believed thaii the town itself had some cause to be thankftil for what Mr. Moore had done in it, not merely in connection with that chapel, but in what some would call secular work, namely, teaching a thorough knowledge of music. (Applause.) Mr. Fieldhouse then mentioned that for the subscriptions they were very much indebted to other denominations besides their own, including Church people, and particularly to their friends at Wycliffe. There had been little difficulty in collecting the money as the subscriptions had been of a most spontaneous char- acter. (Hear, hear, and applause). The Rev. E. MOORE, in acknowledging the presenta- tion, referred also to the gift that had been made to him by his late Sunday school class. This had been very acceptable to him and had, indeed, delighted him beyond measure. His whole connection with the Sunday school had been of the most delightful and pleasant character, and he could not recall a single incident with regard to the Sunday School that could give him the slightest pain or discomfort. (Hear, hear.) He scarcely thought he deserved all the kind things that had been said of him, but during his ministry he had always simply tried to do his duty as well as circumstances would permit. He did not pretend to have been by any means perfect, either as a pastor or as a preacher, and there had been faults he was sure incident to his first pastorate. So far as his relations with the congregation personally and socially were con- cerned they had been almost wholly of a pleasant char- acter. Ile had tried to win the esteem and affection of all people with whom he had come in contact. He had never offended any man willingly, nor had heever sought the injury of any, and if there was anything in his conduct towards any member of that church or congre- gation which they looked back upon with any regret or feeling of irritation, he hoped they would banish it and he asked their sincere forgiveness. That church would always have a warm place in his heart. lie had made many fast friendships there, and wherever his lot , might be cast in the future he should always think of Warrington with very great interest and of his many friends there with deep affection. (Loud applause.) The Rev. J. YONGE said he had known Mr. Moore as long as Golborne-st. had known him, and he could tell them that he had found him to be in every sense a good man and true. He believed him to be a Godly man, a man who loved God and followed Jesus Christ, and he believed moreover that, taking him all round,the was as good a minister as they would find in a long day's march. (Applause.) He had known his friend in dark days and in bright days, and he might say without the slightest mental reservation that he had never discerned anything in him to cause him to waver in his confidence in or brotherly esteem for him. (Hear, hear). He deserved the kindest word anybody could say 'for him and he (Mr. Yon,ge) believed he did not deserve any un- kind word anybody might say about him. Be made that last remark because he believed there were reasons which called for it. (Applause). He felt perfectly con- fident when he said it the same feeling prevaded his own people at Wycliffe. They all held Mr. Moore in high esteem, and he was glad to be able to tell them that never did Mr. Moore create so happy an impression or did 'such useful service as he did on Sunday last in preaching at Wycliffe. (Applause.) They might rest in confidence that Geed had good work for Mr. Moore to do in some corner of His vineyard, and perhaps better work than he had ever achieved in the past. (Loud Applause.) The Rev. J. W. VARLET said he had known Mr. Moore for five years, and his connection with him had been of the very best kind. Mr. Moore carried with him the very heartiest good wishes for his future well-being. He (Mr. Varley) was rather sorry that the people of Latch- ford had not been appealed to for subscriptions, but he, as their representative, could tell Mr. Moore that they would keep him in kindest remembrance. (Hear, hear, and applause.) The Rev. E. H. Jecasox alsospoke of his great affection and pleasant relations with Mr. Moore and his family, and also of the great regard in which Mr. Moore was held by the Wesleyans of the town. The Rev. F. R. ROBERTS said he could testify to the • sterling character of their friend. In their intercourse together, although they did not altogether agree in their theological views, he gad learned to regard Mr. Moore as one of the best men he had ever met in his life. He also referred to the great help that Mrs. Moore had been to to her husband. The only mystery to himi was why they were met there that night. He could not understand why they should all be say- ing those good things, and yet letting Mr. Moore go. (Hear, hear.) It seemed to him little short of a mockery that a man who as appreciated so much as Mr. Moore had been should be allowed to slip away as he was doing. It seemed to him that if Mr. Moore was gone that church, would be the poorer, the town would be the poorer and dissent would be the poorer. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Mr. W. ROBETITS said, as his brother had just expressed it, he could not for the life of him understand hew that thing had coin about. He had been associated with Mr. Moore in various movements, and especially' in the temperance movement, andhe could tell them that the removal of Mr. Moore would be a very serious loss to the town. (Hear, hear.) He believed that the few people who had expressed any unkindness toward Mr. Moore could be counted on the fingers of one hand, and he (Mr. Roberts) hoped they would make up their minds that the cause he had referred to should not suffer by M. Moore's removal, and if an-one amongst them tried to sow the seeds of discontent', chuck him out of the place. (Loud applause.) Mr. GOUGH said he thought the subscriptions showed how much Mr. Moore was appreciated by people not only

in their own connection but all over the town. He hoped the warm feeling between that place and Wycliffe would continue to exist. .(Applause.) M. Worro, in:moiing a vote of thanks to the chair- me (21r. Hisll held Mr."Fieldhouse) referred to the great services always rendered him by his wife. He could truly say that he had a model minister's wife. (Arr.+ plause.) _ _ _
• Mr. (iOUGH seconded the proposition, which having been carried, the meeting concluded.
PRESENTATION-BY THE BIBLE CLASS.

Mr. Moore has also been presented with a handsome gold pencil case by the members of his late Bible Class. Along with the pendl case the following letter was sent: —" Golborne-st. Sunday School, February. 10th 1890. Dear Mr. Moore,—We (the members of yourßible Class) cannot let you leave us without thanking you very sincerely for the warm interest you have always taken in our spiritual welfare. We all feel that we have bene- fited by your kind and earnest teaching, and it is with heart-felt respect that we now take our leave of you as our teacher. We ask your acceptance of the enclosed gift, as a token of 'affection, and assure you we shall always remember with pleasure the time we have spent with you." To the letter the names of the Bible Glass were ' appended. In acknowledginc, the gift Mr.,Moore wrote: —" I shall always look back with great pleasure to the pleasant afternoons we have spent together over the Hely Word. I trust that the same memory will always be cherished by you. Pleased as lam with this token, of your, affection, there is one thing that would please me still more, and that would be to know that the greatest principles and truths we have discussed together might become the ruling forces of your own lives and charactevs„ and above all, that you might every one become avowed and Nithful disciples of the Lord Jesus, about whom we have so often talked. May it be my happy lot to hear, and not in the distant future, that such has become the unalterable resolution of each of you."

div.head: STATE OF IRELAND.
div.p: STATE OF IRELAND.

- ARREST OF EVICTED TENANTS. • A Maryborough telegram states that twenty-five more arrests have been made in connection with thb building of huts on the Clongoray estate, County Kildare. The campaigners, it is stated, are determined ta persist.
IMPRiSONMENT FOR INTIMIDATION.

At the Crimes Act Court at Cork, on Saturday, John Slattery, president of the South of Ireland Cattle Trade Association, was sentenced to six months' imprisonment for refusing to give bail for his good behaviour on a charge of intimidation towards a man who allowed some pigs, field by a caretaker of an evicted farm, to be lodged en his premises. ALLEGED MURDER NEAR QUEENSTOWN.

A Queenstown correspondent says that information has been received there that the gatekeeper of the Royal Victoria Docks (Passage West), distant two miles from Queenstown, was killed early on Sunday morning. One of the crew of the steamship Manhattan, now Viol; at the dock wharf, is in custody, charged with the crime. He is a fireman, named Daniel Mac. ,

div.head: DEATH SENTENCE AFFIRMED.
div.p: DEATH SENTENCE AFFIRMED.

The Irish Queen's Bench gave judgment on Saturday over-ruling the points raised on behalf of Michael O'Brien, who, at last Nenagh Assizes, was convicted of having poisoned his father-in-law, and was sentenced to be hanged in Limerick on the 14th ult., execution being respited pending the argument. Sentence was affirmed. The convict listened attentively to the judgments. •A PARNELLITE LIBEL ACTION. The hearing of the action by Mr. Henry Canipbell, M.P., against the "Belfast News-Letter," to recover £5,000 damages for alleged libel, came on in Dublin, on Tuesday, before Mr. Justice O'Brien. The statement complained of was alleged to have been made in a speech by Mr. Porter, a Donegal gentleman, and was to the effect that it had been shown in the O'Donnell v. Walter action that Mr. Campbell wrote the order for the knives for Mrs. Byrne, for the Phenix Park murders.—Plain- tiff's case having closed, Mr. James Henderson, pro- prietor of the "News-Letter," Mr. Allen, sub-editor, and Mr. Watkin, the correspondent who supplied the report of Mr. Porter's speech, were examined. The manuscript of the speech could not be found. Counsel on both sides having spoken, Judge O'Brien summed up, and the jury returned a verdict for the plaintiff—damages £2OO. ARCHBISHOP WALSH ON SECRET SOCIETIES.

In his Lenten pastoral the Roman Catholic Archbishop of Dublin says :—" As secret societies are most detri- mental to public order, as well as to the best interests of our religion, several Popes, including the present, have pronounced a sentence of excommunication against their members and of all who hale in any way promoted the interests of these unhappy organizations. 'Hence Catholics becoming Freemasons, Ribbonmen, Penians, Good Templars, or members of any similar secret society, or taking part in their meetings, balls, &c., incur the censures of the Church." The table of regulations for Lent, which are relaxed in consequence of the epidemic of influenza, concludes with a caution to the Catholics of the diocese to be on their guard alainst a "political movement" that has lately sprung into life, having for its object the rearing of destitute children born of Catholic parents in the Protestant faith.

div.head: DROPPIisTG FROM RUNCORN BRIDGE
div.p: DROPPIisTG FROM RUNCORN BRIDGE
LIVELY SCENE.

Runcorn Bridge, on Thursday afternoon, was the scene of another daring feat by Tommy Burns, the noted athlete and swimmer, of Liverpool. It was announced that at two o'clock he would drop from the bridge into the Mersey, by means of a parachute, and some time before that hour, thou- sands had assembled on the Widnes shore, and hun- dreds on the Cheshire shore, in anxious anticipa- tion. A large number, of persons also gathered on the lofty structure itself. In preparation for the "drop," a rope about eight feet long dangled from the railings, which protect the footwalk on the first girder, and about a quarter past two, Burns, at- tended by " Bits " Kendrick, of Widnes, and red Savage, an old athlete of Salford, appeared on the scene. Burns quickly divested himself of his apparel, and stood attired in ordinal y swimming costume. Mounting the rails, he rapidly descended the rope hand over hand, and after placing a toy parachute to his mouth, was about to release his hold, when -the warning voice of Hulse the pilot, who was in charge of a, boat on the river, caused him to pause, and for several momenta he was suspended in the air, 70 feet above the water. Then a piece Of wood, having floated by, a cheery "All right" sounded from below, and Burns dropped with tearful velocity, feet first. lie struck the • water with great force spray fly- ing in all directions, and be descended in the water so far, that at least half a minute elapsed befbre he again appeared on the surface, his, re-appearancebeing greeted with loud cheers. He was soon taken on board the boat in attendance, and no doubt to keep bkoself•warm, took a haadat•the oars in rowing back to the ferrg slip. He dressed at the Mersey Hotel, and on iiresenting himself in the large room he received a cordial reception from a large number of his admirers. Mr. Montague, of rfengler's Circus, Liverpool, came forward, and on behalf of Mr. Savage, of Salford, presented Burns with a silver goblet in commemoration of his feat that afternoon. Burns, said, Mr. Montague, had been acknowledged as the champion of the world for swimming, div- ing, and running, for many years past, and "had beaten time against all competitors"; and his friends Mr. Green, of Liverpool, and Mr. Herriman, of Widnes, would back him against any man in the world for 8200. He intended to take Burns to Ireland and America, and hoped to return from the latter continent with many Yankee dollars_ As a gymnast of 25 years experience, he considered that Burn's performance was a great credit to him, and there were several members of Hengler's Circus troupe present, who were agreed that they had never in the wholeof their existence seen such a drop as the'one performed that day by Burns, whom he hoped would be as successful in the future as in the past.—Burns accepted the present, and cordially shook hands with Mr. Savage. In the course of conversation the announcement was made that Thos. Dawson, of Oldham, would dive from the bridge at three o'clock on Sunday afternoon and afterwards walk from Runcorn to Lou-- don And back in six days. Burns stated that he would be present at the time stated, and would undertake to beat Dawson. It should be stated that a considerable , sum was collected for Burns from amongst the specta- tors. •

it is reported that the Russian Government has de- manded from the Bulgarian Government the payment of three million roubles, arrears of the sum due to Russia on account of the cost of her occupation of the Principa- lity in 1879. . . . .

-SHOCKING Faratr7v.-7,A shocking affair is reported from Fleecethorpe Farm, near Worksop. Two men„ named respectively Ringrose and Minnit, went to sleep, near a fire which they had Related in a sheep-bouse, Shortly afterwards the farm bailiff found Itngrose dead from suffocation, and plinn4 not only unconscious bt with one leg very badly burnt.

div.head: LATE EARL SYDNEN.
div.p: THE LATE EARL SYDNEN.

The funeral of the late Earl Sydney took' place, on Thursday, at Chislehurst Amongst those who sent wreaths and crosses to be placed on the coffin were the Queen, the Prince of Wales, the ea.-Empress Eugenie, and the Duchess of Albany. THE LLANERCH DISASTER. . - -

It is announced that £12,000 has been raised for the relief of the widows and orphans of the victims in the Llanerch colliery disaster. Effoits are being made to raise £25,000 for the permanent relief of the sufferers. , Work was resumed at the pit on Wednesday. About 200 men and boys went down safely. Lamps were used. '

div.head: THREE POACHERS SENTENCED TO DEATH.
div.p: THREE POACHERS SENTENCED TO DEATH.

At Worcestershire Atsizes the trial of Joseph Boswell, Satntel Boswell," and Alfred Hill, for the murder of Frederick Stephens, a gamekeeper on the Due d'Aumale's estate near Evesham, was resumed on Wednesday. The jury were three hours in deliberating, and' after mid- nightreturned a verdict of guilty, and the prisoners were sentenced to death.

RITUALISM AND THE LAITY.

Sir,—Ritualism is on the increase in the Established Church. It is the favourite of the hour., What is the secret of its strange fascination? I think the reason is to be found in the laity of the Church of England. They and not the clergy are responsible for its rise. They have their Prayer Book, the Articles, and the Bible, and the Church invites them to compare them. If the lay- man thinks his clergyman teaches contrary to these, why, he may surely tell him so. Churchmen, however, seem to have an aversion to troubling themselves with thinking about such things. It is so much easier to tell the parson to do it all, and accept all he says as Gospel. But he is not infallible, and they have responsibility, too, though they may not realise it. Laymen, however, have not the share in governing their Church which they should. This is what makes Convocation little more than a Clerical Debating Society. And when laymen and clergymen do meet in Diocesan Synods and the like, they are hampered by restrictions which no other denomination requires. 'thus, I believe that the cure for Ritualism is an educated laity, a laity who shall know what true religion is and who will have nothing else in its place; and the best way to make lay- men take greater interest in Church matters is to give them, from Convocation downwards, a larger portion of its control. _
I trust you will allow me to lay these few remarks before your readers. FIDES.
"FACTS FOR ROBERT FOULKES.

Sir,—Last week "Robert Foulkes" sent me some "facts." Now, if there is one thing more than another that I am partial too,it is " facts," for they are stubborn things. I have carefully gone through his epistle, and, like " Sam Weller," net being provided 'with an extra- ordinarily strong magnifying glass, I tail to discover them. The only conclusion I have arrived at is, that " Robert "is again troubled by the bishops. This time the principal offender is Bishop Jayne. But why write to the paper about him? Why not sing a hymn to the tune of" My Pretty Jane P" I will help" Robert "to the first verse. How's this P

My Jayne, my Jayne, my Bishop Jayne, Oh, don't do things so sly, For on you and your goings on I've got my watchful eye. For we, the true sound Protestants, Know what you are about, And you, with all your Popish tricks, Will soon be put to r ut. Chorus. My Jayne, &c. I night say I have tried the above classical poetry to a tin whistle and a disused salmon tin,and they both stood it, which proves its solidity. I have a yard or two more in stock, and " Robert " can have it for asking. I might say more, but patience and space alike forbid: but, hark you, frind Robert. a word in your ear: throw to the winds your Protestantism ,with its narrow, cribbed, confined ideas, and become a Christian. The bishops will ceaseto trouble you, and your mind will be at rest. SAMOTHNEDE.

div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL.
THE WORK AT THELWALL.

The work of the Thelwall section of the Ship Canal is being pursued with great vigour. Almaist each week sees the men working increased hours, the promoters being determined to make the best of their opportunities and to finish the work within the prescribed time. The locks, which are the great centre of public attraction, have reached a most interesting stage of their develop- ment. The old river bed of the Mersey is rapidly being filled up with soil. Railway lines have been laid along the river bank, and wagons of earth are constantly being "tipped "into the old course. The damage effected bv the recent floods has been almost completely rectified, and the embankment which was the cause of the cutting being immersed in water has been materially strengthened. At Latchford the German navvy is per- forming wonders, the whole width of the canal having been excavated for some distance past Latchford Station in the direction of Thelwall. The smallersteam navvies are following in its course, beginning a lower "lift."

CONCERT AT MORRIS BROOK. A very enjoyable concert was given, on Tuesday even- ing, at Morris Brook, in connection with the recently established Mechanics Institute. There was a large attendance, and an excellent programme was submitted. Before the concert was commenced, Mr. J. Price declared a new bagatelle board open for play, and he then pre- sided over the first portion of the programme, in the absence of the Mayor of W irrington(Alderman Francomb) who had been announced to take the chair. When one or two songs had been contributed, however. Mr. Francomb arrived, and it was explained that he had lost his way, and had not been able to find his destination earlier. la the course ad a few introductory remarks the Mayor said that the work of cutting the canal had so thoroughly cut up the roads, and diverted old land marks, that it was almost impossible for even a person who knew the neighbourhood not long ago to find his way. He found that the former residence of Major Pickmere had disappeared bodily. The constructi)n of the Ship Canal was, he continued, the greatest undertaking that ever the ingenuity of man had attempted to carry out. The wish was general teat the canal should be successfully made, for it would no doubt be a very great blessing to the people of Lancashire. During the evening songs were given by Miss Jones, Mr. Snell, Mr. Marshall, and Mr. J. H. Price, several encores being demanded, and Professor Weber's entertainment filled the second part of the programme. The vocalists were accompanied by Mr. Jackson, who also played a pianoforte solo. Mr. T. Price. called upon for a speech, mentioned that a Band 'of Hope had been formed amongst the children on that section of the works. A portion of the concert was repeated on Wednesday evening.

STRIKE OF NAVVIES AT BARTON. About 200 nav-vies employed on the Ship Canal Works at Barton have gone out on strike for an advance of id., per hour more pay, their present rate being 40. an hour. The strikers up to the present have refrained from molesting those at work, who considerably outnumber them. The places of the men on strike are being stead- ily filled, and ere long, there will be no vacancies. The authorities have made ample preparations to cope with any disturbance which may arise, an additional staff of police having been requisitioned, and so far the men on strike have maintained peace and order. They consider that for the nature of the work they have to perform they are justly entitled to at least sd. an hour, but they are not sufficiently united to gain the advance.

div.head: STORAGE OF EXPLOSIVES.
div.p: THE STORAGE OF EXPLOSIVES.

Mr. Stevens, a 'surveyor in the employ of the Man- chester Ship Canal Company, applied to Mr. J. H. P. Leresche and Mr. W. W. Cooke, at the Manchester County Police Court, on Tuesday morning, for permission, under the Explosives' Act, to build a store on the part of the canal works opposite Mode Wheel, for the storage of 2001bs. of mixed explosives for use in the excavations. Mr. Superintendent Bent, who is an inspector under the Explosives' Act, said that he had visited the proposed site and found that the company had complied with the regu- lations. A plan of the proposed buildings and its situa- tion having been put in, the bench granted the applica- tion.

div.head: CANAL AND RIVER POLLUTION.
div.p: THE CANAL AND RIVER POLLUTION.

The public inquiry into the application of the Stock- port Corporation for powers to acquire lands and pro- perty compulsorily for the purpose of constructing sewage disposal works near Cheadle, and for effecting street and other improvements within the borough, was continued on Saturday, at the Court Rouse, Stockport, before Mr. Arnold Taylor, commissioner for the Local Government Board.—Mr. Dobson, solicitor, examined by counsel, statud that the Altrincham Local Board had brought pressure to bear upon the Stockport Corporation under the Rivers Pollution (Prevention) Act to compel them to take the sewage of the town out of the River Mersey. Acting under this pressure the Corporation had entered into an agreement with the trustees of the War- rington Grammar School for the purchase of 98 acres of land at Cheadle Heath, the price being £15,700, and the Charity Commissioners had given their assent to this arrangement. '

The hearing of the charges against the Bishop of Lin- coln as resumed on Thursday morning, at Lambeth Palace. Sir W. Phillimore, on behalf of the Bishop, pro- duced a Dutch book giving an account of the coronation of William of Orange, and containing a picture of West- minster Abbey, showing two large candles burning on the altar and a lamp above.

div.head: DOUBLE MURDER IN AMERICA.
div.p: DOUBLE MURDER IN AMERICA.

A horrible murder is reported from Omaha city, near which place the bodies of an old couple have been found hidden in a heap of refuse behind a barn and riddled with bullets. Two men who had sold some cattle be- longing to the deceased have been arrested en suvicion of having committed the crime. •

div.head: LIBERAL CLUB BUILDING COMPANY,
div.p: LIBERAL CLUB BUILDING COMPANY,
LIMITED.

An extraordinary general meeting of the share- holders of this Company is to be held on Friday eveningnext, with the object of considering a pro- position for winding up the Company. It hat been felt for some time that some step of this kind should be taken. as by the death of a number of the original members,shares have passed into the hands of people who have little interest in •the undertaking, and who desire to be relieved of any responsibility in connection with it. Besides this, the Club has not for some time been regarded as sufficiently central for the members, and the need of taking some step with a view to re-organisation has already been considered. The circular calling the meeting says "It is with much regret that your directors feel themselves compelled to issue the accompanying notice. They are, however, decidedly of opinion that the heavy annual expenses connected with the property of the Company are more than our tenants —the Liberal Club and the Liberal Association— can sustain in the shape of rent. Your Directors are ' also of opinion that the situation of the Com- pany's premises is not sufficiently central to enable them .to be of that service and con- sequently to ensure that success which it is the ' desire of all members of the party to secure. Having carefully considered the financial position of the Company your directors believe that the only prudent course for the shareholders to adopt is to pass the resolutions contained in the notice here- with. Your directors will also endeavour to arrange that the convenience of the members of the Liberal Association and of the Liberal Club shall suffer the least possible interference, and everything that can, will be done to facilitate a satisfactory re- arrangement a the varied interests of the Liberal party."

div.head: WARRINGTON WAIER WORKS COMPANY. . HALF YEALLY MEETING.
div.p: WARRINGTON WAIER WORKS COMPANY. . HALF YEALLY MEETING.

The ordinary half-yearly meeting of the share- holders of this Company was held on Wednesday afternoon, at the offices of the company in Cairo-st. In the absence of the chairman, Lord Winmarleigh, Sir. Gilbert Greenall, M.P., the deputy-chairman, presided' There were also present the Rev. A. Kenworthy, Messrs'. J. Geddes, J. C. Parr, P. Stubs, J. Matson, J. Jolley, W. MaAvdsley, R. Davies, T. W. Mellor (Ashton-under-Lyne), T. J. Ridg way, H. Neild, W. Fairhurst, T. B. Foster (Manchester), .7. Hedgcock, J Shaw Green, J. Wright Booth, A., I Smith, K. J. Nicholson (law clerk), and John Rose, I secretary. The directors submitted the following report:— "The revenue account shows a balance,including£l,o43 10s. id. brought from the previous half-year, of £5,132 15s. The preference charges amount to £9OO, leaving a balance of £4,232 15s, out of which the directors recom- mend that there be paid for the half-year a dividend at the rate of seven per cent. oer annum on the £30,000 ordinary seven per cent, share capital, and a further dividend of one-half per cent thereon, so as to make up the dividend upon those shares for the year 1889 to their maximum statutory dividend of seven per cent perannum, a dividend at the rate of seven-and-a-half per cent, per annum on the £15,000 ordinary seven-and-a-half per cent share capital, and a further dividend of one per cent, thereon, so as to make up the dividend upon those shares for the year 1889 to the ir maximum statutory I dividend of seven-and-a-half per cent, per annual ; and a dividend at the rate of nine-and-a-half per cent, per annum on the £30,000 ordinary ten per cent, share capi- tal, which will make the dividend upon those shares for the year 1889 eight per cent. per annum; the dividend paid for the first half-year of 1889 having been at the rate of six-and-a-half per cent. per annum upon all three classes of shares. The balance ta be carried forward is the sum of £1,045 55., as against £l,OOB 3s. 3d. carried forward at the end of 1888. The reserve fund amounts to the sum of £3,743 10s. The directors congratulate the shareholders upon the steady improvement in the Company's income which has taken place of late years. For the last half-year, ended 31st December, 1889, the net income balance of £3,189 4s. lid., a -ailable for divi- dend upon the ordinary share capital after deducting the sum of £1,043 10s. id. brought forward from the pre- vious half-year, was more than sufficient to pay the full maximum statutory dividends of £lO, £7l, and £7 per cent, upon the three classes of ordinary shares. A Bill, entitled • The Warrington Extension, Water and Im- provement Bill, 1890,' containing provisions vitallv affect- ing the Company, has been deposited by the Corporation of the borough of Warrington for promotion in the ensu- ing Session of Parliament. It provides, amongst other matters, for the compulsory sale and transfer to the Corporation of the Company's entire undertaking. The directors will strenmously oppose the Bill on behalf of the C,ompanyouid haft given instructions for the presenta- tion- of a petition against it, and for the taking of all such steps as may be considered necessary, with a view to it rejection by Parliament. The directors who retire by rotation are Lord Winmarleigh, Mr. James Matson, and Mr. Vrilliam Fairhurst, who are eligible and offer themselves for re-election. The auditor who retires by rotation is Mr, J. Stialv Green, who is eligible and offers himself for re-election."

The report was unanimously adopted, and dividends according to the recommendations ef the directors declared. The retiring directors vrerc unanimously re- elected, and Mr. Shaw Green was re-ehicted auditor. On the motion of Mr. R. Davies, seconded by Mr. T. J. Rideway, the remuneration of the ditectors for the year 1890 was fixed at the sum of £3OO. On the proposition of Mr. H. Neild, seconded by the Rev. A. Kenworthy, a vote of thanks was accordid Sir (Whert Greenall for presiding, and on the motion of Mr. J. C. Parr, seconded by Mr. Geddes, a vote of thanks was passed te Lard Winmarleigh, the Chairman of the Company, for his consent to continue in office. The proceedings then terminated.

div.head: MISS TIALLWOOD'S CONCERT.
div.p: MISS TIALLWOOD'S CONCERT.

A grand ballad concert, promoted by Miss Hall- wood, was given in the Warrington Public Hall, on Wednesday evening. The concert, from a musical point of view, was of a very high class, all the artistes who took part holding prominent positions in the musical world. In regard to attendance, however, there was much to be desired. las the audience in some parts of the hall was of decidedly meagre proportions. The poorness of the patronato of so excellent a concert is probably due to the fact that Ash Wednesday is in some respects an unsuitable day for such a gather- ing, and also to the circumstance that there have been numerous attractions of various kinds in the town dur- ing the week. The artistes were Madame Anderson, Miss Hallwood, Mr. Thomas Barlow, Mr. Charles Williams, Mr. Edward Grime, Mr. Richard Holland, Mr. Thomas Shaw, Madame Theresa Burnett, and Mr. W. H. Jude. The programme was an admirably arranged one and it was capitally rendered in every particular. The appre- ciation of !the audience was unmistakeably displayed after every item, and all the performers were warmly recalled, though in most instances they contented themselves with bowing their acknowledg- ments. The proceedings began with a trio, "Turn on, Old Time," composed of Miss Hallwood and Messrs. Barlow and Grime. Mr. Charles Williams followed with the song" In cellar cool," for the excellent singing of which he was re-called. Later in the evening Mr. Williams sang' Thy s,entinelam I " in an equally suc- cessful manner. Miss Bellwood met with a cordial reception on appearing to sing Sullivan's ballad, "The great oak tree, and having given a fine rendition of this piece the 'applause was renewed with greater vigour till Miss Hallwood re-appeared to bow her acknowledgments. Miss Hallwood afterwards sang " Grannie's Spiry," a new song by Hubi Newcombe and V. H. Jude, and this proved to be an exceedingly popular reature of the programme. She was accom- panied by the composer, Mr. Jude. The violin solos of Mr. Shave, who has been not inaptly described as the "the Liverpool Paganini" were greatly admired and Mr. Shaw complied with an enthusiastic encore. Madame Marie Andel son has a charming style and a singularly clear enunciation, and these qualities combined with a voice of great power quite won the approval of the audience, and Miss Anderson was encored after singing the "Three Wishes." On her appearance dur- ingthe second part of the concert, her song being "Pack clouds, away," she met with the same marks of appre- ciation. Mr. W. H. Jude's fantasias, in which he dis- played his wonderful skill as a musician, met with a storm of applause' and the audience would be satisfied with nothing less than a repetition of the performance. Mr. Edward Grime, in both his songs. "Fetters of Gold" and "The Wonders of the Deep," upheld his high repu- tation, and the buffo songs of Mr. Richard Holland were also fully appreciated. "The death of Nelson," and "The Maid of the Mill," were successfully sung by Mr. Barlogo, who possesses a fine tenor voice. There was also a performance on the piano and violin by Madame Burnett and Mr. Shaw, which was deservedly admired. The accompaniments, it need hardly be said, were very skilfully played by Madame Burnett.

div.p: 0 RPHE US ORCHESTRAL SOCIETY.

The first concert of this new and promising musical organisation, was held, in the Public Hall, on Thursday evening, when there was a fair atten- dance, especially in the front seats. The balance in. the proceeds is to be devoted to the' funds of the Warrington Infirmary. The members cf the orches- tra are as follows :—First violins: Mr. J. Roberts (leader), Mr. A. Barrett, Mr. Jones, Miss 31. Nunner-- ley, Miss J. Nunnerley, Miss Rummer, Miss A. Garnett; second violins: Mr. W. E. Atkin, Mr. J. Hulme, Mr. Dix, Miss Smith, Miss Perry, Mr. Hall; 'violas: Mr. E. W. Reynolds, Mr. W. R. Earp ; 'cellos: Mr. C. It. Crossley, Mr. W. Sever, Mr. H. N. Hough- ton; double basses: Mr. Grounds, Mr. Butterworth; flute :Mr. Podmore; oboes: Mr. F. Whittle, Mr. J. P. As it hap- pened four of the first violinists were unable to be present at the concert, and it was found necessary to engage two professional players whose services were undoubtedly of value in giving steadiness to the maiden efforts of the local orchestra. The vocalists engaged for the occasion were Miss Nellie Mein and Mr. Miller. The latter sang the songs allotted to him in fairly good style, which calls, how- ever, for no special comment. Miss Mein possesses a voice-of great strength and purity, which she uses with great advantage. The two charming songs "Absence,' and "The Evening Sky," composed by the conductor, Mr. F. H. Crossley, were sung by her in an exceedingly effective manner, and she was cordially encored. She was also re-called after singing "Last Night," a splen- did song, which was capitally rendered. The orchestra acquitted themselves, on the whole, exceedingly well. They showed themselves, as might have been expected, somewhat timid at the commencement, but, having overcome this feeling, they played with precision and effect, and at times with brilliancy even. The orchestral variations on an original air, composed by Mr. Crossley, were, for instance, very well presented, and the same may be said of Haydn's symphony in G major, Arditi's gavotte, and Mendelssohn's march. Mr. F. VV. Reynolds acquitted himself admirably at the pianoforte. He has a delicate and yet a powerful touch, and his exe- cution was throughout much applauded. The encores caused the entertainment to last till something after ten o'clock, and for a iirst performance of the society, it must be said that the concert was most successful.

div.head: AN EXTRAORDINARY BLUNDER.
div.p: AN EXTRAORDINARY BLUNDER.
ENTERING THE WRONG HOUSE.

An extraordinary blunder, arising iii;;;gri intoxi- cation,was narrated at the St. Helens Town Hall, on Monday. Before Alderman J. Harrison and Mr. A. Sinclair, John Roberts, a young man, residing at 8 Napier-et., was charged with breaking into the dwelling-house of Samuel Lawson, at 22 Wilson-st. Mr. J. 0. Swift appeared for the prisoner. The evidence showed that on Saturday afternoon the Lawsons journeyed to Liverpool and stayed until Sunday night. About midnight on Saturday, however, a next door neighbour named Bolton heard some one in Lawson's house. It seemed as if some one was tumbling the furniture about, and shortly afterwards there was a smash of glass. An ex-policeman named Hughes was informed and he entered the back yard. The place was in darkness but on calling " Hello " the prisoner came to the window of one of the back bedrooms and shouted •6 Hello "in response. At Hughes' request the prisoner came downstairs, unfastened the back-door and let Hughes in. It was then found that the furniture and other articles had been disarranged in the kitchen and rooms upstairs; that the prisoner had taken off his boots, coat and hat, which he had left downstairs, while he had also taken off his waistcoat and scarf which were in the back room. He was only wearing his shirt and trousers, and the prisoner told the parties that he had made a mistake.—Mr. Swift, on behalf of the prisoner, contended, and it was admitted by the prosecution, that the prisoner lived in the next street to Wilson-st., that his home was in a row of houses exactly similiar to that of Lawson's,and that like Lawson's the house was two doors from the end of the row. It was contended that the prisoner, whilst slightly under the influence of drink, mistook Wilson-st., for Napier-st., that he then proceeded to the house which he thought was his own home, and finding that no one responded to his knocks at the door he pushed against the front door and it flew open. He then entered, and made preparations for going to bed without obtaining a light.—Mr. Swift said his client had a vague idea at the time there was something wrong, but he could not account for it until the next door neighbour and the ex-policeman appeared on the scene.—The Bench remarked that there appeared to be some suspicious circumstances in the case, hut there was not sufficient evidence to convict and he would be discharged.

div.head: WEST HAM MYSTERY.
div.p: THE WEST HAM MYSTERY.

Although several of the most experienced police - officers- are engaged on the West Ham murder case noth- ing of importance to throw light on the affair has been. ascertained. The authorities have received from all parts of the country many commueications offering sug- gestions for elucidation of the mystery, but none of these- have been of any assistance. The deceased girl Amelia Jeffs and her parents are natives of Neath, South Wales, and some of their relatives from that part of the country on Tuesday visited the mortuary and saw the body. No one has yet been found who saw a girl in company with any suspicious man on the night of deceased's disappear- ance. As an illustration of the intense indignation in the locality, it may be mentioned that at a public-house nearly opposite the scene of the murder a sum of nearly £9O was collected within 24-hours after the inquest for a reward fund. The Mayor of West Ham, Mr. Frederic Smith, -LP., on Tuesday night issued bills offering a reward of £lOO for information leading to the conviction of the murderer.

A London correspondent writes :—The murder of a girl under atrocious circumstances at West Ham directs the attention of the public to the reputation the locality bears as a resort of desperate characters. A well-known Police official tells me that it is within the knowledge of the Scotland Yard authorities that somewhere in the neighbourhood is located a band of men who make it a business to kidnap children in all parts of London. Near- ly every disappearance is placed to their credit, and it was owing to the fact that the police firmly believed the murdered girl Jeffs had fallen into their clutches, that there was so much delay in searching the vicittity. The gang, which cannot be traced, invariably selects young girls, and they are shipped to the Continent with evil intention. On an average every week at least one dis- appearance is brought to the attentibn of the police. Occasionally a truant is found, but in by far the major- ity of instances no tidings are gathered of the missing one, and the public never know of the case save by a . brief reference to it in a police court record. FUNERAL OF AMELIA JEFFS. _

The funeral of the girl Aineli;:-.T7fis:Tvijo'W. as so foully murdered, took place on Thursday, and both at West Ham Church, where the first part of the service was conducted, and at the cemetery. there were large crowds. Many beaut ful wreaths were sent to be placed upon the coffin.

div.head: _IMPORTANT DISCOVERY.
div.p: _IMPORTANT DISCOVERY.

The police, it is stated, are in the possession of clues which are regarded as of a very promising character. They ascertained that the deceased girl had niade ac- quaintances not known to her parents, and it is con- sidered as decisive that the criminal was not only welt acquainted with her, but was a resident in theneighbour- hood, and that he obtained entrance to the house by a key which fitted the front door.
