At the request of the General Purposes Committee the following report with regard to the financial) aspects of the Waterworks question has been pre- pared by Mr. J. L. Tunstall to be submitted to the Committee and Town Council:—

" Gentlernen,—ln accordance with your instructions I beg to report upon the statement with reference to the proposed purchase of the undertaking of the Warrington Water Works Company, submitted to me, as follows : assume for all the purposes of this report that the pub- lished accounts of the Water Works Company are cor- mt. My calculations are based entirely upon the revenue of the undertaking as exhibited in those acconnts, and I have not in any way considered the state of the Com- pany's works or any circumstances that may arise neces- sitating the expenditure of additional capital. The costs of promoting the Bill now before Parliament have also been disregarded, inasmuch as I presume they, will in any case become a charge upon the borough rate, and; as mentioned in your statement; the purchase of the Water Works is only one of many matters dealt with in that Bill.

The following are, as I am given to understand, the proposed terms of purchase :—"The Corporation to pur- chase the undertaking of the Company for a sum equi- valent to 30 years' purchase of the maximum annual dividends which the Company is authorized to pay upon the present paid up capital, taking over all the assets of the Company except a sum in cash representing the re- venue undivided at the vesting period, and assuming all, the liabilities of the Company then existing. Your statement as to the Company's capital is correct, aid for convenience of reference Ire-produce it. The rateable value of the Borough on the 25th March, 1889, was £148,505, and each penny of Borough rate levied during the year ended at that date iealized £560, or thereabouts. The present rateable value of the Borough is £151,137, and the proportionate yield of each penny of rate will be £570. If the Borough be extended as proposed, there will be an addition to the rateable value of £13,280, raising it to £184,397, and each penny in the 2, if the yield be proportionate, will realize £620. The area to be annexed will, in all probability, yield more than its proportion, inasmuch as it does not contain so large a proportion as the present Borough of property in reSpect of which discount will be allowed on rates. Assuming then that the net profit from the undertaking of the Company and the rateable values of the respective areas remain stationary at the figures named above, the charge upon the rates during each of the first three years of possession by the Corporation will be as shewn in the following statement : Payment • Be- Amount Amount to Sinking Net ficieney in the in the E Fund. dr: ' First Year... 13472 8595 4877 8.556 7.866 Second Year 13323 3595 4728 8.295 7.626 Third Year... 13175 8595 4580 8'035 7 387 I have disregarded, in these calculations, any loss of interest that may arise by reason of small sums remain- ing in the Sinking Fund from time to time earning nominal interest only; but if the instalments named above were paid into the Sinking Fund half-yearly in- stead of yearly the charge upoa the rates would be some- what less, even after ample provision for such loss. There is, however, no necessity whatever to incur so heavy a charge upon the rates. The matter may be ar- ranged so as to considerably lighten the burden of -the pre- sent ratepayers by establishing a Sinking Fund on the principle of redemption by equal yearly, or preferably half-yearly instalments of principal and interest, and in my opinion' looking to the character of the undertaking, this would be the more equitable course to pursue. Now, in order to ascertain the amount of the required instalment, it will be necessary to consider at what rate of interest the accumulation of the Sinking Fund can be in- vested, and as I understand the Waterworks Company may possibly make it a condition that the dividends on their preference stock, amounting to £l,BOO shall be paid for by annuities, irredeemable for 60 years, except at the annuitants option, some part of the fund to be applied to the purpose of such redemption will necessarily have to be invested in other securities. The capital value of these annuities is £54,000. They will cost 3 per cent. per annum upon this sum, and it will probably be safe to assume that 3 per cent, can be realized on the invest- ment of the Sinking Fund. For the remainder of the capitalized dividends, amounting to £186,750 I under- stand the Company -would probably accept payment either in cash, or by way of annuities redeemalie at the option of the Corporation at any time. If a loAl of this amount could immediately be obtained at 3± per cent. , per annum it would of course be more advantageous to borrow the money and pay the Company in cash, and the necesssary Sinking Fund would in this event be smaller. For the sake of safety, however,l take more unfavourable terms as a basis for my calculations and assume that

annuities aregranted redemmbe at any time at tin option of the Corporation. These annuities would con the Corporation 3f per cent, per annum, and on the parts of the fund applied from time to time to their redemptius, which might be effected by half-yearly dra.lvings, 31 per cent. per annum would be saved, which for the purpose of Interest calculations would be equivalent to investing the money at that rate. To provide, however for the ex- penses connected with the loan of such sums as may be so raised, and ta provide also for the lo3s of interest do an sums temportrily uninvested ,•1* I arming a small raW of interest, I think It well to assume the'rate to be earned as 3 per cent per annumenlv. There remains a sum Si £33,250 to pay off the Company's leans and to provide for minor matters already referred to. This I assume would be borrowed at 3f per cent, per attnum, and the parts of the fund applied to the redemption of this loan would practically earn 3 per cent, per annum. The basis on which the payments to the Sinking Fund must be calculated would then be as follows The Corporation raise a sum of £274,000, of which £54,000 cost 31 per cent, per annum, the Sink- ing Fund Investments realizing 3 per cent, per annum. £186,750 cost 3f per cent, per annum, the Sinking Fund Investments realizing 3f per cent. per annum. £33,250 cost 3f per cent, per annum, the Sink- ing Fund Investments realizing 31 per cent per annum. The annual sum to be provided under these conditions for the establishment of a Sinking Fund te pay the annual charges upon and to redeem the capital sum of ; £274.000 by equal half-yearly instalments of principal I and interest, extending over 60 sears, would amount to I £10,639 10e. Assuming again the net annti d revenue of the undertaking to remain stationary at £3,595, the annual .deficiency, chargeable upon the 'yes would amount to £2,044 10s., a sum equivalent to 3.587 d. in the £ on the present area of thefforough, or 3.298 d. in the £on the proposed extended area. The charge saved to the rates during the first year by this system of Sink- ing Fund, as compared with that first named, would thus be 4169 d. in the £ calculated upon the present rateable value, or 4.568 d. in the' 4 upon the, rateable value of the proposed extended area. /t may be well to reiterate that in those calculations I have taken existing facts as my basis,and entirely ignored any and every ele- ment of prospective increment. It is' the fact, as men- tioned in your statement, that the increase in the net income during the year 1889 over the year 1888 was £698 and the increase during each of the last three years has been as follows:

Firstyear -.10639 10 9316 1323 10 2.322. 2'135 Second year 10339 10 9526 1113 10 1'954 1196 Third year... 10039 10 10224 415 10 '670 Taking the still more favourable view which you sug- gest, viz. :—That the increase' in the revenue during the first three years would amount to £2,000; and that the Sinking Fund might be suspended for that period,.there would be absolutely no charge upon the rates. An arrangement which would be even more advantageous to the Corporation •'without prejudice to the interest of the Company would be to grant terminable annuities for 60 years in respect of the £240,750 purchase money of the dividends. In this case there would be a simple annual payment of a part of the said sutn 0f110,6391.0§. for 60 years direct to the Shareholders of the Company instead of into a Sinking Fund. All account-keeping in .[ respect of this part of the proposed Sinking Fund would be saved and there would be no loss on investments at lower rates than the cost to the Corporation. I may perhaps with propriety remind you at this point, that no , stamp duty is payable in respect of annuity certificates, , whilst upon mortgages there would be a stamp duty of Zs. 6d. per cent. On the • whole, I arrive at the conclu- sion that the greatest possible risk the purchase would, with a proper arrangement of the Sinking Fund, entail, leaving out of sight all elements of prospective incre- ments, either by an increase of income or of rateable value, or otherwise, would be a charge upon the rates of about 3d. in the whilst in all probability a much more satistactory result would ensue.—l have the honour to / be, gentlemen, your obedient servant, J. div.head: TOWN'S MEETING LAST NIGHT.
div.p: TOWN'S MEETING LAST NIGHT.
THE PROPOSED PURCHASE OF THE WATER- WORKS. LIVELY PROCEEDINGS: THE• MEETING ADJOURNED.

Ltst night a meetinzsf owners of property and ratepayers in ilie-BOFOugli, Was held in the 'Public Hall, Warrington; the meeting,having been convened by the Mayor for the purpose of considering resolu. tions passed by the Town Council, and to authorise the Council to rake such steps as they shall deem ' necessary for promoting a bill in the ensuing session of Parliament._ to extend the boundaries of the Borough, to provide for the purchase of the water- works, and " to make better provision for the health, local government and improvement of the Borough, and for other ,purposes." The Mayor (Alderman Francomb) presided, and amongst those on the platform were Aldermen Burgess, Harrison, Slitton ; Councillors W. Pierpoint, R. Greenall, J. Shaw Green, F: Monks, T. Flood, H. Roberts, Muir, Fleming, R. T. Fairclough, J. Fairclough, J. Taylor, Messrs. Davies, J. L. Tunstall, J: Walker, T. Tunstall, C. J. ,Liolmes, W. Diggle, F. W. Monks. J. Peers, the Rev. F; Lake Good • Brook (town ' clerk), Whittle (deputy town clerk), Longdin (borough surveyor). There was a fairly large gathering in the the body. of the hall. As usual at meetings of this description Mr. Diggle was very much in evidence, and just before the meetirg, he caused considerable amusement by appearing on , •the platform with a retinue of two lads carrying a great variety of bottles in handkerchiefs and a basket, ' Afterwards Mr. Diggle displayed these articles on thei.reporters' table. The Town Clerk having read the nutice convening the meeting,

THE MAYOR MOVES A MOTION. The MAYOR opened the proceedings by reading: the following resolution :—" That this meeting, as re- presenting the owners and ratepayers of the Borough of Warrington as pursuant to the provisions ,of ' the Act of the 35th and 36th Victoria chapter 91, intituled 'An Act to authorise the • application if funds of Municipal Corporations and other govern- ng bodies in certain cases' approve of and consent to the following resolutions of the Council of the said Borough passed at their meeting held in the Town Hall, Warrington, on the 19th day of December, 1889, namely :—" That the Mayor. Aldermen, and Burgesses of the Borough of Warrington acting by the Council (hereinafter called the Corporation) do and they are hereby empowered to apply to Parliament in the session of 1890 for a Bill intituled s' a Bill to extend the bound- aries of the Borough of Warrington to provide for vest- ing the undertaking of the Warrington Waterworks Company in the Mayor, Aldermen, and Burgesses of the Borough of Warrington and to make better provision for the health, local government, and improvement of the Borough and for other purposes. That the costs, charges, and expenses preliminary and incidental to the applying for promoting and passing such Bill into an Act shall he charged upon the Borough Fund and Borough Rate." They were met there as ratepayers of the Borough to take into consideration a Bill which the Corporation had decided to promote in Parliament in order, in pursuance of the Borough Funds Act, to authorise or otherwise the , payment of the expenses of the promotion of the Bill out of the Borough Rate. It was necessary that he should? ' explain to them the propositions contained in the BR. They would all be aware that for several years two Su i -3,- jects had been prominently before the inhabitants of Warsineton. One had bee:: the extension of the Borough boundary and the other the purchase of the Waterworks. With regard to the formerthough from time to time pet off it was now brought forward in consequence of the Boundaries Commission and of the construction of the Manchester Ship Canal. The Boundary Commisstimiers had recommended that the Boundary of the Boneugh should be for administrative purposes the boundary of the ccunty,and it had been thought by the Committee of the Corporation appointed to consider the question and was recommended to them by the Council that so nnich of Grappenhall, Appleton, and Lower Walton as lay between the Manchester Ship Canal And the present boundary of the Borough should be added to the Borough. If left entside they would be absolutely severed from the county of Chester by the Ship Canal and would be difficult to administer for sewerage and other purposes, as part of the area of the Cheshire Authoritv,whereas, on the other hand they would be easily dealt with in the system of drainage which existed in the Borough in Latchford. it was proposed also to bring the whole ' Arpley within the Borough. That suggestion was made so long at'm as when the charter of the Borough was obtained, but at that time it met withebjection from the land owners. In the face of the advent of the Ship Canal there was every prospect of Arpley becoming a busy area' and the Corporation considered that it should be under their control for a municipal and publie health matters.. At the present time it was absolutely severed from the county of Lancaster by the interposition of the Borough, and could neither be watched norotherwise dealt with by the County with that convenience *hich it could be by the Borough. There were no roads repairable by the inhabitants at large in it, and it waa highly desirable that all new roads should be made in accordance with the requirements of the Corporation. The new road which was being made to connect Cheshire with Lancashire would have to be made and perfected before the Borough could be called upon to take it over. With regard to the northern, eastern, and western boundaries, it was proposed to ex-

tend them with the object of bringing in house property that it might be under the local -government of the Borough, and that any additional property erected might be subject to the bye-laws and contrql eti the Borough: The original recommendation of the Commit- tee, and which was in the Bill, was to extend in those directions to a much greater extent than they now pro- posed to ask the House of Commons to sanction. The Corporation were now prepared to undertake to ask the Committee of the House of Commons to grant the exten- sion of the boundary en the north and west, sides as limited in the plan number 2, being the second recom- mendation of therCorporation. Now, with regard to the desirability of extending the boundary, although there was considerable land in some parts still unbuilt upon, yet-there was a constant tendency to erect buildinga im- mediately outside the Borough boundary, and it is thoieght by the Corporation to be highly desirable, that the popu- lation should be under the junsdittion of the Borougtv. There had been an exception taken to the extension in Poulton, and it would be amatter for the, Corporation to consider as to whether :or not, that extension could be modified, when the Bill was In Committee of the House. He thought that the ample fact that it might bring works within the Borough, and thereby increase -the payment of rates, ought not without great justification, to be al- lowed to interfere with the proposed scheme,and he might mention that two of the largest works, and certainly the largest rateable value that would be added to the Borough, were owned by gentlemere orby companies con-1 Isiah* of gentlemen who did not raise any objection what- ever on the ground of the extension of the Borough embrao- ing theirlindertakings. He meant WiLderspool Brewery,. and Messrs. -Monks, HAII, and Co. He submitted' that it was so eminently desirable that the extension should take place, now that be hoped as far as thatmatter was concerned the resolution would be carried unanimouily. With regard to the purchase of the Waterer-elks, as they were aware, the Corporation had from timeto time during the last twenty years had this matter inconsideration. So long ago as 1888 it was nearly accomplished. Since pre- paringthe Bill, as deposfited, in which power was takento purchase both by compulsion or by agreement.overtures had been made by the Corporation to the Wiiterworks Company, and the Corporation had undertaken to modify the Bill when in Committee of the House, by striking out the purchase by compulsion. He was, however, in a position to state the terms which had been proposed to the directors of the Waterworks Company, and which there was evet i raison to beliovo they were pr4p4sea 1e recommend for the acceptance of their shareholders. Those terms were based, on the actual revenue, as shown by the Company's balance sheet, and, assuming that Parliament allow sixty year for repay- ment of the purchase money, and that the amount was repaid by equal instalments of principal and interest, and that the revenue of the Waterworks did not lecrease or the ratable value of the Borough did not inerease, the total charge on the Borough rate would be 30. in the 20 On the other hand, assuming that the same gradual increase in the revenue of the Waterworks continued that had existed during the last three years, and that the rateable value of the Borough would be increased by the extension of the boundary and by the steady existing, increase in the rateable value, the charge on the Borough rate in the first year would be 2d., In the second year about lid and the third year id. in the 2, and might subsequently be expected to disappear . altogether. Application would be made to the Committee of the House of Commons for a three years' suspension of the I Sinking- Fund, and if that was granted there wthild be no charge on the rate whatever. The possession by the local authority of the •• Waterworks • had been so thoroughly admitted to be desirable all through the country that it was scarcely worth while pointing out the desirabilities of their acquiring it. He might say, however, that apart from .being an improv- ing financial undertaking, it would give them power at no additional cost to have a supply of water for thoroughly-flushing sewers, And watering the streets, and put them in a position to have a supply of water for manufacturing purposes in a manner which was suggested by an Engineefat the time when they appeared in the Ship Canal Committee in the House .of Commons. i It would further put them in a position, if t became desirabler of taking a supply of two million gallons aday of the excellent water which the Liverpool Corporation were getting from the Vyrnwy Waterorks. Tha water would cost sd. per 1000 gallons, which supply even if supplied for domestic purposes would leave a profit to the Corporation if they charged thetiame price charged by the Water Works' Company. The. enorineu saving to the public in the use of an excellent soft water I was something that was unrealised unless once experi- enced and tried even in matter of soap and, tea. With regard to the application for an increase of the Museum, and Library rate, it was suggested by the Committze of the Museum and Library that they should have power to charge up to 2d. in the 2. There was of course no reason why they should levy that rate unless it was necessary for the purposes of the Library and Museern, but 1-e must point out that there were very few towns where there existed a Library, Museum, and Art Gallery of the value that the ratepayers of Warringtonhad in theirs and that whatever additional money was expleided by the ratepayers in maintaining the perfection of those institutions they themselves would get the whole benefit of it, and the increased rate would enable the Library Ccimmitteeto issue the books free of charge. They how- ever, considered the bill of such importance that they would not fora moment think of allowing it to be wreckcd by any opposition to the maximum 21. rate. If the ge- neral sense of the meeting tha, a maximum of lid. would be sufficient, the Corporation would be ready to alter the bill in that respect in the House of Commons. He also wished to point out that the greater part of the expenses in connection with the carrying of the Bill through Parliament,. assuming that it would only be opposed for the purpose of inserting clauses (those expensesamounted to probably £1,000), and seeing that it was the most opportune time for the extension of the Borough boun. dary and for the acquisition of the Waterworks, it would' he 'nothing less than r,a catastrophe if '' the 'BSI *ere not , now :prokeeded with.

Alderman Buttouss seconded the proposition and said he thought it undesirable that anything should be said to place the Bill in jeopardy, and he should try to avoid anything of that kind. Whilc the responsibility of the matter was great, there was nothing depressing about it,..and he had so much confidence in the work that this g Bill was calculated to do, and the effect it would have for the benefit of Warrington, that he prcv heeded with the duty he had undertaken with a feelidg that if they succeeded, they would have contributed a very great-deal to thefuture prosperity of the town. (Applause,)- Ls to the proposed extension of the borough boundary, he might announce that they had no need te fear any opposition from the County Council, in applying for this BM. The borough as it now existed hadanacreage of I,442iheres, and a population of 50,000, and the land now unbnilt upon would accommodate a further popu- lation o", 000, so that they had not much land left available within the borough. The population of the town grave an average of 35 per acre, which was .too dense for proper conditions of health that should per- tain to-a town like Warrington. If the borough wae extended* the population would be equal to .an ahLerage 0118 'per acre. The acreage proposed to be added to the borough was I,sl9af_gres,sothat it would about doubly the acreage of the borough. The number of houses in the area they proposed to take in were 810 and the popula- tion 41;8eff. The rateable value was £13,044 105.., And ' id the resent municipal rates were equal to a rate of 4s. .. in the £ a year. This rate would produce £2.636 2s. .' on the proposed area and it was fair to consider what charge this area would bring upon the borough. In the first: place they would require two miles of main road' to keep in repair, £240 a year ; there would bag 3)T; miles of subsidiary roads, which would require, I.te, a year to. , keep in proper repair; .and ; scaverict-• ing would cost £ll5 a year. Therefore they had £2,636 derivable from a rate , such as was levied in the borough at the present time, : and they had £2.005 of, liability incurred formiainten- ance of roads, lighting, &c.,, leaving £631-to the•eredit of the rates, or, in other words, instead of any losaaeCTU- ing to the inhabitants of theeborough by the extension of its boundaries, there would be a profit of.£B3tas„ Bcl. Dealing with the sanitary aspect of the question, Alderman Faargess said they had around them, under the control of the Rural Sanitary Authority, A tolerably large area.. Alderman HARRISON, in the course of his remarks, said a inorb important bill than that which they were about to.consider that night was never before he ventured to say, submitted to the arbitrament oft the. ratepayers of Warrington, inasmuch as one item alone involved an ex- penditure of more than a quarter of a million of money. It might fairly be asked of those who had taken an active part in trying to promote the purchase of the Water Works, why they had done an, andi he admitted they were in duty bound to give some good and satisfac- tory reason, but he might say that the necessity for the purchase had been a plant of slow growth', and had forced itself upon them, in a most unwelcome manner. For instance, their Public Baths were practii• cally of no real use to them, for want of water. It was quite true, they could have water supplied for that purpose,but it would involve a large annual expenditure to have an adequate supply. Then again they had not 'tally sufficient to enabte them to flush the sewers, and to water the streets, and the supply for other sanitary purposes was miserably inadequate. Then again, they were practically unprotected from the ravages of fire in nearly all the principal streets and thoroughfares of the town. The Water Company were only bouud to put down mains oX sucb cluzeti.stootia wouicl be sufficient

for domestic purposes, and as a rule a 3 inch main was sufficient for that purpose but absurdly inadecpate for extinguishing fires, and in respect to that queSion a very grave responsibility devolved upon the TOWU Council.. The Water Company was &imply a commercial , undertaking, and in that light alone it must be viewed and treated,,and as such could claim rights and pri- vileges that hardly seemed compatibiewith the freedom with which governing bodies liked to act. Therefore, the necessity for acquiring the absolute control of the water supply, in Ow interests of the inhabitants, seemed indisputable, and it was to be hoped, far the sake of , saving a few pennies in the £ for five years, the epPer- tunity of controlling the water supply Tiould not be, lost, , for the advantages acaruing` to them Would be far reaching in their' beneficial effects. In the High Court of Justice, Chancery Division, Mr. Justice Chitty, in the matter of the Companies Acts 1867 and 1877 and in the matter of THE ST. HELENS ' COPPER COMPANY LIMITED AND REDUCED. , MOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN, that a petition 11 has been presented to her Majesty's High Court of , Justice, for confirming a resolution of the above company for reducing its capital from £lOO,OOO to £50,000. A list of the persons admitted to have been creditors of the company on the list day of January, 1890, May be inspected at the offices of the company at St. Helens, LaUcashire, or at the offices of their solicitor MARESCO PEARCE, ABCHURCH CHAMBERS, ABCHURCH YARD, IN THE CITY OF LONDON, at any time between the hours of 10 a.m. and 5 p.m., on payment of the charge of one shilling. Any person who claims to have been on the last mentioned day and still to be a creditor of the company and who is not entered on the said list, and claims to he so entered must on or before the 10th day of March, 1890, send in his name and address, and the particulars of his claim, and the name and address of his solicitor (if any), to the undersigned at Abchurch Chambers, Abchurch-yard aforesaid, or in default thereof he will be precluded from objecting to the proposed reduction of capital. Dated this 7th day of February, 1890. MARESCO PEARCE, solicitor for the said company, Abchurch Chambers, London, B.C.

IN PARLIAMENT.—SEssiox 1890. 1_ ANCHESTER SHIP CA-I>AL (TIDAL OPEN- -11 INGS. An) BILL, AND WIDNES BRINE SUPPLY BILL, At a MEETING of the Widnes Local Board, held at the Board-room, Town Hall. Widnes. pursuant to the Act 35 and 36 Vic., c. 91, this 4th day of February, 1890, the above- named Bills were considered, and the following Resolutions passed, viz. That this meeting having considered the clauses and pro- visions of a Bill intituled " A Bill to alter certain works authorised by the Manchester Ship Canal Act. 1885, and for ether purposes," it is resolved that the Local Board do oppose the said Bill in Parliament. and take all necessary steps for the due protection of the rights and interests of the district of Widnes. as represented by the Local Board for the said dis- trict ; and that the costs, charges, and expenses incurred and to be incurred in such opposition be paid out of the General 11 District Fund, or out of the rates applicable to the pur- poses. That this meeting having considered the clauses and pro- visions of a Bill intituled "A Bill for incorporating and conferring powers upon the Widnes Brine Supply Company, and for other purposes," it is resolved that the Local Board do oppose the said Bill in Parliament, and take all necessary steps for the due protection of the rights and interests of the said district of Widnes, as represented by the Local Board for the said district, sad that the costs; charges. and expenses incurred and to be incurred, in such opposition, be paid out of the General District Fund, or out of the rates applicable to the purpose. JAS. T. ALLEN, Clerk to the Widnes Local Board. Town hall, Widnes, 10th February, 1890.
